Lesson 1 · Chapter 16

Chromosomes and DNA

How can a cell double its DNA without doubling its chromosome sets?

Required time
75 minutes
Advanced Learning
21 optional minutes

Learning goal

Distinguish packaging, genes, chromosomes, homologous sets and sister copies, and interpret a karyotype within its resolution.

Before you begin

Cells store hereditary information in DNA. A copy and a set are different counting units. An image shows features only at its own scale and in its sampled material.

In the textbook

Chapter 16 · 552–553 #5,7–12; 555 #4

Open at p. 552

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

chromosome
An organized DNA–protein structure. Before copying, it contains one DNA molecule. After copying, it contains two attached copies; when they separate, each is counted as a chromosome.
gene
A region of DNA whose information contributes to a functional RNA molecule or protein.
homologous pair
Two chromosomes with corresponding gene positions, usually one inherited from each parent; they may carry different versions of the same genes.
sister chromatid
One of the two DNA copies of a replicated chromosome, initially joined to its sister at the centromeric region.

Learn · Part 1

DNA packaging

DNA
Deoxyribonucleic acid: a long molecule whose sequence of chemical units carries hereditary information.
chromatin
DNA together with associated proteins that package and regulate genetic material in the nucleus.
chromosome
An organized DNA–protein structure. Before copying, it contains one DNA molecule. After copying, it contains two attached copies; when they separate, each is counted as a chromosome.
gene
A region of DNA whose information contributes to a functional RNA molecule or protein.
locus
A defined chromosome position or DNA region used to locate a gene or marker.
karyotype
An organized display or description of chromosomes used to examine number and large-scale structure.
mitosis
Nuclear division that separates replicated sister chromatids into genetically similar daughter nuclei.
allele
One of two or more DNA-sequence versions at a gene or locus.
protein
A molecule made of a chain or chains of small building blocks called amino acids; its sequence and folded shape help determine its function.
base
One of the information-bearing chemical units in DNA or RNA; ordinary DNA uses A, T, G and C, while RNA usually uses U in place of T.
RNA
Ribonucleic acid: a molecule related to DNA whose chemical units usually use U instead of T; different RNAs carry information, help assemble proteins or carry out other cellular functions.

DNA stores biological information in the order of its chemical units, called bases. A gene is a region of DNA whose instructions can be used to make a product, often RNA or protein. Using those instructions is called gene expression. A locus is a position on a chromosome. Different versions of a gene, called alleles, can occupy corresponding loci. These terms describe related levels of organization, rather than interchangeable objects.

DNA associates with proteins to form chromatin. A chromosome is an organized DNA–protein structure carrying many loci. During much of the cell cycle, chromatin is relatively dispersed, allowing activities such as gene expression and replication. Before chromosome separation, it becomes more condensed and easier to distinguish in suitable images. Condensation changes its organization; it does not create DNA that was absent before division.

A long DNA molecule must be copied and separated accurately. Packaging helps organize this task, while proteins control access and movement. When reading a diagram, distinguish a chromosome from a short gene region marked on it. A visible band or coloured segment may represent a model feature, not the exact size of one gene. Connect each label to its scale before using the diagram to count or explain inheritance.

Worked example

A drawing labels a whole chromosome “one gene” and a short DNA region “one chromosome.” Repair the hierarchy.

  1. Start with DNA wrapped around associated proteins as chromatin.
  2. Identify a chromosome as one organized DNA molecule with its associated proteins at an unreplicated stage.
  3. Place many gene regions along that DNA rather than equating one region with the whole chromosome.

A gene is a region of DNA; a chromosome contains a much longer DNA molecule and many such regions. Packaging changes visibility without creating new genes by itself.

Stop and check

Does condensation during mitosis create additional chromosome sets?

Compare your thinking

No. Condensation changes packaging. Set number must be tracked independently from how compact the chromosomes look.

Advanced LearningDifferent views of the same material7 minutes

Different views of the same material

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced dna packaging. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A sequence diagram emphasizes bases, a chromosome drawing emphasizes organization, and a karyotype emphasizes whole-chromosome comparisons. Each view omits information present in another. Switching views requires keeping the scale and biological unit explicit. A tiny sequence change may be invisible in a karyotype, while an extra chromosome may be obvious. Choose a representation that can actually answer the question being asked.

An unreplicated chromosome contains one long DNA molecule with associated proteins. Replication makes two attached sister copies; the chromosome count changes when they separate, not merely when DNA is copied. Compare corresponding loci on homologues to see why inherited counterparts can have different alleles.

Match the representation to the scale of the claim. A chromosome image can reveal a number difference without resolving an altered base, while a short sequence cannot inventory the whole chromosome complement. The two observations answer complementary questions. Packaging and image resolution do not themselves establish a change in gene number.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Different views of the same material — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Sequence viewResolves base order within a DNA region.
Karyotype viewCompares whole chromosomes but not every small sequence change.

Limitation: Packaging and image resolution do not themselves establish a change in gene number.

Learn · Part 2

Sets and copies

homologous pair
Two chromosomes with corresponding gene positions, usually one inherited from each parent; they may carry different versions of the same genes.
sister chromatid
One of the two DNA copies of a replicated chromosome, initially joined to its sister at the centromeric region.
centromere
A chromosome region involved in joining sister chromatids and attaching the chromosome to the cell-division machinery.
haploid
Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.
diploid
Having two chromosome sets, conventionally written 2n.
polyploid
Having more than two complete sets of chromosomes; this differs from gaining or losing only one chromosome.
DNA replication
Copying DNA so that each resulting double-stranded molecule has one original strand and one newly made strand.
daughter chromosome
A former sister chromatid counted as a separate chromosome after sister separation.
meiosis
A two-division process following one DNA replication that produces haploid cells and generates genetic variation.

Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding gene loci and belong to different inherited sets. In a typical diploid cell, one member of a pair comes from each parent. They can carry different alleles. Sister chromatids, in contrast, are the two copies formed when one chromosome replicates. They remain joined before separation, including at a region called the centromere. Homologues and sisters therefore represent different relationships.

Haploid means one complete chromosome set, diploid means two, and polyploid means more than two complete sets. Replicating DNA increases copies without adding another homologous set. For example, a diploid cell with eight chromosomes has eight chromatids before replication and sixteen chromatids afterward. It still contains eight duplicated chromosomes and two sets while the sisters remain joined.

Chromosome counting depends on the stage and boundary. Once sister chromatids separate, each is counted as a daughter chromosome. A whole dividing cell can temporarily contain twice the chromosome count that will enter each daughter nucleus. State whether you are counting one cell, one pole or one completed product. An extra single chromosome is also different from an extra complete set; the latter changes ploidy.

Worked example

A model cell has 2n = 4. Count sets, chromosomes and DNA molecules before replication and just after replication.

  1. Before replication, identify two sets containing two chromosome types each.
  2. Count four unreplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules.
  3. After replication, keep four chromosomes but count eight sister-chromatid DNA molecules.

Before replication: two sets, four chromosomes, four DNA molecules. After replication: two sets, four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules.

Stop and check

Does an X-shaped replicated chromosome count as two homologous chromosomes?

Compare your thinking

No. It is one replicated chromosome composed of two sister chromatids. Its homologue is a separate chromosome of the corresponding type.

Advanced LearningDrawings need a counting key7 minutes

Drawings need a counting key

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced sets and copies. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

An X shape is a visual convention, not the definition of a chromosome. A chromosome may be unreplicated or replicated, and many stages do not display a clear X shape. Use centromere relationships and the stage label rather than counting strokes. A good diagram also distinguishes homologues by origin or allele labels while keeping sister copies together until their separation is the event being modelled.

Follow each centromere relationship while adding the sister copy. Drawing an X doubles the strokes but does not add a homologous set. Recording DNA molecules separately makes the copying event visible without mislabelling the cell's ploidy.

In the related worked example: Before replication: two sets, four chromosomes, four DNA molecules. After replication: two sets, four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules. An X shape is a drawing convention, not a universal chromosome definition.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Drawings need a counting key — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Before replication, 2n = 4Two sets; four chromosomes; four DNA molecules.
After replication, 2n = 4Two sets; four chromosomes; eight DNA molecules.

Learn · Part 3

Reading karyotypes

autosome
A chromosome other than a sex chromosome in the classification being used.
sex chromosome
A chromosome associated with sex determination or sex-linked inheritance in a specified organism.
sample
A selected subset of observations used to investigate a larger population or process.
evidence
Observations or results used to evaluate a claim, together with their method and limitations.
aneuploidy
A chromosome number with one or more individual chromosomes added or missing rather than a complete set change.
phenotype
An observable or measurable characteristic produced through genotype, gene expression, development, and environment.
autosomal
Located on, or inherited through, an autosome.
individual
One organism or labelled case in the stated population or pedigree.
transmission
Passage of genetic information from a parent through a gamete to offspring.
privacy
Control and appropriate protection of personal information, including genetic information.
consent
An informed and voluntary agreement to a specified use or procedure; one agreement does not authorize every later use.
substitution
Replacement of one nucleotide or chromosome segment with another.
uncertainty
A transparent description of limits in measurement, sampling, models, evidence, or prediction.

A karyotype is an arranged set of chromosome images. To find matching chromosomes, compare their size, centromere position and stained bands. In a typical human body-cell display, most chromosomes form homologous pairs. Autosomes are the chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes. Identify the sex chromosomes separately. Their pairing and pattern of inheritance can differ from those of a matched autosomal pair.

Start by counting the chromosomes. Then look for large changes in their structure. A karyotype can show these features, but it usually cannot show a single changed DNA base or every allele. Three copies of one chromosome support a claim about chromosome number. That image alone cannot show a person's whole phenotype, health needs or future development.

Aneuploidy means an unusual number of particular chromosomes. Polyploidy means an unusual number of whole chromosome sets. Compare an extra chromosome with an extra complete set before choosing a term. Also ask which cells were sampled. Sometimes one organism has cell lineages with different chromosome sets or counts. This is called mosaicism. One sample may not show every lineage. Record what the image shows, then state what further evidence an inference needs.

Worked example

A fictional karyotype contains three copies of one chromosome type and two copies of each remaining autosomal type. What can the image support, and what remains unmeasured?

  1. Use the supplied size and banding key to identify the chromosome types.
  2. Count the copies of each type rather than grouping by colour alone.
  3. Report the observed extra copy without inferring a complete sequence or every future trait.

The image supports an extra copy of the identified chromosome type in the sampled cell. It does not reveal every DNA variant, all tissues in the organism or a complete developmental outcome.

Stop and check

Can a normal-looking karyotype exclude every single-gene sequence change?

Compare your thinking

No. Most small sequence changes are below its resolution. A different method is needed to test those changes.

Advanced LearningA sampled cell is not every cell7 minutes

A sampled cell is not every cell

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced reading karyotypes. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Chromosome observations come from sampled cells and a preparation method. If different cell lineages have different chromosome complements, one sample may not represent every tissue. This possibility does not invalidate a karyotype; it limits the scope of the claim. State the observed pattern and sample context, then distinguish it from a claim about all cells. Resolution and sampling are separate limits that may require different follow-up evidence.

Chromosome testing can bring unexpected findings as well as the result being sought. Consent, privacy, disability perspectives and the wishes of affected people matter when communicating uncertainty. Follow a person’s or community’s preferred language. Chromosomes do not reveal personality, worth or gender identity, and a classroom display is not a clinical interpretation.

Distinguish a resolution problem from a sampling problem. Higher image detail may help identify a chromosome feature, but cannot establish whether an unexamined tissue shares it. State both the preparation and the sampled population when reporting the result. A karyotype does not reveal every variant, tissue or developmental outcome.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

A sampled cell is not every cell — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Observed sampleChromosome pattern in the prepared cells.
Whole organism claimWould require information about other cell lineages and tissues.

Limitation: A karyotype does not reveal every variant, tissue or developmental outcome.

The Cell Cycle

What can a snapshot of cells reveal about a process unfolding over time?

Learning goal

Track interphase DNA changes, explain control points and calculate conditional duration estimates from supplied population counts.

Before you begin

Replication produces sister copies. A proportion is a part divided by a whole. A snapshot count and a direct time measurement are different kinds of evidence.

Learn · Part 1

Interphase

G1
The interphase interval before DNA replication, when a cell grows and carries out normal activity.
S phase
The interphase interval in which DNA is replicated.
G2
The interphase interval after DNA replication and before mitosis, including preparation and checks.
cytokinesis
Physical division of a cell's cytoplasm into daughter cells.

Interphase includes G1, S phase and G2. During G1, a cell carries out its functions and grows under suitable conditions. During S phase, it replicates its DNA. During G2, it continues preparation for division and checks aspects of the replicated material. The names describe stages in a cycle, but cells can differ in how long they spend in each stage or whether they continue toward division.

DNA replication forms sister chromatids. It doubles the DNA amount in a typical cycling cell without changing its ploidy. A diploid cell remains diploid after S phase. Counting the chromosome sets requires identifying homologous representatives, rather than simply measuring DNA quantity. A high DNA measurement may be consistent with replication, but the cell's starting ploidy and stage also matter.

Interphase is active. Cells synthesize molecules, use genetic information and maintain their internal organization. Chromosomes may be difficult to distinguish individually because the chromatin is less condensed. A lack of visible chromosome-shaped objects does not mean that the cell lacks chromosomes. When comparing images or measurements, connect the observation to the process and state what the method cannot directly show.

Worked example

For a model cell with 2n = 6, compare G1, the end of S phase and G2.

  1. In G1, record six chromosomes and six DNA molecules.
  2. During S phase, DNA is copied without separating sister centromeres.
  3. At the end of S phase and in G2, record six duplicated chromosomes and twelve DNA molecules.

The DNA amount doubles through S phase, while chromosome count and ploidy remain unchanged before division.

Stop and check

Is interphase a stage in which the cell performs no activity?

Compare your thinking

No. It includes growth, normal cell functions, DNA replication during S phase and preparation for division. Not every cell is committed to continuing through the whole cycle.

Advanced LearningDNA amount as population evidence7 minutes

DNA amount as population evidence

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced interphase. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A measurement of DNA amount can help distinguish cell-cycle populations, but it is not a complete stage image. Cells with intermediate amounts may be copying DNA, while cells with doubled amounts may occupy several later stages. Combine the measurement with structural evidence and knowledge of the organism's ploidy. A peak in a DNA-amount graph should not automatically be labelled a new chromosome set.

A short pulse of a labelled DNA building block chiefly marks cells making DNA in S phase. A later observation can follow those labelled cells through the cycle. This method measures incorporation into DNA; it differs from simply counting visible mitotic shapes. Cells can also leave the dividing cycle for a non-dividing state while remaining metabolically active.

Interpret a doubled DNA signal only after checking starting ploidy and the population being sampled. Several post-replication stages can share a similar amount. Combining a structural observation with the measurement narrows the stage claim without inventing a new set of homologues. DNA amount alone is not a complete stage identification.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 2

Control and division

checkpoint
A regulatory control point that can delay cell-cycle progression when conditions or molecular events are unsuitable.
cell-cycle regulation
Control of when and whether a cell proceeds through growth, replication and division.
sister separation
Movement of sister chromatids apart, after which each is counted as a daughter chromosome.
segregation
Separation of chromosomes or chromatids during cell division. In Mendelian inheritance, allele segregation describes separation of allele-bearing homologues so each normal gamete receives one allele copy at a locus.

A cell-cycle checkpoint is a control process that can delay the next step in the cycle. It involves molecules that work together, not a separate organelle seen in a cell image. These controls help the cell respond to growth conditions, DNA damage and chromosome attachment. When conditions are suitable, the cell moves on. If a problem is detected, it may pause or begin another response.

Mitosis separates the copied chromosomes into new nuclei. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. These processes must work together so each daughter cell receives the proper chromosomes. Some errors can escape the controls. Damaged DNA may be copied, or chromosomes may separate incorrectly. The change may then pass to daughter cells. Cancer involves changes in the control of cell growth and survival. Several changes often contribute; there is no single cause for every cancer.

Consider treated cells whose chromosomes stay aligned at the middle of the cell. The total cell count hardly changes. One explanation is a delay in mitosis, rather than faster production of new cells. Compare treated and untreated groups over time. Count both new cells and cells that die. The stage pattern helps you ask a question about cell control. It does not identify the exact faulty molecule or provide a clinical diagnosis.

Worked example

A fictional model allows a cell with unrepaired DNA damage to continue into replication and division. Explain one consequence without claiming that every damaged cell becomes a tumour.

  1. Identify the checkpoint function that would normally help delay progression.
  2. Trace copying or segregation of damaged genetic material to daughter cells.
  3. Distinguish an increased possibility of abnormal outcomes from an inevitable final disease.

Failure of control can allow damaging changes to persist or spread through a lineage. The outcome depends on the change, repair, later controls and the tissue context.

Stop and check

Does one checkpoint failure prove that all later control mechanisms are absent?

Compare your thinking

No. Different controls can act at different stages. Evidence about one failed response does not establish the state of every other response.

Advanced LearningCell control, stem cells and chromosome ends6 minutes

Cell control, stem cells and chromosome ends

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced control and division. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Cell-cycle control combines DNA integrity, replication, size, growth signals, contact and chromosome attachment rather than one universal gate. Cyclins help regulate CDKs, enzymes that modify other proteins during transitions. A delay alone does not identify the responsible molecule. Repair or programmed cell death can stop a damaged lineage. Proto-oncogenes normally support growth and survival; some changes make their signals inappropriately active. Tumour-suppressor functions restrain growth or support protection, while repair defects can allow further changes. These interacting roles explain why failure of one modelled control does not guarantee a tumour. Isolate a condition, predict its effect, then test whether the prediction still holds when another relevant condition changes.

Stem cells renew themselves and produce specialized descendants. Pluripotent cells can form the body's main cell types; multipotent cells have a narrower range, such as blood lineages. Adult tissue stem cells are generally multipotent. Induced pluripotent cells are specialized cells reprogrammed in a laboratory, not proof that ordinary adult stem cells were already pluripotent. Totipotency includes embryonic and supporting extraembryonic lineages and, under suitable conditions, a whole organism. The zygote has this capacity, and some very early cleavage cells can retain it. Potential depends on stage, species and the experimental test; neither every early cell nor every stem cell has identical capacity. Research comparisons also need evidence about cell source, consent, feasibility and ethical perspectives.

Telomeres are repeated DNA with protective proteins at chromosome ends. They help distinguish an end from a broken strand and often shorten with repeated ordinary body-cell division. Telomerase adds repeats in some cell types; short or damaged ends can trigger a stable division stop or other responses, not a fixed organism-lifespan countdown. Tumours can contain different cell lineages. Variants that support survival, division, resource access, immune escape or treatment resistance may become more common: somatic evolution. A driver contributes to expansion; a passenger accompanies it without causing that advantage. Timing, frequency and functional comparisons help distinguish these roles.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 3

Measuring cell populations

mitotic index
The proportion of observed cells that are in mitosis at a particular time.
relative duration
The share of total time occupied by one stage, estimated only under appropriate sampling/model assumptions.
metaphase
A division stage in which chromosomes align near the middle of the cell with attachments to the spindle.
photomicrograph
A photograph obtained through a microscope; it records actual observed material rather than a schematic drawing.

The mitotic index is the fraction of counted cells that are in mitosis. Count the mitotic cells and divide by the total number observed using the same sampling rules. If 28 of 100 cells are classified as mitotic, the index is 0.28, or 28%. Include interphase cells in the denominator. Counting only the visibly dividing cells would answer a different question.

Under restricted assumptions, the fraction in a stage can help estimate its relative duration. If an asynchronously dividing population is roughly steady and cells have similar cycles, a stage occupying a larger fraction may take more time. With a 20-hour model cycle, 6% in metaphase corresponds to an estimated 1.2 hours. The calculation is a model-based estimate, not direct timing of a single cell.

Sampling and biology can challenge those assumptions. Cells may enter the cycle at different rates, pause at a checkpoint or die at different stages. Conveniently selecting a dense field of dividing cells can also bias the estimate. Plan representative image selection, state classification rules and record uncertain cases. Compare repeated fields before treating a single count as a characteristic of the whole tissue.

Worked example

The supplied synthetic count has 72 interphase cells out of 100. Under an explicitly simplified steady-population model with a 20-hour cycle, estimate the interphase duration.

  1. Calculate the observed fraction: 72/100 = 0.72.
  2. Multiply by the model cycle length: 0.72 × 20 hours.
  3. State the sampling and steady-population assumptions; these counts were supplied, not obtained from the five authentic example images.

The model estimate is 14.4 hours. It is a conditional estimate from a synthetic population count, not a direct timing measurement of one cell.

Stop and check

Why might the fraction of cells in a stage fail to equal the fraction of one cell's cycle spent there?

Compare your thinking

Sampling bias, changing growth conditions, cell loss and unequal entry into the cycle can break the simple assumption. A snapshot is not the same as following individual cells through time.

Advanced LearningReal images and synthetic tables have different roles6 minutes

Real images and synthetic tables have different roles

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced measuring cell populations. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Authentic micrographs support practice in recognizing visible structures. A synthetic table can provide enough observations for a clear calculation without pretending that those observations came from the displayed images. Keep the two sources labelled. A real duration study would need a sampling design or time-lapse method suited to the biological question. The mathematical operation may be identical while the strength and origin of the evidence differ.

Microscope counts and cultured-cell comparisons can test a mechanism without diagnosing a person. Tissue, inherited and acquired changes, exposures, age, immune conditions and access to care all affect the broader context. Cancer is not evidence of personal failure. Use respectful language and keep classroom findings distinct from clinical interpretation.

For the supplied model, 72/100 multiplied by 20 hours gives 14.4 hours. That arithmetic estimates time from a population fraction under stated assumptions. It does not convert five displayed micrographs into a hundred observed cells or directly time one cell. The 14.4-hour result depends on the simplified steady-population assumption.

Lesson 3 · Chapter 16

Mitosis

How do duplicated chromosomes reach two daughter nuclei?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Sequence chromosome changes, explain counting during anaphase and classify authentic cell images from visible features.

Before you begin

A duplicated chromosome has sister copies. A whole cell and one pole are different counting boundaries. Plant and animal cells form division boundaries differently.

In the textbook

Start with four words

Learn · Part 1

Preparing to separate

prophase
An early division stage when chromosomes condense, the spindle forms, and nuclear organization changes.
spindle
A system of protein fibres that positions and moves chromosomes during cell division.
kinetochore
A protein attachment structure at a chromosome’s centromere that connects it to spindle fibres.
anaphase
The division stage when separated chromosomes or chromatids move toward opposite poles.
limitation
A boundary on what a method, dataset or model can establish.
mutation
A change in DNA sequence that can create a new allele; whether it reaches offspring depends on the cell lineage and reproduction.

During prophase, copied chromosomes condense and become easier to distinguish. Protein fibres form a spindle. A kinetochore is a protein structure at each chromatid's centromere region where spindle fibres can attach. In a typical animal cell, the nuclear envelope changes as the cell moves toward metaphase. This allows the spindle to reach the chromosomes and attach to them.

At metaphase, duplicated chromosomes line up near the middle, or equator, of the cell. The two sister chromatids of each chromosome are still joined. Through their kinetochores, they attach to fibres leading to opposite spindle poles. This prepares the sisters to move apart. In a metaphase drawing, keep the sisters joined. Once they separate, they are daughter chromosomes and the cell has moved into anaphase.

Classify an image using features you can see. Condensed chromosomes may suggest an early stage of mitosis. A clear line of chromosomes at the equator supports metaphase. In a microscope image, the cell may be tilted or its structures may overlap. Name the visible feature and explain any uncertainty. Use the textbook drawing as a guide, then check whether the real image provides the same evidence.

Worked example

A cell image shows condensed chromosomes, and a later image shows chromosomes arranged near the equatorial plane with spindle attachments. Sequence the observations.

  1. Use condensation as evidence consistent with prophase progression.
  2. Use equatorial chromosome alignment and appropriate attachments as evidence of metaphase.
  3. Keep observations about visible structures separate from details too small to resolve in the image.

The condensation stage precedes the aligned metaphase arrangement. Stage identification should be justified from the visible structures, not merely a memorized picture position.

Stop and check

Does seeing dark condensed material alone prove metaphase?

Compare your thinking

No. Condensation occurs before metaphase. Evidence of chromosome arrangement and attachment is needed for a stronger stage assignment.

Advanced LearningStages describe a continuous process6 minutes

Stages describe a continuous process

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced preparing to separate. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Named stages are useful boundaries within a continuous sequence. An image near a transition may show features associated with more than one textbook stage. Explain which feature supports the label and identify uncertainty when the image is unclear. Forcing every image into a category without a reason can hide limitations in focus, orientation or staining. A defensible classification may include a qualified label.

In the typical animal-cell model, centrosomes help organize spindle microtubules, which are protein tubes. Nuclear-envelope breakdown during the prophase-to-metaphase transition is often called prometaphase. Each sister has its own kinetochore at the centromere region. Attachment signals help delay anaphase until suitable connections are established; an aligned chromosome has no intention or goal.

Treat stage names as summaries of observable relationships. A transitional image may show some but not all features expected in a textbook drawing. Recording the decisive feature and the uncertainty makes classification more defensible than relying on the image's position in a sequence. Real stages are continuous; a poorly resolved image may warrant a qualified label.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Stages describe a continuous process — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Condensation evidenceChromosomes become visibly compact.
Alignment evidenceChromosomes occupy the equatorial region with suitable attachments.

Limitation: Real stages are continuous; a poorly resolved image may warrant a qualified label.

Learn · Part 2

Separating copies

telophase
A late division stage when chromosomes reach the poles and new nuclear organization forms.

Anaphase begins when the links holding sisters together are released. Each separated chromatid now counts as a daughter chromosome. Spindle activity moves these chromosomes toward opposite poles. Each side receives a copy of the original chromosome set. Mitosis separates sisters. It does not pair up maternal and paternal homologues and reduce them to one set, as meiosis I does.

State the boundary when counting. A cell entering mitosis with eight duplicated chromosomes has sixteen daughter chromosomes just after the sisters split. Eight move toward each pole. Each new nucleus normally receives eight and remains diploid. The whole-cell count and the count at one pole differ because they describe different groups. Neither count should be used without its boundary.

In telophase, the chromosome groups are apart and nuclei begin to re-form. The chromatin becomes less condensed as cells return toward interphase. Mitosis normally preserves the chromosome complement. This does not prove that every DNA base is unchanged. A copying error could still have occurred. Separate the claim about balanced chromosome sets from a claim about perfect sequence identity.

Worked example

A 2n = 4 model cell reaches mitotic anaphase. Count chromosomes in the still-undivided cell and at each pole.

  1. Before separation, the cell has four duplicated chromosomes.
  2. When sister centromeres separate, each former chromatid is counted as a chromosome.
  3. Count eight chromosomes across the whole cell, with four moving toward each pole.

The whole anaphase cell temporarily contains eight chromosomes by this counting convention; each future daughter nucleus receives four. This is not evidence that each daughter becomes tetraploid.

Stop and check

Why must an anaphase chromosome count name the boundary being counted?

Compare your thinking

The whole cell and one pole contain different totals during separation. Omitting the boundary can make two correct counts appear contradictory.

Advanced LearningConservation through changing labels6 minutes

Conservation through changing labels

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced separating copies. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The amount of DNA does not double at anaphase merely because the chromosome count changes. The count changes when joined sister copies become independent chromosomes. Follow the same labelled DNA molecules through the event to see that distinction. A conservation table can list molecules, chromosome units and destination nuclei separately. This is more reliable than assuming every change in a count means that new material was synthesized.

Release of links between sisters permits separation. Shortening of kinetochore microtubules and changes in spindle geometry contribute to movement toward opposite poles. Follow the same DNA copies through the movement: the count of chromosome units changes, while no extra round of synthesis occurs at that moment.

Track the same DNA molecules as their relationship changes. Once sisters separate, each is counted as a chromosome; the material has not doubled again. A whole-cell count and a per-pole count therefore differ without requiring a new stable ploidy for each daughter. The counting boundary must be stated before comparing totals.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Case or measureBiological interpretation

One future daughter nucleusReceives four chromosomes.

Models and Data Lab: Track sets and copies through division

Learn · Part 3

Finishing cell division

cleavage furrow
The inward pinching of an animal cell membrane during cytokinesis.
cell plate
A plant-cell structure formed during cytokinesis that develops into new membranes and a separating cell wall.

Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm during or after nuclear division. In many animal cells, a ring beneath the cell surface tightens. This forms a groove called a cleavage furrow between the daughter nuclei. As the furrow deepens, the cell splits into two. Its position and timing must fit chromosome separation. The new boundary should not cut through chromosomes that have not yet moved apart.

Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, so they divide in a different way. Small vesicles gather near the centre and help form a cell plate. The plate grows outward until it reaches the existing cell boundary. New separating membranes and a wall form from this structure. Compare the directions: a plant cell builds a barrier from the centre outward; an animal cell pinches inward from the outside.

Keep nuclear division separate from cell separation. In some cases, nuclei divide before the cytoplasm fully splits. Seeing two nuclei therefore does not prove that two separate cells exist. First locate the nuclei or chromosome groups in the image. Then trace the outer cell boundary and look for a furrow or plate. Use both observations to explain how far division has progressed.

Worked example

Compare how a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell divide their cytoplasm after nuclear division.

  1. In the animal model, trace constriction of a cleavage furrow.
  2. In the plant model, trace cell-plate formation and development of the separating boundary.
  3. Keep these cytokinesis mechanisms distinct from chromosome separation during mitosis.

Both mechanisms partition cytoplasm into daughter cells, but they form the separating boundary differently. Mitosis and cytokinesis are related processes with distinct events.

Stop and check

Does completion of nuclear division alone prove that two separate cells already exist?

Compare your thinking

No. Cytoplasmic division may still be incomplete or may differ by cell type. Count nuclei and cell boundaries separately.

Advanced LearningThe boundary constrains the mechanism6 minutes

The boundary constrains the mechanism

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced finishing cell division. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A plant cell's surrounding wall changes how a new division boundary can form. A simple animal-style pinching diagram therefore does not transfer directly to a plant cell. This illustrates how a shared outcome can arise through different structural mechanisms. When comparing divisions, identify the shared function first, then show how each cell's existing structures shape the route to that function.

The animal contractile ring contains actin and myosin, proteins that generate constriction. Plant vesicles instead contribute to the expanding cell plate. After division, cells with comparable chromosome complements may use different genes as they develop; matching sets do not guarantee identical expression or the absence of every mutation.

Begin with the shared function of partitioning cytoplasm, then account for the different surrounding structures. The cell wall constrains how a new boundary forms in the plant model. Similar chromosome complements after division do not require identical gene expression afterward. An animal pinching diagram cannot be transferred unchanged to a walled plant cell.

Observation and simulation

simulation
A model run under specified rules to examine how its outcomes change; simulated results are not automatically real observations.
communication
Presenting a question, method, evidence and explanation clearly enough for another reader to assess them.

A photomicrograph is an image made with a microscope. It records a real specimen under stated conditions. A drawing or simulation is a model that highlights chosen features. Examine the supplied textbook cell images for diffuse nuclear material, condensed chromosomes, alignment or separated groups. State what you can see. Do not treat the model's clear arrows as features visible in the real image.

Start the investigation with a question and a consistent rule for naming stages. Two separated chromosome groups may support anaphase or telophase more strongly than metaphase. Record the feature used for each choice. Mark an unclear case as uncertain. Compare your choice with a supplied alternative. Explain which visible feature resolves the disagreement or which missing feature leaves it open.

Use the separate synthetic counts for calculation: 72 interphase, 12 prophase, 6 metaphase, 4 anaphase and 6 telophase/cytokinesis cells. These are not counts from the five real images. They give a mitotic index of 28%. A 20-hour-cycle model can also give phase-duration estimates, but needs timing and sampling assumptions. Reading supplied images demonstrates reasoning, not physical microscope skill or live teamwork.

  2. Record the observed feature before selecting a stage label.
  3. Compare the label with the guide and revise any assignment whose supporting feature is absent or unclear.

This independent exercise models evidence-based communication but does not certify physical microscopy or actual group-work performance.

Question 2

Compare cytoplasmic division in a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell. Name the boundary-forming structure and direction of its development in each. Both images show two daughter nuclear regions, but only one shows a complete boundary between them. Explain why counting nuclei alone cannot establish the number of separate cells.

Up to 500 characters can be saved in this response. Longer writing stays visible for copying and revision.

Attempt the question to open the feedback.

One complete response

An animal cleavage furrow constricts inward from the surface. A plant cell plate forms near the centre and expands outward, developing a new separating wall and membranes. Both partition cytoplasm. Mitosis separates the nuclear chromosome complements; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm. Two nuclear regions without a completed cell boundary need not be two separate cells.

Contrast inward furrow constriction with outward cell-plate formation, connect both to cytoplasmic partitioning, and distinguish nuclear regions from completed cell boundaries.

Lesson 4 · Chapter 16

Meiosis Part A

Which separation event reduces chromosome sets?

Required time
105 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Trace homolog pairing, exchange and two meiotic divisions, comparing them with mitosis using explicit counts.

Before you begin

Homologues carry corresponding loci; sisters are replicated copies. Ploidy counts homologous sets. DNA replicates before the two-division meiotic sequence.

In the textbook

Chapter 16 · 563 #20–22; 566 #23–25

Open at p. 563

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

Close pairing of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.

Learn · Part 1

Pairing and exchange

synapsis
Close pairing of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.
tetrad
The four-chromatid structure formed when replicated homologous chromosomes pair during meiotic prophase I.
crossing over
Reciprocal DNA exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.
chiasma
The visible physical connection between homologous chromosomes associated with an earlier crossing-over event.
parental
Coming from a parent or original generation. In a linkage cross, parental combinations match allele arrangements present on the original parental chromosomes; distinguish that narrower use from recombinant combinations.
recombinant
An offspring or gamete allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangements.

Meiosis follows DNA replication, so each chromosome has two sisters. During synapsis, homologous chromosomes pair closely. The two joined homologues form a tetrad with four chromatids. Corresponding gene regions line up. This brings the chromosome from one inherited set beside its partner from the other set. The paired homologues may carry different alleles at the same gene locus.

Crossing over exchanges corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids. A chiasma is a visible connection linked to an exchange as the homologues begin to separate along their lengths. Trace the two chromatids that take part. Each can now carry a new mix of parental alleles. The process usually reshuffles existing alleles rather than creating a new allele sequence.

Correct alignment matters. Exchange between mismatched regions can leave some products with extra or missing material. In a model of normal exchange, line up matching positions and follow the segments into the products. Do not show all four chromatids blending together. Name the two taking part and check that each balanced product retains the expected sequence regions.

Worked example

In a 2n = 4 model, one homologous pair carries A and a. Show crossing over between nonsister chromatids without exchanging an entire chromosome set.

  1. Replicate each homologue before pairing.
  2. Pair corresponding homologues and select one chromatid from each for an exchange at matching regions.
  3. Track the exchanged segments while preserving chromosome number and the overall homologous pair.

Crossing over can create new allele combinations along chromatids. It exchanges corresponding DNA regions between nonsister chromatids rather than creating extra sets.

Stop and check

Would exchanging matching segments between identical sister copies usually create the same new allele combinations as exchange between different homologues?

Compare your thinking

No. Sister copies initially carry the same sequence, whereas homologues can carry different alleles. The identity of the participating chromatids matters.

Advanced LearningAn exchange is not a new allele by itself6 minutes

An exchange is not a new allele by itself

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced pairing and exchange. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Recombination can rearrange existing variants into new combinations without creating a new base sequence at a locus through mutation. Keep those two sources of variation separate. A labelled chromosome model can demonstrate the difference by tracking unchanged allele labels across an exchanged segment. Real recombination has molecular details beyond the classroom model, but the distinction between rearranging variants and originating variants remains useful.

Keep the allele labels visible as nonsister chromatids exchange corresponding regions. New combinations can then be recognized without inventing a new allele at every exchange. This distinguishes recombination's contribution from the origin of sequence variants.

In the related worked example: Crossing over can create new allele combinations along chromatids. It exchanges corresponding DNA regions between nonsister chromatids rather than creating extra sets. The segment model omits molecular details and does not imply extra chromosome sets.

Models and Data Lab: Track sets and copies through division

Learn · Part 2

First meiotic division

metaphase I
The meiotic stage when homologous chromosome pairs align before their separation.
independent orientation
The way one homologous pair can align independently of another pair in meiosis I.
anaphase I
The meiotic stage when homologous chromosomes move toward opposite poles while sisters remain associated.
reduction
A decrease in chromosome-set number from diploid to haploid during the first meiotic division.
meiosis II
The meiotic division in which sister chromatids separate without another preceding DNA replication.
haploid product
A cell containing one complete chromosome set after a specified division or life-cycle transition.
gamete
A haploid reproductive cell—sperm or egg lineage cell—that can contribute one chromosome set at fertilization.

At metaphase I, homologous pairs arrange near the cell's equatorial region. The orientation of one pair can be independent of another pair's orientation. This creates different possible combinations of maternal and paternal homologues moving toward a pole. The sisters of each chromosome remain joined, while homologues are arranged for separation into opposite products.

During anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate. This is the reduction step: each product receives one chromosome from each homologous pair and therefore one set. A starting cell with two pairs has four duplicated chromosomes. After the first division, each product has two duplicated chromosomes in one set. Its DNA amount is reduced, but each chromosome still contains sister chromatids.

Reduction describes the number of sets, not whether every chromosome is already unduplicated. The products after meiosis I are haploid even though DNA copies remain joined. When reading an anaphase I diagram, distinguish the whole cell from one pole. The whole cell still contains both sets during movement, while each separating group receives one. Label the boundary before writing a chromosome count.

Worked example

A replicated 2n = 4 cell completes meiosis I. Count chromosomes and sets in one daughter cell and name what separated.

  1. Start with two homologous pairs, each chromosome duplicated.
  2. Separate the homologues of each pair while sister chromatids remain joined.
  3. Count two duplicated chromosomes in each product, representing one complete set.

Each product is haploid, n = 2, with two duplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. Homologues, not sister chromatids, separated in this division.

Stop and check

Why is meiosis I called a reduction division even though its products still contain duplicated chromosomes?

Compare your thinking

It reduces homologous sets from two to one. Remaining sister copies affect DNA amount, not the number of homologous sets.

Advanced LearningRandom orientation changes combinations6 minutes

Random orientation changes combinations

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced first meiotic division. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Different homologous pairs can orient independently at the first division under the simple independent-assortment model. This changes which parental homologues travel together without changing the number each product receives. Draw two possible orientations for the same 2n = 4 starting cell and compare the resulting combinations. Independence applies to the orientation of different pairs; it does not mean all loci on one chromosome behave as unlinked.

Draw the same starting pairs twice with different orientations. Comparing the products shows variation in combinations while preserving the required count per product. The independence concerns different pair orientations, not an assertion that every pair of loci is unlinked.

In the related worked example: Each product is haploid, n = 2, with two duplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. Homologues, not sister chromatids, separated in this division. Independent assortment of chromosome pairs does not erase linkage within a chromosome.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 3

Second meiotic division

Meiosis II separates sister chromatids in the cells formed by meiosis I. There is no second S phase between the divisions, so DNA is not copied again. Each chromosome still has the two sisters made before meiosis I. During meiosis II, the chromosomes line up and the sisters move apart. New nuclear groups form, each with one chromosome set.

Follow a model that starts with 2n = 4. After meiosis I, each product has two duplicated chromosomes. After meiosis II, each final product has two unduplicated chromosomes. There are normally four haploid nuclei from the original diploid cell. The number of separate cells and useful gametes can differ between reproductive systems. Always say what you are counting: nuclei, cells or functional gametes.

Like mitosis, meiosis II separates sisters. The key difference is its starting point: meiosis I has already separated homologous pairs, leaving one chromosome set in each cell. Meiosis II separates copies within that set. It does not halve the number of sets again or make a cell 'half-haploid'. Later, two haploid gametes can join at fertilization and restore the diploid number.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How two divisions produce cells with one chromosome set.

Worked example

Each product of meiosis I in a 2n = 4 model has two duplicated chromosomes. Describe meiosis II and the final per-cell counts.

  1. Begin without another S phase.
  2. Separate sister chromatids in each of the two cells.
  3. Partition the separated chromosomes into four final products, each with one set.

Each final product has n = 2: two unduplicated chromosomes and two DNA molecules. Meiosis II separates copies without another reduction in homologous-set number.

Stop and check

Would inserting a normal full DNA-replication phase between meiosis I and II preserve the intended simple sequence?

Compare your thinking

No. The usual model has one replication before two divisions. Adding another replication changes the material being partitioned.

Advanced LearningA repeated-looking division can serve a different sequence6 minutes

A repeated-looking division can serve a different sequence

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced second meiotic division. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Meiosis II resembles mitosis in separating sister chromatids, but it begins with a haploid complement produced by meiosis I. The earlier division therefore changes the context of the same broad separation event. Compare starting ploidy, replication history and final products before calling two processes equivalent. Looking only at the shape of an anaphase drawing can hide these important differences.

Compare what entered the division before comparing the shapes of its stages. Similar-looking sister separation has a different history after homologues have already separated. In the 2n = 4 model, final meiotic products each retain two chromosomes and two DNA molecules.

In the related worked example: Each final product has n = 2: two unduplicated chromosomes and two DNA molecules. Meiosis II separates copies without another reduction in homologous-set number. There is no additional replication or homologous-set reduction between the two meiotic divisions.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 4

Comparing divisions

genetic variation
Differences in DNA sequences or chromosome content among cells or organisms. Mutation can originate variants, and recombination can create new combinations; environment and development also affect phenotypes without necessarily changing inherited DNA.
asexual reproduction
Reproduction from one parent without gamete fusion, usually producing genetically similar descendants except for mutation.
gametophyte
A multicellular haploid stage that produces gametes by mitosis in a plant life cycle.
spore
In the plant life cycles studied here, a haploid reproductive cell that grows by cell division into the haploid stage without first joining another reproductive cell.

Mitosis normally has one DNA replication and one nuclear division. Sisters separate and two nuclei receive chromosome complements with the original ploidy. Homologues do not undergo the same pairing and reduction as in meiosis I. Depending on the organism, mitosis can support growth, repair or asexual reproduction. Its role depends on the cell and life-cycle stage being studied.

Meiosis normally has one replication and two nuclear divisions. Homologues pair and may exchange segments before separating in meiosis I. Sisters separate in meiosis II. The products have half the starting number of sets. Exchange and independent pair orientation can also change allele combinations. The products therefore differ from the starting cell in more than simply their number.

Compare seven features: replications, divisions, pairing, structures separated, product number, ploidy and genetic similarity. Explain each row instead of using only the words same or different. Also keep sources of variation distinct. Crossing over can rearrange existing alleles. Mutation can change a sequence. Mitosis normally preserves the complement, but does not guarantee that no mutation occurred during copying or later cell activity.

Worked example

Compare mitosis and meiosis for a replicated 2n = 4 starting cell, using products and separation events.

  1. Mitosis separates sister copies in one division and normally produces two diploid daughters.
  2. Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sister copies.
  3. Count four haploid products after the full meiotic sequence, while retaining the simplified successful-division assumptions.

Mitosis normally preserves set number in two products; meiosis reduces it in four products after two divisions. Replication precedes both sequences but occurs only once before the two meiotic divisions.

Stop and check

Is the difference adequately described as “mitosis makes body cells; meiosis makes sperm” for all organisms?

Compare your thinking

No. That shortcut omits oocytes and organisms in which meiosis produces spores. The chromosome behaviour and life-cycle context provide a more general comparison.

Advanced LearningThe cell division and its later role6 minutes

The cell division and its later role

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced comparing divisions. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A division mechanism does not identify the entire reproductive strategy. In plants, haploid spores formed by meiosis can divide by mitosis to form gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis. The same separation rules still apply. Add the organism's life-cycle stage to a comparison table so that the cell's later role does not replace the actual definition of the division process.

Add the organism and stage to the division table. In plants, meiosis can produce spores whose descendants later form gametes through mitosis. The later reproductive role cannot replace the chromosome-based definition of the original division.

In the related worked example: Mitosis normally preserves set number in two products; meiosis reduces it in four products after two divisions. Replication precedes both sequences but occurs only once before the two meiotic divisions. Meiosis does not directly produce gametes in every life cycle.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Lesson 5 · Chapter 16

Meiosis Part B

How can variation and chromosome errors arise from the same division sequence?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Compare gamete development, sources of combinations, error timings and twin origins with bounded developmental claims.

Before you begin

Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sisters. Gamete content, cytoplasmic size and developmental timing are different features. Fertilization combines two contributions.

In the textbook

Chapter 16 · 568 #26; 570–571 #27–30; 572 #1–10

Open at p. 568

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

independent assortment
Independent orientation and separation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing independent allele assortment for unlinked loci.
nondisjunction
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during a cell division.
aneuploidy
A chromosome number with one or more individual chromosomes added or missing rather than a complete set change.
identical twins
Twins arising when one early embryo separates into two; they are also called monozygotic twins and need not share every later trait.

Learn · Part 1

Gamete development

spermatogenesis
Development of sperm through mitosis, meiosis, and cellular differentiation in the testes.
oogenesis
Development of female gametes through mitosis, growth, meiosis, and unequal cytokinesis.
polar body
A small haploid cell produced by unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis that usually does not become an egg.
meiotic pause
An interval during which a meiotic process is arrested at a particular stage.
generation
A group or stage in a parent-to-offspring sequence, defined for the population being studied.

Gametogenesis means the development of gametes. Human sperm and oocyte pathways both use meiosis, but differ in timing and cell size. One primary spermatocyte can produce four haploid spermatids. These cells then change form and mature toward functional sperm. Their tails and other structures support later movement and interaction with the oocyte. Meiosis alone does not provide every mature sperm function.

Oogenesis includes unequal cell division and long pauses. A primary oocyte begins meiosis before birth, then pauses in the first division. Later, a selected cell completes meiosis I. It forms a large secondary oocyte and a small polar body. The ovulated cell usually pauses in metaphase II. Sperm entry triggers completion. Most cytoplasm stays with the larger cell rather than being shared equally.

Both pathways reduce chromosome sets before fertilization. One haploid maternal set and one haploid paternal set then restore diploidy. This prevents a doubling of sets in each generation. Other organisms can have different timing and life cycles. State the organism and stage when explaining a count. Four meiotic nuclei do not mean four equally sized, equally functional gametes in every system.

Worked example

Compare a typical spermatocyte lineage with a typical human oocyte lineage in chromosome reduction and cytoplasmic allocation.

  1. Both lineages use meiosis to reduce homologous sets.
  2. A successful primary spermatocyte lineage produces four spermatids through relatively even divisions.
  3. Oogenesis retains most cytoplasm in one large cell, with polar bodies, and includes characteristic meiotic pauses.

Both pathways reduce sets, but their products differ in size, developmental timing and allocation of cytoplasm. An ovulated secondary oocyte typically remains paused in metaphase II.

Stop and check

Does an unequal division of cytoplasm necessarily imply an unequal number of chromosome sets in the two meiotic products?

Compare your thinking

No. Cytoplasmic volume and chromosome allocation are separate features. A small polar body can receive a haploid set.

Advanced LearningTiming adds another source of difference6 minutes

Timing adds another source of difference

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced gamete development. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A diagram drawn only as a branching tree can hide long pauses and later differentiation. Add time annotations to distinguish the chromosome divisions from the maturation of the resulting cells. The products' size and form relate to their roles, but those comparisons do not establish an individual's reproductive capacity. A useful classroom model explains the mechanism while keeping personal conclusions outside the evidence it supplies.

Human sperm-producing lineages can renew and divide after puberty, whereas oocytes may remain paused for years. The first oocyte pause is in prophase I; the later pause is usually metaphase II. Timing and repeated cell divisions create different contexts for errors. Population age patterns cannot identify one segregation event without chromosome evidence or determine a pregnancy outcome. Unequal oocyte divisions retain most cytoplasm, organelles and stored molecules in one large cell. Sperm-producing divisions yield smaller products that later acquire specialized form. Nuclear sets and cytoplasmic amounts are different contributions. Their unequal sizes do not imply that one gamete carries greater genetic value.

A primary spermatocyte completes meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes. These complete meiosis II to produce spermatids, which differentiate toward sperm. Cell maturation changes shape and function without adding another reduction division. Human sperm-producing lineages normally continue after puberty; the usual oocyte supply was established earlier.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Timing adds another source of difference — comparison

Chromosome reductionBoth typical gamete-producing pathways reduce sets.
Timing and cytoplasmPauses, differentiation and allocation differ between pathways.

Limitation: Population timing patterns cannot determine one person's reproductive outcome.

Learn · Part 2

Sources of variation

independent assortment
Independent orientation and separation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing independent allele assortment for unlinked loci.
random fertilization
The combination of gametes without a fixed pairing pattern in the model, adding new allele combinations.
linked loci
Gene positions on the same chromosome; nearby positions tend to be inherited together because crossing over separates them less often.
sampling uncertainty
Chance difference between a sample result and the underlying probabilities or population because only a finite sample was observed.

Crossing over changes allele combinations along homologous chromosomes. Independent assortment changes which homologues from different pairs enter a gamete together. Random fertilization combines one gamete with another from the possible types. These processes can produce a new mix of existing alleles. They do not need to create a new DNA sequence at every locus to generate varied offspring.

If n chromosome pairs orient independently, they give 2ⁿ combinations of whole homologues before counting crossing over. Three pairs give eight combinations. This is a count of whole parental chromosomes, not every possible allele sequence. Exchange adds combinations within a chromosome. Linked loci can also differ from a simple independent-locus model. State what the count includes and leaves out.

A possible outcome is not a promised outcome. A small sample can omit some gamete types by chance. Mutation provides another source of variation by changing a sequence. Keep these mechanisms separate in an explanation. If a diagram shows swapped parental segments, use crossing over. If it shows a new base, consider mutation. Name the actual change before making a broader claim.

Worked example

Separate three sources of new combinations: crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization.

  1. Crossing over exchanges corresponding regions between homologous nonsister chromatids.
  2. Independent assortment changes combinations of homologues from different pairs in gametes.
  3. Fertilization combines one gamete from each parent, adding another combination step.

These processes reshuffle existing genetic variants at different stages. Mutation is a separate source of new sequence variants and need not occur for every new combination.

Stop and check

Does independent assortment alone require an exchange of DNA segments between homologues?

Compare your thinking

No. It concerns the orientation and separation of different homologous pairs. Segment exchange is crossing over.

Advanced LearningCounting possibilities has assumptions6 minutes

Counting possibilities has assumptions

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced sources of variation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

For n independently orienting chromosome pairs, 2^n describes combinations of parental homologues before adding crossing over. It is not the total number of possible DNA sequences or the number of guaranteed offspring types. The count assumes distinguishable parental homologues and the stated independent orientation model. State those conditions before using a large number as evidence of variation.

Name what each factor of two represents: an alternative orientation for one distinguishable pair. The result counts combinations in that bounded model, not every possible DNA sequence. Adding another source of variation requires its own assumptions rather than reinterpreting the original number.

In the related worked example: These processes reshuffle existing genetic variants at different stages. Mutation is a separate source of new sequence variants and need not occur for every new combination. The count is not a guaranteed set of offspring types.

Learn · Part 3

Nondisjunction

meiosis I error
A segregation error in the first division, such as homologues failing to separate normally.
meiosis II error
A segregation error in the second division, such as sister chromatids failing to separate normally.
nondisjunction
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during a cell division.

Nondisjunction is failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during a division. If one homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I, both members can move into the same product. After meiosis II, two final products contain an extra copy of that chromosome and two lack it. All four are abnormal for the tracked chromosome in this simplified sequence.

If meiosis I is normal but sisters fail to separate in only one meiosis II cell, the pattern differs. One product receives two copies, one receives none, and two products retain the usual single copy. Fertilization involving an abnormal gamete can produce aneuploidy in the zygote: an unusual number of specific chromosomes. This differs from gaining or losing a complete set.

Trace the error and each product before naming a count. For a gamete that should have n chromosomes, the abnormal products may be n+1 or n−1 for the tracked event. Outcomes depend on which chromosome is involved and on later development. A classroom model does not determine one individual's phenotype or prognosis. It provides a mechanism that can be tested against suitable chromosome and cell-lineage evidence.

Worked example

In a simple two-division model, homologues of one pair fail to separate in meiosis I. Compare the four gametes with a case in which sister separation fails in one meiosis-II cell.

  1. For the meiosis-I error, send both homologues to one first-division product and neither to the other.
  2. After normal meiosis II, obtain two n+1 and two n−1 gametes for that chromosome.
  3. For the stated meiosis-II error, obtain two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1.

The distribution differs by timing: all four gametes are affected in the simple meiosis-I case, while two remain normal in the specified meiosis-II case.

Stop and check

Does n+1 mean that a gamete has acquired an entire additional chromosome set?

Compare your thinking

No. It means one extra chromosome relative to the haploid count. An extra complete set is a different change.

A memorized percentage can fail when the starting case changes. Draw the affected pair and follow each product to the end before counting outcomes. State whether the error affects one division, one pair and one cell, and whether later divisions proceed normally. This method makes the assumptions visible and prevents a result from a simple model being applied to every possible segregation error.

Trace the affected pair through both divisions before counting normal and altered products. The familiar proportions follow from one precisely stated error, not from the word nondisjunction alone. Changing the affected pair, cell or later events changes the model.

Learn · Part 4

Twins and early development

fraternal twins
Twins arising from two separate fertilizations; they are also called dizygotic twins.
identical twins
Twins arising when one early embryo separates into two; they are also called monozygotic twins and need not share every later trait.
zygote splitting
A simplified label for separation of one early embryonic lineage into two developing embryos.
environment
The physical, biological and other surrounding conditions relevant to an organism or process.

Dizygotic, or fraternal, twins begin when two oocytes are fertilized separately. Two zygotes form, each with its own mix of parental alleles. Their genetic relationship is much like that of other siblings with the same parents. Sharing a pregnancy does not give them identical genomes. Each zygote follows its own early series of cell divisions.

Monozygotic, or identical, twins begin from one early embryo that gives rise to two embryos. They share a zygote origin and much of their inherited genetic information. Their supporting membranes can be arranged in different ways. They may have separate or shared chorionic structures. Do not define monozygotic twins by saying that they always share one placenta or chorion.

A shared origin does not guarantee identical development. Later mutations, differences in gene expression and different environments can affect the twins. Compare three things separately: their origin, their inherited information and their conditions during development. A picture of two fetuses or one shared membrane cannot settle every question about their genes. Explain which origin model the evidence supports and what is still uncertain.

Worked example

Compare two embryos arising from one fertilized egg that later separates with embryos arising from two separately fertilized eggs.

  1. One zygote followed by separation supports a monozygotic origin.
  2. Two oocytes fertilized separately support a dizygotic origin.
  3. Distinguish the origin of genetic similarity from later differences in development, environment and acquired changes.

Monozygotic twins arise from one zygote and are usually highly genetically similar. Dizygotic twins arise from separate fertilizations and have a genetic relationship comparable to other full siblings in the stated family model.

Stop and check

Does a monozygotic origin guarantee identical traits throughout life?

Compare your thinking

No. Developmental conditions, environments, gene regulation and later changes can differ. Genetic similarity does not make every outcome identical.

The timing of embryonic separation can relate to placental and membrane arrangements, but those arrangements should not be treated as a complete shortcut for determining every twin relationship. Clinical interpretation uses specific observations and context. For the classroom comparison, begin with the number of zygotes and then add qualified developmental information. Avoid making one visible feature stand in for the entire history.

Start the comparison with fertilization history, then add qualified information about subsequent separation and membranes. Similarity in one visible support structure cannot substitute for every earlier event in that history. Genetic similarity also need not mean identical later traits.

In the related worked example: Monozygotic twins arise from one zygote and are usually highly genetically similar. Dizygotic twins arise from separate fertilizations and have a genetic relationship comparable to other full siblings in the stated family model. Membrane arrangements alone are not a complete determination of every twin relationship.

Lesson 6 · Chapter 16

Reproductive Strategies

How do organisms place meiosis and fertilization in different life cycles?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Compare sexual and asexual strategies and annotate moss, pine and selected animal cycles without merging their distinct stages.

Before you begin

Mitosis preserves the current set number; meiosis reduces it and fertilization restores it. Haploid cells can divide by mitosis. Reproductive success depends on context.

In the textbook

Start with four words

asexual reproduction

gametophyte
A multicellular haploid stage that produces gametes by mitosis in a plant life cycle.
sporophyte
A multicellular diploid stage that produces haploid spores through meiosis in a plant life cycle.
