Learn · Part 1

Sexual and asexual reproduction

clone
A cell or organism descended asexually from one source and therefore highly similar genetically, though not necessarily identical in phenotype.
sexual reproduction
Reproduction involving meiosis and fusion of gametes, generating new combinations of genetic information.
Daphnia
A genus of small aquatic crustaceans used here to compare environmentally influenced sexual and asexual reproductive strategies.
sea anemone
An animal used here to compare sexual reproduction with asexual processes such as budding or fission.
polyp
A usually attached body form of some cnidarians; its life-cycle role depends on the species.
medusa
A usually free-swimming body form of some cnidarians; not all cnidarians have this stage.
genotype
The allele combination an organism or cell carries at one or more loci.
nuclear DNA
DNA contained in the nucleus, including the chromosomes used in ordinary nuclear inheritance models.
mitochondrial DNA
DNA contained in mitochondria; its inheritance pattern differs from that of nuclear chromosomes in many organisms.
binary fission
Asexual cell reproduction in which one cell copies its genetic material and divides into two cells.
bacterial conjugation
Transfer of DNA from a donor bacterium to a recipient through direct cell contact; transfer itself does not make an additional cell.
somatic-cell nuclear transfer
A cloning method that transfers a body-cell nucleus into an oocyte whose nucleus has been removed.

Sexual reproduction joins gametes. Asexual reproduction forms new organisms without that fusion. It can involve division, budding or growth from part of a parent, depending on the species. A clone is an organism or lineage produced with close genetic similarity to its source through such a process. Mutations can still arise in a clonal lineage, so close similarity does not mean every base stays unchanged forever.

Asexual reproduction can preserve a successful genotype, meaning an allele combination. It may allow fast growth in numbers without finding a mate. Sexual reproduction can produce varied combinations that matter when conditions change. It also has costs linked to making and combining gametes. Neither mode is always best. Compare speed, resources, variation and the environment in the stated case.

Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission: DNA is copied, the copies separate and one cell divides into two. This is not mitosis, because bacteria lack the eukaryotic nucleus and mitotic spindle. In bacterial conjugation, DNA passes from a donor to a recipient through direct contact. That transfer can change a recipient without increasing cell number. Gene transfer and making another organism are different events.

A species may use different modes under different conditions. Plants and animals have other pathways, so name the organism before describing its cellular steps. A group that looks alike is not necessarily a clone. Evidence must show its origin and genetic relationship, rather than only a similar visible trait.

Watch and make sense of it

Worked example

A fictional plant population can produce runners or seeds after fertilization. Compare inheritance and one ecological tradeoff.

  1. Runners develop through mitotic growth from the parent and usually preserve its genotype apart from new changes.
  2. Sexual reproduction combines gametes and can reshuffle parental variants.
  3. Compare speed, resource investment and variation in the stated environment rather than ranking one strategy as universally superior.

Asexual propagation can rapidly preserve a successful genotype; sexual reproduction can generate new combinations. Their relative effects depend on conditions, and neither guarantees survival.

Stop and check

Does asexual reproduction mean that no genetic change can ever occur?

Compare your thinking

No. Mutations can arise in asexual lineages. Asexual reproduction lacks the same gamete-combination process but is not immune to sequence change.

Advanced LearningVariation and success are different quantities6 minutes

Variation and success are different quantities

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced sexual and asexual reproduction. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A more varied set of offspring is not automatically more successful in every environment. Some combinations may perform poorly, while a stable environment may favour an existing genotype. Changing conditions can alter that comparison. A careful study measures both genetic variation and a defined outcome such as survival or reproduction. It should not use one as an unmeasured substitute for the other.

Sexual reproduction can require finding a mate, specialized structures and time spent producing gametes. Each offspring receives part of each parent’s nuclear genome. Assortment and exchange create combinations, but neither diversity nor speed is an automatic advantage in every environment. Sexual and asexual strategies have different trade-offs rather than forming a ladder of progress.

Measure both quantities rather than using one as a proxy for the other. A genotype preserved by asexual propagation may perform well under stable conditions, while changed conditions alter the comparison. Neither strategy occupies a universal higher rung of biological progress. Greater variation does not guarantee greater success in every environment.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Variation and success are different quantities — comparison

Genetic variationDifference among inherited combinations.
Measured successSurvival or reproduction in a defined environment.

Learn · Part 2

Life-cycle transitions

sporophyte
A multicellular diploid stage that produces haploid spores through meiosis in a plant life cycle.

Many plants alternate between a multicellular diploid sporophyte and a multicellular haploid gametophyte. The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis. A spore can grow without fusing with another cell. Through mitosis, it develops into a gametophyte. This haploid stage then produces haploid gametes by mitosis, because a reduction division is not needed to reduce a set that is already single.

Fertilization combines two gametes to form a diploid zygote. The zygote grows by mitosis into a new sporophyte. The complete sequence therefore links meiosis, mitosis and fertilization at specific transitions. Spores and gametes are both haploid in this model, but their next actions differ: a spore grows, while a gamete participates in fusion.

Do not assume that meiosis directly makes gametes in every life cycle. In the usual human model it does; in the plant cycle described here it makes spores. Also distinguish plant alternation of generations from an animal switching between sexual and asexual reproduction. Alternating reproductive modes does not automatically mean the organism alternates between multicellular haploid and diploid generations.

Worked example

Trace a moss life cycle from a diploid sporophyte through spores, gametophytes and fertilization. Compare the corresponding ploidy transitions in pine.

  1. Meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores.
  2. Spores grow by mitosis into haploid gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis.
  3. Fertilization restores diploidy; pine retains these broad transitions with much reduced gametophytes associated with the dominant sporophyte.

Meiosis changes 2n to n, fertilization changes n to 2n, and intervening mitosis preserves the current set number. Plant spores and gametes are different stages.

Stop and check

Must every haploid cell immediately fuse with another cell rather than divide?

Compare your thinking

No. Haploid stages can divide by mitosis. Moss gametophytes illustrate a multicellular haploid stage.

Advanced LearningVisibility can hide a life-cycle stage6 minutes

Visibility can hide a life-cycle stage

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced life-cycle transitions. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A large tree makes the diploid sporophyte conspicuous, while its gametophytes are much smaller and associated with reproductive structures. Size does not remove those stages from the life cycle. Use ploidy labels and the two transition events to identify them, rather than assuming the largest visible organism represents every stage. This also prevents a familiar animal life-cycle model from being imposed unchanged on plants.

Compare three arrangements. In a diploid-dominant animal cycle, meiosis leads to gametes and fertilization restores two sets. In a haploid-dominant cycle, the zygote undergoes meiosis and most growth occurs with one set. Plant alternation includes multicellular stages of both ploidies. Mark the reduction and fusion arrows; their positions distinguish the cycles.

Locate the two ploidy-changing arrows before interpreting the largest visible stage. Mitosis between them preserves the current set number, even when the stage is small or hidden within another structure. Spores and gametes remain distinct in the plant sequence. Visibility or size does not determine ploidy or erase a life-cycle stage.

Learn · Part 3

Animal strategies

Daphnia are small aquatic crustaceans. Under favourable conditions, females can produce offspring without fertilization. This is called parthenogenesis. Under other conditions, sexual reproduction can produce embryos that persist through harsh periods. The value of each mode depends on the environment. Producing many offspring quickly and surviving a difficult season are two different challenges.

Sea anemones can reproduce sexually using gametes. In some species, they can also split or bud to produce offspring asexually. Their adult body form is a polyp. Many jellyfish have both a polyp stage and a medusa stage. Their cycles can include asexual production of new stages, while the medusa produces gametes for sexual reproduction. Label each organism's cycle carefully. A sea anemone does not have every stage of a jellyfish cycle.

Polyp and medusa describe body shapes. They do not mean haploid and diploid generations. Both forms are typically diploid in the animal cycles compared here. Label the chromosome sets and the kind of division at each arrow. Then compare the plant cycle: its multicellular gametophyte is haploid, while its sporophyte is diploid. Similar cycle drawings can therefore show quite different changes in chromosome sets.

Worked example

Compare a Daphnia model that switches reproductive modes with a jellyfish model containing a polyp stage and a medusa stage. Avoid adding a medusa stage to a sea-anemone cycle.

  1. Identify which Daphnia conditions in the supplied model favour asexual or sexual reproduction.
  2. In the jellyfish example, distinguish mitotic asexual production from gamete formation and fertilization.
  3. Treat the sea-anemone example separately because a medusa stage is not part of its life cycle.

Different animals can combine reproductive strategies in different sequences. Shared vocabulary does not establish that their complete life cycles are identical.

Life-cycle diagrams are often visually similar: arrows connect adults, offspring and reproductive cells. The organism label is therefore part of the scientific content, not a decorative caption. Check which stage is sexual, which stage can reproduce asexually and which conditions trigger transitions in the supplied example. A general comparison should preserve those differences rather than compress several organisms into one universal cycle.

Learn · Part 4

Evidence and applications

cloning
Producing genetically closely related cells or organisms from a source lineage; environmental and later genetic differences can remain.
benefit
A favourable outcome for a specified person, group or system, evaluated using stated criteria.
experimental control
A comparison or controlled condition that helps isolate an interpretation of an experimental result.
control
A comparison condition or regulated variable used to make an investigation interpretable.

Cloning technology can extend an asexual principle through a planned method. In somatic-cell nuclear transfer, a body-cell nucleus is placed in an oocyte whose nucleus has been removed. If development proceeds, much of the nuclear genome comes from the donor. Mitochondria and the growth environment can differ. The result is not a copy of every donor trait or experience. Most mitochondria come from the egg cytoplasm, so most mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg donor rather than the transferred nucleus.

Name the goal before judging a technology. A project might aim to copy a useful genotype, study development or aid conservation. An early embryo is evidence of one step, not proof of a healthy adult. A conservation project also needs suitable habitat, behaviour and varied breeding lines. A method that copies DNA cannot solve every problem that limits a species' recovery.

Consider a fictional choice between fast clonal growth and maintaining varied breeding lines. Explain the benefit, limit and result to measure. An initial preference for speed may change after considering future environmental shifts. Revise the plan using the biological mechanism and the stated goal. This shows how a technology can expand capability while still needing evidence about the wider need it aims to meet.

Worked example

A fictional nursery compares cloned cuttings with seedlings across a stable treatment and a changing treatment. What would make the comparison informative?

  1. Define an outcome such as survival or growth over the same interval.
  2. Replicate groups and control starting size, care and sampling while recording the reproductive origin.
  3. Compare variation and performance separately, then revise a claim that one method must always win.

The study can test outcomes under its stated conditions. It cannot establish a universal ranking without evidence across other genotypes and environments.

Stop and check

Would one successful cutting and one failed seedling establish that asexual reproduction is always more effective?

Compare your thinking

No. The comparison is too small and confounds reproductive method with individual differences and conditions.

Advanced LearningReplication, nuclear transfer and the limits of a clone6 minutes

Replication, nuclear transfer and the limits of a clone

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced evidence and applications. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Repeating a comparison across individuals helps reveal whether an apparent advantage persists beyond one case. Repeating it across environmental conditions answers a broader question about context. These are related but different forms of evidence. A nursery recommendation should state the conditions under which its measured advantage occurred and identify the uncertainties that matter before scaling up the practice.

Dolly the sheep developed after nuclear transfer from an adult body cell. This showed that a specialized nucleus could support a new developmental program under suitable conditions. The egg supplies cytoplasm, including mitochondria, and development occurs in a different environment. A nuclear clone therefore need not have every trait, DNA variant or life experience of its donor. Dolly alone cannot establish that all clones age early. A later study examined 13 cloned sheep aged seven to nine years and found no major clinical signs of the assessed metabolic, cardiovascular or musculoskeletal diseases, although some joints showed mild changes. That result concerns surviving adults and the conditions measured. It does not erase embryo losses or prove that every cloning procedure is safe. Compare samples, survival and measured outcomes before making a general claim.

Embryo splitting and nuclear transfer are different cloning methods. Nuclear transfer places a nucleus in a new cytoplasmic and developmental setting and requires changes in gene regulation. Epigenetic state, prenatal conditions and later experience can differ. Telomere length in one cloned animal cannot establish a universal rule for ageing or lifespan.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Replication, nuclear transfer and the limits of a clone — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Repeated individualsTests whether a measured difference persists beyond one case.
Repeated environmentsTests whether that difference depends on conditions.

Limitation: One clone or surviving sample cannot establish a universal safety or ageing rule.

Illustrated walkthrough

1. Sexual and asexual reproduction

A fictional plant population can produce runners or seeds after fertilization. Compare inheritance and one ecological tradeoff.

  1. Runners develop through mitotic growth from the parent and usually preserve its genotype apart from new changes.
  2. Sexual reproduction combines gametes and can reshuffle parental variants.
  3. Compare speed, resource investment and variation in the stated environment rather than ranking one strategy as universally superior.

Asexual propagation can rapidly preserve a successful genotype; sexual reproduction can generate new combinations. Their relative effects depend on conditions, and neither guarantees survival.

2. Life-cycle transitions

Trace a moss life cycle from a diploid sporophyte through spores, gametophytes and fertilization. Compare the corresponding ploidy transitions in pine.

  1. Meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores.
  2. Spores grow by mitosis into haploid gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis.
  3. Fertilization restores diploidy; pine retains these broad transitions with much reduced gametophytes associated with the dominant sporophyte.

Meiosis changes 2n to n, fertilization changes n to 2n, and intervening mitosis preserves the current set number. Plant spores and gametes are different stages.

3. Animal strategies

Compare a Daphnia model that switches reproductive modes with a jellyfish model containing a polyp stage and a medusa stage. Avoid adding a medusa stage to a sea-anemone cycle.

  1. Identify which Daphnia conditions in the supplied model favour asexual or sexual reproduction.
  2. In the jellyfish example, distinguish mitotic asexual production from gamete formation and fertilization.
  3. Treat the sea-anemone example separately because a medusa stage is not part of its life cycle.

Different animals can combine reproductive strategies in different sequences. Shared vocabulary does not establish that their complete life cycles are identical.

4. Evidence and applications

A fictional nursery compares cloned cuttings with seedlings across a stable treatment and a changing treatment. What would make the comparison informative?

  1. Define an outcome such as survival or growth over the same interval.
  2. Replicate groups and control starting size, care and sampling while recording the reproductive origin.
  3. Compare variation and performance separately, then revise a claim that one method must always win.

The study can test outcomes under its stated conditions. It cannot establish a universal ranking without evidence across other genotypes and environments.

Lesson 7 · Chapter 17

Genes, Alleles and Traits

Why can different genotypes produce the same scored phenotype?

Required time
75 minutes
Advanced Learning
18 optional minutes

Learning goal

Use genetic notation accurately and distinguish dominance, allele frequency and environmental contributions to traits.

Before you begin

A gene region can have alternative alleles. Diploid individuals carry two copies at a typical autosomal locus. A measured trait depends on a stated expression model.

In the textbook

Chapter 17 · 587 #1; 590 #6–9

Open at p. 587

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

genotype

heterozygous

Learn · Part 1

Inheritance language

homozygous
Having two copies of the same allele at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.
heterozygous
Having two different alleles at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.
dominant
Describes an allele whose scored phenotype appears in a heterozygote under specified conditions.
recessive
Describes an allele whose scored phenotype in simple dominance is usually observed only without a dominant allele.
allele product
An RNA or protein output associated with a gene variant, contributing to how a genotype affects a trait.
notation
The symbols and conventions used to represent biological quantities or relationships.

A gene has a position, or locus, in chromosome DNA. Alleles are different forms of the gene at that locus. A typical diploid individual has two homologous chromosomes, so it has two alleles at an autosomal locus. These can match or differ. The allele pair is its genotype for that locus. A phenotype is a trait you can observe or measure under stated conditions.

Homozygous means the two alleles match, as in AA or aa. Heterozygous means they differ, as in Aa. Define the letters before using them. A letter labels an allele in a model; it does not explain how that allele works. A population can have many forms of an allele even though one typical diploid individual has only two at the autosomal locus.

Keep genes and observations separate. A genotype label names the inherited allele pair. A phenotype label describes something such as flower colour or enzyme activity. Allele products and other influences link the two. Two genotypes can give the same phenotype in one model. One genotype can also give different measurements in different conditions. Before predicting a result, name the locus, define the allele symbols and state the trait you will measure.

Worked example

In a stated one-locus model, A is completely dominant to a. Translate AA, Aa and aa into genotype and phenotype descriptions.

  1. Define the alleles before interpreting the letters.
  2. Identify AA and aa as homozygous and Aa as heterozygous.
  3. Under the stated complete-dominance model, group AA and Aa by the dominant phenotype while retaining distinct genotypes.

There are three genotypes but two phenotype categories in this model. The notation does not say which allele is common, beneficial or older.

Stop and check

Can the dominant phenotype alone distinguish AA from Aa?

Compare your thinking

No. Both can show that phenotype under the stated model. Additional evidence is needed to distinguish their genotypes.

Advanced LearningA symbol needs a model6 minutes

A symbol needs a model

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced inheritance language. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Capital and lower-case letters are convenient when two alleles follow complete dominance. Other inheritance patterns need notation that does not imply a false dominant–recessive relationship. Define allele symbols, phenotype rules and locus assumptions before constructing a cross. This makes the calculation reproducible and prevents a learner from importing a familiar ratio into a different biological model.

Dominant describes the heterozygote’s phenotype under a defined model. It does not mean common, stronger, healthier or more desirable, and it does not predict that an allele must increase in a population. A notation choice cannot supply evidence for an inheritance relationship.

Write the allele key and phenotype rule before using a cross. A capital letter is a notation choice, not evidence that the allele is common or advantageous. Keeping these claims separate prevents the expected inheritance pattern from being mistaken for a population trend. Dominant does not mean stronger, healthier, older or more desirable.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

A symbol needs a model — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Dominance notationDefines the phenotype of a heterozygote in a stated model.
Population frequencyCounts how common an allele or phenotype is.

Limitation: Dominant does not mean stronger, healthier, older or more desirable.

Related worked example: Worked example: Inheritance language

Learn · Part 2

Trait expression

pedigree
A diagram of reported trait occurrence and relationships across generations, interpreted probabilistically and with privacy safeguards.

Dominant and recessive describe an allele relationship for a stated trait. In complete dominance, the heterozygote has the same scored phenotype as one homozygote. That allele is called dominant in this comparison. The other is recessive. These terms do not show which allele is more common, more useful or newer. They describe how the chosen trait appears in a genotype.

An allele can affect a protein or how much of it a cell makes. One functional copy may provide enough product for the scored trait. In that case, a low-function allele can be recessive. Other mechanisms give other patterns. One allele does not erase the other. The dominance relationship can also depend on whether the study measures a visible trait or a molecular product.

In a fictional A/a model with complete dominance, AA and Aa share a phenotype while aa differs. A dominant phenotype therefore leaves two possible genotypes. An aa inference also relies on the stated model of trait expression. Define the assumptions before using a cross or pedigree. A simple classroom rule should not be treated as a general rule for a complex human trait.

Worked example

A fictional population contains mostly aa individuals even though A is completely dominant. Is the observation contradictory?

  1. Use dominance to predict the heterozygote's phenotype.
  2. Use population counts to describe allele or phenotype frequency.
  3. Keep the expression rule separate from the frequency measurement.

There is no contradiction. Complete dominance describes expression in a heterozygote; it does not require the dominant allele or phenotype to be common.

Stop and check

Does dominant mean that an allele must improve survival?

Compare your thinking

No. Dominance and effects on survival are different relationships. Either allele can have context-dependent effects.

Advanced LearningExpression can depend on biological scale6 minutes

Expression can depend on biological scale

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced trait expression. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A dominance label often describes one measured phenotype. At a molecular level, both alleles may still produce detectable products, even when an organism-level trait falls into one category. State what trait was measured and how it was classified. This helps explain why different descriptions of the same heterozygote can be compatible when they refer to different biological levels.

Define the measured feature before applying a dominance label. Two descriptions can be compatible when one concerns an organism-level category and another concerns molecular products. The different scales explain the apparent disagreement without changing the underlying genotype.

In the related worked example: There is no contradiction. Complete dominance describes expression in a heterozygote; it does not require the dominant allele or phenotype to be common. A dominance label for one phenotype need not describe every biological measurement.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Expression can depend on biological scale — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Organism-level traitMay place a heterozygote in one phenotype category.
Molecular measurementMay detect products associated with both alleles.

Limitation: A dominance label for one phenotype need not describe every biological measurement.

Related worked example: Worked example: Trait expression

Learn · Part 3

Genes and environment

polygenic trait
A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.
environmental influence
An effect of surrounding conditions on development, expression or performance of an organism.
continuous variation
A range of measured trait values, often influenced by several genes and environmental conditions.
polygenic
A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.
probability
A numerical measure of how likely an event is under a stated model, from zero to one.

A polygenic trait is influenced by more than one locus. Many allele combinations are then possible. Their effects, together with the environment, can produce continuous variation: a spread of measurements rather than only a few distinct groups. Height is one example with many genetic and environmental inputs. A range of values does not mean one allele exists for each exact height.

Conditions can affect growth, gene use and the measured trait. Nutrition or temperature may change the result from a given genotype. Genes and environment can both matter. To study their roles, define the population, trait and range of conditions. A family resemblance alone cannot separate shared genes from shared experiences. A stronger comparison needs a design that tests those alternatives.

Heritability describes genetic contributions to measured variation in a studied population and environment. It does not assign a genetic percentage to one person's trait. It also does not mean change is impossible. Tongue rolling, freckles and earlobe attachment are not reliable universal one-gene human models. Use fictional traits for simple crosses, and explain why their rules need not fit a real complex trait.

Worked example

Two fictional plants share a stated genotype but grow to different heights under different light conditions. Does this disprove inheritance?

  1. Identify the shared genotype and the changed environment.
  2. Recognize height as an outcome that can depend on several genes and environmental conditions.
  3. Seek a controlled comparison before attributing the entire difference to light.

The observation is compatible with environmental influence on an inherited developmental system. It does not show that genes are irrelevant or that one environmental difference is the only cause.

Stop and check

Would a continuous height distribution automatically support a single complete-dominance locus?

Compare your thinking

No. Many genes, environmental variation and measurement can contribute. A specific model needs evidence beyond the shape of the distribution.

Advanced LearningInteraction differs from simple addition6 minutes

Interaction differs from simple addition

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced genes and environment. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The effect of an environmental change can differ among genotypes. If one genotype responds strongly to added light and another responds weakly, the response is not captured by one universal environmental increment. A comparison across both genotypes and conditions can reveal that pattern. The conclusion should describe the measured interaction rather than assigning every difference exclusively to either genes or environment.

Differences in survival, scoring, environment or allele expression can alter an observed ratio even when segregation proceeds normally. Meiotic drive means unequal transmission of alternative alleles through gametes; it is another possible departure from the equal-probability model. Linkage and other inheritance patterns require their own evidence. Eye colour and other complex human traits should not be forced into a universal one-gene binary.

Environmental context includes nutrition, health, social conditions, learning opportunities and physical surroundings. Random developmental events and measurement choices can also affect observations. A gene–environment interaction means that a genetic effect differs across conditions; it cannot be reduced to two fixed percentages describing one individual.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Interaction differs from simple addition — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Genotype comparisonCompares inherited alternatives under stated conditions.
Environment comparisonTests whether their responses differ across conditions.

Limitation: A complex individual trait cannot be divided into two fixed genetic and environmental percentages.

Lesson 8 · Chapter 17

Mendelian Genetics

How can a cross test a model of allele transmission?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Connect segregation with meiosis, define inheritance notation and use offspring observations as probabilistic evidence.

Before you begin

Gametes carry one allele per locus in the model. Phenotype rules must be stated separately from genotype combinations. A small sample need not equal an expected ratio.

In the textbook

Chapter 17 · 588–593 #3–6,8–12; 591 Practice Problems 1–2; 596 #4,5

Open at p. 588

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

segregation
Separation of chromosomes or chromatids during cell division. In Mendelian inheritance, allele segregation describes separation of allele-bearing homologues so each normal gamete receives one allele copy at a locus.
true breeding
Producing the same specified trait when self-fertilized or crossed within the line under the simple model; the relevant loci are homozygous.
Punnett square
A grid that organizes possible gamete combinations to calculate offspring genotype probabilities under stated assumptions.
test cross
A cross with a homozygous recessive partner used to infer an unknown genotype or gamete frequencies.

Learn · Part 1

Controlled crosses and evidence

P generation
The parental generation in a defined genetic cross.
F1
The first offspring generation produced by the specified parental cross.
F2
The second offspring generation, often produced by crossing F1 individuals in the stated model.
true breeding
Producing the same specified trait when self-fertilized or crossed within the line under the simple model; the relevant loci are homozygous.
reciprocal cross
A comparison that switches which parental sex carries each trait or genotype.
expected count
The number predicted for a category by a specified probability model and total sample size.
sample size
The number of observations or individuals included in the sample.
inheritance model
A stated set of rules linking parental alleles, gametes and offspring genotypes/phenotypes.

Mendelian models grew from repeated crosses made under controlled conditions. The chosen parents form the P generation. Their offspring are the F1 generation. Crossing F1 individuals, or allowing them to self-fertilize, commonly produces the F2 generation. A true-breeding line keeps producing the scored trait under those breeding conditions. Such lines provide a clear starting point for testing inheritance.

Follow a simple complete-dominance cross. Two true-breeding parents have contrasting traits. Their F1 offspring are heterozygous but show one parental phenotype. Crossing the F1 can produce an F2 ratio near three dominant phenotypes to one recessive phenotype in a large sample. The recessive trait has reappeared. This supports separate inherited factors that can be passed on without showing, rather than a permanent blend of the parents' traits.

A reciprocal cross switches which parental sex supplies each phenotype. Compare its result with the first cross to see whether the direction matters. Record the sample sizes and actual counts before stating a rule. A close fit to a predicted ratio supports the model and its assumptions. It does not rule out every other explanation. Repeated observations and controlled methods provide stronger evidence than one small cross.

Worked example

A fictional true-breeding AA parent is crossed with aa under complete dominance. Predict the first generation, then identify the next cross that tests segregation.

  1. Each AA parent gamete carries A and each aa parent gamete carries a.
  2. All first-generation offspring are Aa under this model.
  3. Cross two Aa individuals and compare the next generation with the predicted genotype and phenotype proportions.

The first generation is all Aa with the dominant phenotype. Aa × Aa predicts 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and, under complete dominance, 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

Stop and check

Does observing only the first generation establish the full 3:1 second-generation prediction?

Compare your thinking

No. That prediction requires the next cross and the model assumptions. The first-generation observation supplies only part of the evidence.

Advanced LearningControlled pollination narrows alternatives6 minutes

Controlled pollination narrows alternatives

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced controlled crosses and evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A controlled cross must establish which parents supplied the gametes. Otherwise unintended pollen or uncertain parentage can produce offspring inconsistent with the proposed cross for reasons unrelated to the inheritance model. Controls and records therefore contribute directly to interpretation. Before changing a biological explanation, check that the observed offspring actually came from the stated parental combination and that the phenotype categories were applied consistently.

Unexpected offspring can arise from a mistaken cross record as well as an incorrect inheritance model. Check parentage and classification before revising the segregation explanation. These controls remove competing explanations that a larger offspring count alone would not resolve.

In the related worked example: The first generation is all Aa with the dominant phenotype. Aa × Aa predicts 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and, under complete dominance, 3 dominant : 1 recessive. A ratio cannot be interpreted independently of the crossing and scoring records.

Controlled parentageChecks which parents supplied the gametes.

Models and Data Lab: Test one-locus inheritance probabilities

Learn · Part 2

Segregation

allele pair
The two allele copies at a locus in a diploid individual, one associated with each homologue.
Punnett square
A grid that organizes possible gamete combinations to calculate offspring genotype probabilities under stated assumptions.

Segregation is the separation of the two alleles at one locus into different gametes. An Aa individual has A on one homologue and a at the matching locus on the other. During ordinary meiosis, the homologues separate. Each gamete receives one allele. In this simple model, half the gametes are expected to carry A and half to carry a.

Build an Aa × Aa cross one parent at a time. Each can supply A or a. The four combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa, each with a one-quarter chance. Aa and aA contain the same allele pair, so combine their chances. The genotype ratio is one-quarter AA, one-half Aa and one-quarter aa. Under complete dominance, both AA and Aa show the dominant trait. That gives three-quarters dominant and one-quarter recessive phenotypes.

These chances are not a schedule for four offspring. A small sample can contain four dominant offspring without breaking the segregation rule. Also distinguish two rules. Segregation concerns the two alleles at one locus. Independent assortment concerns how alleles at different loci combine in gametes. It applies under suitable chromosome relationships. Showing segregation at one locus does not prove that two loci assort independently.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How parental alleles separate and pass to offspring.

Worked example

Connect an Aa parent's two allele types with meiosis and its predicted gametes.

  1. Place A and a at corresponding loci on homologous chromosomes.
  2. Follow homolog separation during meiosis I and the later separation of sister copies.
  3. Under the stated equal-transmission model, assign probability 1/2 to A and 1/2 to a in a gamete.

The two alleles segregate into gametes; a gamete carries one of them at this locus. The 1/2 probabilities are predictions across many gametes, not a guarantee for every small sample.

Stop and check

Does an Aa gamete normally carry both A and a in this simple diploid model?

Compare your thinking

No. The gamete is haploid at this locus and carries one allele. Aa describes the diploid parent's genotype.

Advanced LearningA probability is not a required sequence6 minutes

A probability is not a required sequence

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced segregation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A 1/2 probability does not mean gametes must alternate A, a, A, a. Independent sampled events can form runs and uneven small groups. Compare the overall sampling distribution with the model rather than judging a short sequence by whether it looks balanced. Deviations can arise by chance, but persistent departures with adequate controls may motivate testing other biological explanations.

An independent event is not forced to compensate for the preceding one. An A gamete does not make an a gamete obligatory next. Compare repeated sample patterns with the model while retaining the possibility that persistent controlled departures deserve another biological explanation.

In the related worked example: The two alleles segregate into gametes; a gamete carries one of them at this locus. The 1/2 probabilities are predictions across many gametes, not a guarantee for every small sample. An uneven small sample alone does not refute equal gamete probabilities.

Learn · Part 3

Inheritance modes and notation

autosomal dominant
A model in which a trait-associated allele on an autosome is expressed in the heterozygote.
autosomal recessive
A model in which two copies of a trait-associated autosomal allele are required for the specified phenotype.
gamete probability
The probability that a gamete carries a specified allele combination under a stated genetic model.
phenotype ratio
The relative numbers or probabilities of specified observable trait classes, written in a stated order; for example, dominant:recessive = 3:1 in a simple complete-dominance cross.
independent trials
Events whose probabilities are unchanged by the outcomes of earlier trials under the model.
affected
A pedigree label indicating the specified phenotype; it is not a judgment about the person.
unaffected
A pedigree label indicating absence of the specified phenotype; it does not necessarily establish genotype.

An autosomal locus lies on a chromosome other than a sex chromosome. In a simplified autosomal dominant model, one dominant allele is enough for the scored phenotype. In an autosomal recessive model, two recessive alleles are required for that phenotype. Define which phenotype the notation represents. The terms affected and unaffected in a fictional case are scoring labels, not complete descriptions of a person.

A Punnett square organizes gamete combinations. Write each parent's genotype first, derive the gametes and their probabilities, then place one parent's possibilities across the top and the other's along the side. Each cell combines one gamete from each parent. Add cells belonging to the same genotype or phenotype. If gamete probabilities differ, the square's cells cannot simply be counted as equally likely.

For Aa × aa, the first parent supplies A or a, while the second supplies only a. Expected offspring are one-half Aa and one-half aa. Under complete dominance, half have each scored phenotype. A useful answer includes parental genotypes, gametes, assumptions and explanation. A bare ratio does not reveal which categories were counted or why the calculation applies.

Worked example

A supplied model gives heterozygotes a phenotype distinct from both homozygotes. A student applies a 3:1 phenotype ratio to a heterozygote cross. Repair the prediction.

  1. Define the three genotype-to-phenotype relationships first.
  2. Construct the heterozygote × heterozygote genotype probabilities: 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
  3. Keep the three phenotype categories because the heterozygote does not share either homozygote's phenotype.

The phenotype prediction is 1:2:1 in this model. The genotype probabilities do not change merely because the expression relationship differs from complete dominance.

Stop and check

What should be written before drawing a Punnett square?

Compare your thinking

The allele symbols, parental genotypes, inheritance model and any relevant assumptions about transmission and survival.

Advanced LearningThe same square can support different phenotype summaries6 minutes

The same square can support different phenotype summaries

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced inheritance modes and notation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A Punnett square combines gametes; it does not supply the expression rule by itself. Two models can share the same four genotype cells but group them differently into phenotypes. Place a phenotype key beside the square and apply it afterward. This separates the combinatorial calculation from the biological interpretation and makes it easier to find the source of an incorrect ratio.

Complete the genotype calculation before assigning phenotypes. The same heterozygote cross can yield a 3:1 or 1:2:1 phenotype summary depending on the supplied expression rule. Separating the two operations reveals whether an error concerns combination or interpretation.

In the related worked example: The phenotype prediction is 1:2:1 in this model. The genotype probabilities do not change merely because the expression relationship differs from complete dominance. The square itself does not supply a dominance rule.

Models and Data Lab: Test one-locus inheritance probabilities

Learn · Part 4

Probability and test crosses

test cross
A cross with a homozygous recessive partner used to infer an unknown genotype or gamete frequencies.
independent event
An event whose occurrence does not change the probability of another event under the stated model.
sample fluctuation
Chance variation among finite samples drawn under the same probability model.

A test cross pairs an individual with an uncertain dominant-phenotype genotype with a homozygous recessive tester. Under the simple A/a model, the unknown parent could be AA or Aa. The tester contributes only a. An aa offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent supplied a, identifying that parent as heterozygous under the stated assumptions.

If every observed offspring has the dominant phenotype, the result is less decisive. An AA parent predicts that outcome, but an Aa parent can also produce an all-dominant small sample by chance. For an Aa × aa model, four dominant offspring in four independent trials have probability (1/2)⁴=1/16. Larger repeated samples can strengthen an inference without making an impossible claim about what a small sample proves.

An independent event has a probability unaffected by the other event being considered under the model. Earlier offspring do not use up future outcomes. If parental genotypes remain Aa and Aa, a previous recessive child does not change the next child's one-quarter recessive probability. Sample fluctuation is the difference between realized counts and model expectations. Distinguish that variation from evidence that a biological assumption failed.

Worked example

An individual with a dominant phenotype is crossed with aa. Four observed offspring all have the dominant phenotype. Does this prove that the unknown parent is AA?

  1. Compare AA × aa, which predicts all dominant offspring, with Aa × aa, which predicts 1/2 dominant per offspring.
  2. Under independent outcomes, calculate the chance of four dominant offspring from Aa: (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
  3. Use the observation as evidence without treating a possible outcome as impossible.

The result is more consistent with AA under the simple alternatives, but it does not prove AA. An Aa parent could produce this small sample with probability 1/16.

Stop and check

What would one recessive offspring imply under the stated complete-dominance, accurate-parentage model?

Compare your thinking

The unknown parent contributed a, supporting Aa rather than AA. That conclusion depends on the stated model and reliable observations.

Advanced LearningEvidence strength depends on sample size6 minutes

Evidence strength depends on sample size

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced probability and test crosses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Repeated dominant offspring progressively change how well the two parental hypotheses fit the data, but no finite all-dominant sample makes the Aa probability exactly zero in this model. A full probability about the parent's genotype also requires prior information about the alternatives. Keep “probability of these offspring given Aa” distinct from “probability the parent is Aa given these offspring.”

Compare the likelihood of the observations under each parental hypothesis. All-dominant offspring fit AA particularly well, but remain possible under Aa. Increasing sample size can make one explanation less plausible without turning a finite sample into logical proof.

In the related worked example: The result is more consistent with AA under the simple alternatives, but it does not prove AA. An Aa parent could produce this small sample with probability 1/16. Do not reverse the conditioning to infer a genotype probability without the needed prior information.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Parent is Aa given those offspringRequires prior information as well as the offspring likelihood.

Single and Two Trait Crosses

Which assumptions make a familiar inheritance ratio valid?

Learning goal

Construct mono- and dihybrid crosses, apply probability rules and compare model expectations with supplied samples.

Before you begin

Use the parental genotypes to list the possible gametes, as in the previous lesson. Keep genotype and phenotype separate. Here you will first solve one-locus crosses, then combine independent events, then compare expected and observed results.

Four anchor words

Start with four words

product rule
A probability rule that multiplies probabilities along a sequence of independent or conditional events.
sum rule
A probability rule for mutually exclusive alternatives: add the probabilities of the separate outcomes.
independent assortment
Independent orientation and separation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing independent allele assortment for unlinked loci.
expected count
The number predicted for a category by a specified probability model and total sample size.

Learn · Part 1

Monohybrid crosses

genotype ratio
The relative numbers or probabilities of specified genotype classes, written in a stated order; for example, AA:Aa:aa = 1:2:1.
observed count
The number actually measured in a category before comparison with a model.

A monohybrid cross follows one locus. Begin by identifying the parental genotypes and the allele relationship. Derive the possible gametes rather than copying a remembered ratio. For Aa × Aa, each parent contributes A or a with equal probability. The four combinations yield a 1:2:1 genotype ratio. Complete dominance combines AA and Aa into the same phenotype, yielding a 3:1 phenotype ratio.

Other parental combinations give different predictions. AA × aa produces only Aa offspring, while Aa × aa produces equal Aa and aa probabilities. A genotype ratio and phenotype ratio answer different questions. If heterozygotes have a distinguishable phenotype, the phenotype categories may also follow 1:2:1 rather than 3:1. State the expression model before combining categories.

Use expected probabilities to evaluate observations. A small sample of ten from an Aa × Aa model has expected counts of 2.5 AA, 5 Aa and 2.5 aa. Fractional expected counts are legitimate because they describe averages over repeated samples, not fractions of an actual organism. Record actual whole-number observations separately and consider sample size before deciding whether a difference challenges the model.

Worked example

Solve Aa × Aa under complete dominance, showing genotype and phenotype probabilities separately.

  1. List A and a gametes from each parent with probability 1/2.
  2. Combine them to obtain AA, Aa, aA and aa, each with probability 1/4.
  3. Combine Aa and aA as the same heterozygous genotype, then group phenotypes by the stated dominance rule.

Genotypes: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Phenotypes: 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive.

Stop and check

Why are Aa and aA combined in this simple autosomal model?

Compare your thinking

They contain the same two alleles at the locus. The order written in the square does not create a fourth genotype category.

Advanced LearningExpected counts can be fractional6 minutes

Expected counts can be fractional

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced monohybrid crosses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

For ten offspring, the model predicts expected genotype counts of 2.5, 5 and 2.5. Actual offspring counts must be whole numbers. Fractional expectations describe long-run averages across comparable samples, not half an organism. Keep exact probabilities during calculation and distinguish expected counts from observed counts. Rounding every expected category too early can distort the total or the comparison.

A grid represents weighted combinations of gametes. Repeated Aa boxes are two routes to the same genotype, so add their probabilities. Check that all genotype probabilities sum to one and that every genotype enters exactly one phenotype category under the stated scoring rule. Equal boxes are appropriate only when the listed gamete combinations are equally likely.

Fractional expectations describe averages across comparable samples, not fractional organisms. Keep the exact probabilities until calculating each expectation and check their total. Repeated paths to the same genotype must be added before the phenotype rule is applied. Rounding expectations early can distort the total or comparison.

Learn · Part 2

Probability rules

product rule
A probability rule that multiplies probabilities along a sequence of independent or conditional events.
sum rule
A probability rule for mutually exclusive alternatives: add the probabilities of the separate outcomes.
two loci
Two positions on chromosomes being followed in a genetic model; linkage must be specified.
conditional probability
The probability of an event after specified information or a condition is taken into account.
carrier
In simple recessive inheritance, a heterozygous individual who has one recessive allele and usually lacks the associated phenotype.

The product rule finds the chance that independent events both occur. Start with one locus: in Aa × Aa, the chance of aa is one-quarter. At a second independent locus, Bb × Bb gives a one-quarter chance of bb. To find the chance of aabb, multiply one-quarter by one-quarter. The result is one-sixteenth. Check independence first: learning the result at one locus must not change the chance at the other.

The sum rule combines alternatives that cannot both occur in the same outcome. In Aa × Aa, one route to a heterozygote is A from the first parent and a from the second. Its chance is one-quarter. The other route is a from the first parent and A from the second, also one-quarter. Add the routes to get one-half. If categories overlap, simple addition counts the overlap twice. Use separate categories or account for the overlap.

Conditional probability means finding a chance within a group selected by new information. Use the same Aa × Aa cross. Suppose aa shows a recessive condition and every aa individual shows it. Before you know the phenotype, AA, Aa, aA and aa are equally likely outcomes. Two of the four are carriers, so the carrier chance is one-half.

Now you learn that the child is unaffected. Remove aa, because it does not meet that condition. Three equally likely outcomes remain: AA, Aa and aA. Two are carriers, so the chance among unaffected offspring is two-thirds. The cross has not changed. The information has changed the group used as the denominator. Always name that group before choosing a fraction.

Worked example

For independent loci in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance, calculate the chance of aaB_ and the chance that exactly one of two independent offspring is aa.

  1. Solve the first question one locus at a time. Aa × Aa gives P(aa) = 1/4. Bb × Bb gives P(BB or Bb) = 3/4. B_ means either of these dominant-phenotype genotypes.
  2. The loci are stated to be independent. Multiply the two chances: P(aaB_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
  3. For the second question, focus only on the A locus. Each offspring has P(aa) = 1/4 and P(not aa) = 3/4.
  4. List the two orders that meet exactly one: first aa then not aa, or first not aa then aa. Both aa and neither aa do not meet the condition.
  5. The offspring are stated to be independent. Each allowed order has chance (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
  6. The two orders cannot occur together. Add their chances: 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.

The requested probabilities are 3/16 and 3/8. Multiplication uses the stated independence; addition combines non-overlapping alternatives.

Stop and check

Can probabilities for overlapping alternatives always be added without correction?

Compare your thinking

No. Overlap would be counted twice. Either define disjoint alternatives or subtract the overlapping probability.

Advanced LearningIndependence must be justified6 minutes

Independence must be justified

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced probability rules. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Multiplication is convenient, but it can be misapplied when loci are linked or outcomes share an important condition. Start by naming the events and why independence is a reasonable assumption in the given problem. If the assumption changes, revise the calculation rather than retaining the familiar product. Probability rules are general; the biological model determines which rule and inputs fit the case.

Define the events before choosing arithmetic. For exactly one aa in two independent offspring, aa then not-aa and not-aa then aa are separate allowed orders. Their total is 2 × 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/8 under the supplied assumptions.

In the related worked example: The requested probabilities are 3/16 and 3/8. Multiplication uses the stated independence; addition combines non-overlapping alternatives. Multiplication of marginal probabilities requires the stated independence.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Independence must be justified — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Joint independent eventsMultiply their probabilities, such as 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16.
Non-overlapping alternativesAdd their probabilities, such as two orders giving exactly one aa offspring.

Limitation: Multiplication of marginal probabilities requires the stated independence.

Learn · Part 3

Dihybrid crosses

four gamete types
The four allele combinations AB, Ab, aB and ab available from AaBb when the two loci assort independently.

A dihybrid cross follows two loci. For independently assorting loci in an AaBb individual, A or a can combine with B or b. The four gamete types are AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability one-quarter under the model. Their independence can arise from independently orienting different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis I.

In an AaBb × AaBb cross with complete dominance at both loci, the phenotype probabilities are 9/16 A_B_, 3/16 A_bb, 3/16 aaB_ and 1/16 aabb. The underscore means either allele can occupy that position while retaining the stated dominant phenotype. For example, A_ includes AA and Aa. A 16-cell square or separate single-locus probabilities can produce the same result when used reliably.

This prediction has conditions. Linked loci can be transmitted together more often than independence predicts, and other allele interactions can change the phenotype categories. A 9:3:3:1 ratio is therefore a model result, not a universal property of two-trait inheritance. In a test cross AaBb × aabb, equal gamete probabilities instead predict four equally likely offspring classes. Always connect the ratio to its parental cross and assumptions.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How two traits are tracked together in a cross.

Worked example

List gametes from AaBb under independent assortment and predict the phenotype proportions in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance at both loci.

  1. Combine A or a with B or b to obtain AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4.
  2. Combine the two parents' gametes in a 4 × 4 square or multiply single-locus probabilities.
  3. Group the outcomes as A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb.

The predicted phenotype proportions are 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 under the stated assumptions.

Stop and check

Would tightly linked loci in a known parental phase necessarily produce the same four gamete probabilities?

Compare your thinking

No. Linkage can alter gamete frequencies. The independent-assortment result cannot be assumed without checking the model.

Advanced LearningA ratio bundles several assumptions6 minutes

A ratio bundles several assumptions

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced dihybrid crosses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The familiar 9:3:3:1 ratio depends on the parental genotypes, locus independence, complete dominance and suitable assumptions about transmission, survival and classification. A different observed pattern could challenge any of these components. Use a checklist of model assumptions to decide what to investigate rather than naming linkage immediately whenever a sample differs from the ratio.

Treat the ratio as a compressed set of assumptions, not a biological law. Compare the evidence for each assumption before naming a mechanism for a departure. The same unequal category counts may fit several alternatives until an additional discriminating observation is obtained.

In the related worked example: The predicted phenotype proportions are 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 under the stated assumptions. A departure from 9:3:3:1 does not by itself identify linkage.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 4

Testing a model

An observed count is the result recorded in a sample. An expected count is the model probability multiplied by the sample size. To investigate an Aa × Aa model, first predict the 1:2:1 genotype pattern and specify how offspring will be classified. Keep parental genotypes, scoring rules and the inheritance model constant while comparing sample sizes.

The two small samples contain AA/Aa/aa counts of 3/5/2 and 1/7/2, compared with expectations of 2.5/5/2.5 in each ten-offspring sample. The larger samples contain 24/51/25 and 28/48/24, compared with 25/50/25 in each hundred-offspring sample. These are synthetic data for testing a reasoning process. Their larger-sample proportions are closer overall to the model, but increasing a sample does not guarantee every observed category moves closer each time.

Record the observations and expectations in separate columns. Explain a difference using sample fluctuation before claiming a new inheritance mechanism, then consider alternatives such as scoring error or differential survival. A stronger investigation repeats samples and checks the model's assumptions. Respond to the claim that any deviation disproves segregation by using the actual counts and probabilities. Revise your conclusion to state both the support and its limits.

Worked example

Compare the supplied Aa × Aa genotype counts: small samples 3/5/2 and 1/7/2; large samples 24/51/25 and 28/48/24, ordered AA/Aa/aa.

  1. Use 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 as the model probabilities.
  2. Expected counts are 2.5/5/2.5 for each ten-offspring sample and 25/50/25 for each hundred-offspring sample.
  3. Compare proportions and sample sizes without demanding an exact ratio in each sample.

All four samples differ from exact expectations. Such differences alone do not reject the model; interpretation needs sampling variability, replication and checks on the design.

Stop and check

Is the sample 1/7/2 proof that segregation stopped operating?

Compare your thinking

No. A small sample can differ from expected proportions by chance. A stronger claim needs appropriate evidence and alternative explanations considered.

Advanced LearningAbsolute and proportional deviations6 minutes

Absolute and proportional deviations

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced testing a model. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A large sample can have a greater absolute count difference but a smaller proportional difference. For example, compare three individuals away from expectation in a hundred with a similar difference in ten. Both the denominator and the pattern across categories matter. A formal statistical test may extend the analysis, but it does not replace checking parentage, observation quality and the model's biological assumptions.

Compare how likely the observed data are under each proposed genotype or mechanism. Parentage, scoring, penetrance and sample size affect that comparison. Penetrance means the fraction with a genotype who show the defined phenotype. Choose another observation whose predictions differ between the alternatives. Use “supports” or “is consistent with” when an alternative remains possible.

Show both the count difference and its denominator before comparing fit. A larger sample may produce a larger absolute deviation but a smaller proportional one. Statistical comparison still depends on parentage, classification and the biological model being tested. Neither a large count difference nor a close fit identifies a mechanism alone.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Absolute and proportional deviations — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Three away among tenA proportional difference of 3/10.
Three away among one hundredA proportional difference of 3/100.

Limitation: Neither a large count difference nor a close fit identifies a mechanism alone.

Models and Data Lab: Test one-locus inheritance probabilities

See the idea in action

Illustrated walkthrough

1. Monohybrid crosses

Solve Aa × Aa under complete dominance, showing genotype and phenotype probabilities separately.

  1. List A and a gametes from each parent with probability 1/2.
  2. Combine them to obtain AA, Aa, aA and aa, each with probability 1/4.
  3. Combine Aa and aA as the same heterozygous genotype, then group phenotypes by the stated dominance rule.

Genotypes: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Phenotypes: 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive.

2. Probability rules

For independent loci in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance, calculate the chance of aaB_ and the chance that exactly one of two independent offspring is aa.

  1. Solve the first question one locus at a time. Aa × Aa gives P(aa) = 1/4. Bb × Bb gives P(BB or Bb) = 3/4. B_ means either of these dominant-phenotype genotypes.
  2. The loci are stated to be independent. Multiply the two chances: P(aaB_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
  3. For the second question, focus only on the A locus. Each offspring has P(aa) = 1/4 and P(not aa) = 3/4.
  4. List the two orders that meet exactly one: first aa then not aa, or first not aa then aa. Both aa and neither aa do not meet the condition.
  5. The offspring are stated to be independent. Each allowed order has chance (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
  6. The two orders cannot occur together. Add their chances: 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.

The requested probabilities are 3/16 and 3/8. Multiplication uses the stated independence; addition combines non-overlapping alternatives.

3. Dihybrid crosses

List gametes from AaBb under independent assortment and predict the phenotype proportions in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance at both loci.

  1. Combine A or a with B or b to obtain AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4.
  2. Combine the two parents' gametes in a 4 × 4 square or multiply single-locus probabilities.
  3. Group the outcomes as A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb.

The predicted phenotype proportions are 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 under the stated assumptions.

4. Testing a model

Compare the supplied Aa × Aa genotype counts: small samples 3/5/2 and 1/7/2; large samples 24/51/25 and 28/48/24, ordered AA/Aa/aa.

  1. Use 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 as the model probabilities.
  2. Expected counts are 2.5/5/2.5 for each ten-offspring sample and 25/50/25 for each hundred-offspring sample.
  3. Compare proportions and sample sizes without demanding an exact ratio in each sample.

All four samples differ from exact expectations. Such differences alone do not reject the model; interpretation needs sampling variability, replication and checks on the design.

Checkpoint

Can expected counts of 2.5/5/2.5 occur as literal offspring counts in one ten-offspring family?

Up to 120 characters can be saved in this response. Longer writing stays visible for copying and revision.

No. They are model expectations; observed individuals are counted in whole numbers.

Retrieve

Retrieve the idea

For AaBb × AaBb with independent loci, what is P(aaB_)?

Up to 180 characters can be saved in this response. Longer writing stays visible for copying and revision.

P(aa) × P(B_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16 under the stated model.

For Aa × aa, what proportion of offspring is predicted to be aa?

Attempt the question to open the feedback.

Correct. The Aa parent supplies a with probability 1/2; the aa parent always supplies a, so P(aa)=1/2.

Review this choice. The Aa parent can supply a, so aa offspring are possible.

Review this choice. One-quarter aa would fit Aa × Aa, not Aa × aa.

Review this choice. Three-quarters is the dominant phenotype probability in Aa × Aa under complete dominance, not this aa genotype probability.

One complete response

At A, P(aa)=1/4 and P(A_)=3/4. At B, P(bb)=1/4. Thus P(aabb)=1/4×1/4=1/16 and P(A_bb)=3/4×1/4=3/16. Independence permits multiplying across loci; A_ includes both AA and Aa.

Lesson 10 · Chapter 17

Other Modes of Inheritance

How does the expression model change the phenotype prediction from a cross?

Required time
120 minutes
Advanced Learning
30 optional minutes

Learning goal

Compare incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, sex linkage and polygenic/environmental models using explicit notation.

Before you begin

Gamete combinations determine genotypes. A phenotype key interprets those genotypes. A population can contain more allele types than one diploid individual carries at a locus.

In the textbook

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

codominance
An inheritance pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote contribute distinct detectable products or traits.
X-linked
Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.
polygenic
A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.

Learn · Part 1

Incomplete dominance

intermediate heterozygote
A heterozygote with a phenotype between the two homozygous phenotypes under incomplete dominance.
codominance
An inheritance pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote contribute distinct detectable products or traits.

Incomplete dominance occurs when a heterozygote's measured phenotype falls between those of the two homozygotes. In a fictional flower model, RᴿRᴿ is red, RᵂRᵂ is white and RᴿRᵂ is pink. The symbols name two alleles without claiming that one fully dominates. Write the notation first. The model must state which trait is measured before its pattern can be predicted.

Each pink parent can supply Rᴿ or Rᵂ. Crossing two pink plants gives one-quarter red, one-half pink and one-quarter white. Both genotype and phenotype ratios are 1:2:1 because each genotype has a distinct colour here. The alleles still remain separate and segregate. Pink is an intermediate phenotype, not a new blended allele that makes red and white alleles disappear.

A visible colour, pigment amount and protein type are different measurements. The dominance relationship depends on the chosen trait and its mechanism. Compare this cross with complete dominance, where two genotypes share a scored phenotype. State how the categories differ and why. An intermediate appearance is one kind of allele effect, not the only way two alleles can be expressed.

Worked example

In a fictional flower model, RR is red, WW is white and RW is pink. Predict RW × RW and explain why the alleles have not permanently blended.

  1. List R and W gametes from each parent.
  2. Combine them to obtain 1/4 RR, 1/2 RW and 1/4 WW.
  3. Apply the stated phenotype key to recover red, pink and white offspring categories.

The prediction is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Reappearance of both homozygous categories shows that the alleles remain separable rather than being irreversibly blended.

Stop and check

Does an intermediate heterozygote phenotype mean each gamete contains half of both alleles?

Compare your thinking

No. Each gamete receives one allele at the locus in this model. The intermediate phenotype describes the diploid heterozygote's expression.

Advanced LearningAn intermediate trait needs a defined measure6 minutes

An intermediate trait needs a defined measure

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced incomplete dominance. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

“Intermediate” can refer to an observed colour, amount or other measured phenotype. It should not be treated as a universal average of every molecular and organism-level feature. Define the trait and its categories before comparing genotypes. A model can accurately describe a particular phenotype while leaving details of the underlying biochemical pathway for further study.

Define pink as the phenotype being scored, not as an irreversible mixture of inherited units. The heterozygote cross restores both homozygous categories because allele transmission remains separable. A colour category alone leaves much of the biochemical explanation unresolved.

In the related worked example: The prediction is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Reappearance of both homozygous categories shows that the alleles remain separable rather than being irreversibly blended. Intermediate applies to the defined measurement, not every molecular or organism-level feature.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Models and Data Lab: Test one-locus inheritance probabilities

Learn · Part 2

Codominance and multiple alleles

ABO
A human blood-group system controlled by multiple alleles in which IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive.
multiple alleles
Three or more allele versions present at one locus in a population, though a diploid individual carries at most two.

Codominance occurs when both allele-associated products are detectable in the heterozygote. The simplified ABO blood-group model provides an example. Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles support distinct surface antigens, while i does not produce those same functional antigen-modifying effects. IᴬIᴮ individuals display both A and B antigens rather than an intermediate blended antigen. The i allele is recessive to Iᴬ and Iᴮ in this model.

Multiple alleles means that more than two allele forms exist in the population at a locus. A typical diploid individual still carries only two of them at an autosomal locus. Crossing Iᴬi with Iᴮi produces IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii with equal probabilities, corresponding to AB, A, B and O in the stated model. Write the gametes to show how each outcome arises.

Codominance and multiple alleles describe different features: expression within a genotype versus diversity of allele forms across a population. ABO evidence can exclude some proposed combinations in a closed classroom puzzle, but it cannot establish a unique person's identity or a certain relationship in the real world. Other evidence and model qualifications matter. Keep the exercise's inheritance assumptions separate from a medical or identity decision.

Worked example

In the simplified ABO model, cross Iᴬi with Iᴮi. List the possible offspring genotypes and blood-group phenotypes.

  1. The first parent supplies Iᴬ or i; the second supplies Iᴮ or i.
  2. Combine to obtain IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii, each with probability 1/4.
  3. Apply codominance of Iᴬ and Iᴮ and their dominance over i in this classroom model.

The predicted groups are AB, A, B and O, each with probability 1/4. Three allele types exist in the population, while one diploid individual has at most two at this locus.

Stop and check

Does an AB individual carry three ABO alleles because the population has three common allele types?

Compare your thinking

No. The individual has two alleles at this locus: Iᴬ and Iᴮ in the simplified model.

Advanced LearningPopulation options and individual copies6 minutes

Population options and individual copies

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced codominance and multiple alleles. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Multiple alleles describes the range of variants in a population, not extra copies in every individual. A useful notation table separates the available allele types from the two copies carried by a diploid genotype. Real blood-group interpretation can involve additional biology beyond this simplified locus model. Keep classroom inheritance predictions scoped to the assumptions supplied rather than using them as a complete clinical or identity test.

In the simplified ABO model, phenotype A can arise from IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi, and phenotype B from IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi. A phenotype does not always identify a unique genotype. Detecting both A and B antigens in AB is codominance, not a claim that every molecule is half of each type.

Separate the list of possible allele types from the copies carried by one individual. Then apply the phenotype key: A or B phenotype need not identify a unique genotype. The Iᴬi × Iᴮi cross yields four equally weighted combinations under the supplied assumptions. The classroom ABO model is not a complete clinical or identity test.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.
