Learn · Part 3

Sex linkage

X-linked
Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.
Y-linked
Describes a gene located on the Y chromosome and transmitted through Y-bearing lineages.
hemizygous
Having only one copy of a gene or chromosome region in a diploid cell, as for many X-linked loci in XY cells.
X-linked inheritance
Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.

A sex-linked locus lies on a sex chromosome. In a typical XY model, many X-linked loci have no matching copy on the Y. An XY individual then has just one copy at that locus. This is called hemizygous. A recessive allele on that X can be expressed because there is no second allele to mask it. An XX individual usually has two copies, so its allele combinations differ.

Fruit-fly crosses used by Morgan helped link traits to chromosome location. Follow a simple X-linked recessive eye-colour model. A white-eyed male and a homozygous red-eyed female produce red-eyed F1 offspring. Crossing those F1 flies can produce white-eyed sons. Now reverse the parents' traits. A white-eyed female and a red-eyed male produce red-eyed carrier daughters and white-eyed sons. The different results help test X linkage.

In the usual XY pattern, a father passes his X to daughters and his Y to sons. A Y-linked allele can therefore pass from father to son. An autosomal allele can pass from either parent to offspring of either sex. A male-only trait does not prove X linkage. Test other explanations, such as Y linkage, expression limited to one sex or chance in a small sample. Write the possible genotypes and trace their transmission.

Watch and make sense of it

Worked example

For a stated X-linked recessive model, cross XᴬXᵃ with XᴬY. Calculate the chance of an affected son among all offspring and among sons.

  1. List the maternal Xᴬ and Xᵃ gametes and paternal Xᴬ and Y gametes.
  2. The four equally likely outcomes are XᴬXᴬ, XᴬXᵃ, XᴬY and XᵃY in the simplified model.
  3. Count XᵃY once among all four outcomes and once among the two son outcomes.

The probability is 1/4 among all offspring and 1/2 conditional on being a son. The denominator changes with the question.

Stop and check

In this model, does a father transmit his X chromosome to a son?

Compare your thinking

No. The son receives the paternal Y in the stated model. The maternal X supplies the allele at the locus being followed.

Advanced LearningConditional probability and mosaic expression6 minutes

Conditional probability and mosaic expression

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced sex linkage. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Questions about “an affected son” and “an affected child given that the child is a son” describe different events. Write the sample space before calculating. Also state the simplified assumptions about sex-chromosome transmission and equal gamete probabilities. The model explains a particular inheritance pathway; it should not be expanded into unsupported claims about every feature of sex development or identity.

In many cells with two X chromosomes, much of one X becomes inactive early in development. Descendants can maintain that choice, creating patches of cells with different active X copies. This helps explain coat-colour patches in a heterozygous cat. Some genes escape X inactivation, and patterns can be uneven. A calico coat does not prove one universal chromosome pattern: uncommon male cases and other mechanisms exist.

Carrier is a label within a stated inheritance and phenotype model. Some heterozygous individuals with two X copies show effects because of uneven X inactivation or other biological influences. Write the actual allele and chromosome contribution instead of assuming a carrier can never express a trait. Pedigree symbols summarize the supplied model, not personal identity.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 4

Many genes and environment

risk
The possibility and potential consequence of an adverse outcome under specified conditions.

When several loci affect a trait, many genotype combinations become possible. In a simple additive model, more contributing alleles can shift the trait in one direction. Real effects may be unequal or interact. Gene count alone therefore does not fix an exact phenotype. Conditions can also widen or shift the range of measurements, even when the allele combinations stay the same.

Compare a one-locus flower-colour model with height. The flower model can give a few clear groups under its assumptions. Height has many genetic and environmental inputs. Relatives may share both genes and conditions. Their similarity alone cannot tell how much each source contributed. A useful study must separate these possibilities through its design and define the population to which its result applies.

One established gene for high intelligence is not a valid general model of a complex cognitive trait. An association may depend on the studied population and need not show cause. It also does not prove that changing the variant would be safe or effective. Check the measure, effect size, context and validation. Simple crosses help us learn to test models, including rejecting one that does not fit the question.

Worked example

A fictional trait shows a broad continuous distribution rather than two sharply separated categories. What models should be considered before applying a Mendelian ratio?

  1. Check whether several loci can contribute to the trait.
  2. Consider environmental variation and measurement effects.
  3. Seek family, genotype or controlled-condition evidence that can distinguish the proposed contributions.

A polygenic and environmentally influenced model is plausible, but distribution shape alone does not prove the number of contributing genes.

Stop and check

Does a continuous distribution mean that alleles no longer segregate during meiosis?

Compare your thinking

No. Individual loci can segregate while their combined effects and environmental influences create continuous trait variation.

Advanced LearningMultiple inputs and regulation without a sequence change6 minutes

Multiple inputs and regulation without a sequence change

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced many genes and environment. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Several loci with small effects can produce many combinations, even when each locus has only a few genotype categories. Environmental variation can broaden those outcomes further. A classroom model with a few additive loci illustrates the principle, but real effects may interact rather than add neatly. State which simplifications the model uses before interpreting its distribution as a complete account of a human trait.

Epigenetic regulation changes how DNA is used without changing its base sequence. Chemical marks on DNA or associated proteins can help maintain different gene-use patterns in cell lineages. Such marks are not a single universal on/off switch. Their effect depends on location and biological context. Many are reset between generations, so an environmental effect in one person does not by itself demonstrate inheritance by grandchildren. A gene that normally helps restrain uncontrolled cell growth may increase cancer risk when its function is lost. It is therefore misleading to claim that a harmful inherited variant matters only when a gene is switched on. Sequence, regulation and other changes can interact. A school model should explain the mechanism and uncertainty, rather than predict an individual diagnosis from a simple gene-expression label.

Penetrance is the proportion with a genotype who show a defined phenotype. Expressivity describes differences in degree or form among those showing it. Other genes, age, environment, tissue mixtures and measurement definitions can contribute. A risk variant changes a probability under specified conditions; it is not a guarantee of disease. A shifted group average can coexist with substantial overlap between distributions. It cannot identify an individual’s genotype or ability. A few-locus additive exercise illustrates combinations; it does not establish one gene for height, intelligence or athletic performance.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Multiple inputs and regulation without a sequence change — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Additive classroom lociIllustrate how several inherited contributions create combinations.
Observed continuous traitMay also involve interactions, regulation and environmental variation.

Limitation: Distribution shape alone does not prove gene number, individual ability or a diagnosis.

Related worked example: Worked example: Many genes and environment

Learn · Part 5

Comparing model predictions

Begin by writing the allele symbols and the trait being measured. Then compare the models. Complete dominance groups two genotypes into one phenotype. Incomplete dominance gives the heterozygote an intermediate phenotype, so all three genotypes can be distinguished. Codominance allows both allele products to be detected in the heterozygote. Write these predicted categories before comparing them with the observations.

Survival can change which offspring you count. In a fictional Aa × Aa cross, the chances at conception are one AA, two Aa and one aa. Suppose AA offspring die before the count. Remove AA from the comparison. Of the three remaining outcomes, two are Aa and one is aa. The expected ratio among survivors is therefore 2:1. Segregation has not changed; the set being counted has changed.

Use the same steps when a question gives information about sex, phenotype or survival. First list all outcomes. Next remove those that do not meet the condition. Finally calculate the fraction within the remaining set. The model must fit both inheritance and the way observations were scored. If counts do not match, check sample size, classification, survival and linkage before proposing a new allele relationship.

Worked example

A heterozygote cross produces three observed phenotype categories. Compare complete dominance, incomplete dominance and codominance as possible explanations.

  1. Ask whether the heterozygote shares a homozygote's phenotype, has an intermediate phenotype or displays both defined products.
  2. Use the observed phenotype definitions to select a model.
  3. Then calculate genotype probabilities and apply that model's phenotype key.

The category count alone may suggest that simple complete dominance is inadequate, but the actual phenotype evidence distinguishes incomplete dominance from codominance.

Stop and check

Can a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio by itself tell whether the heterozygote is intermediate or expresses both products?

Compare your thinking

No. Both models can yield that ratio. The nature of the heterozygote's phenotype provides the distinguishing evidence.

Advanced LearningA numerical fit is not a unique mechanism6 minutes

A numerical fit is not a unique mechanism

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced comparing model predictions. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Different biological models can predict the same ratio. To choose between them, identify an observation for which their predictions differ, such as the presence of two distinguishable products. This is stronger than repeatedly collecting only the same category counts. A good explanation combines the numerical result with mechanism-specific evidence and states any remaining alternatives.

Ask what observation would differ under the competing explanations. Repeating the same category count more precisely may still leave both models viable. Evidence about an intermediate measurement versus distinguishable products addresses the mechanism that the ratio alone leaves unresolved.

In the related worked example: The category count alone may suggest that simple complete dominance is inadequate, but the actual phenotype evidence distinguishes incomplete dominance from codominance. Three categories do not uniquely determine one expression mechanism.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

A numerical fit is not a unique mechanism — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Numerical ratioMay be shared by different inheritance models.
Product or phenotype evidenceCan distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance.

Limitation: Three categories do not uniquely determine one expression mechanism.

Illustrated walkthrough

1. Incomplete dominance

In a fictional flower model, RR is red, WW is white and RW is pink. Predict RW × RW and explain why the alleles have not permanently blended.

  1. List R and W gametes from each parent.
  2. Combine them to obtain 1/4 RR, 1/2 RW and 1/4 WW.
  3. Apply the stated phenotype key to recover red, pink and white offspring categories.

The prediction is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Reappearance of both homozygous categories shows that the alleles remain separable rather than being irreversibly blended.

2. Codominance and multiple alleles

In the simplified ABO model, cross Iᴬi with Iᴮi. List the possible offspring genotypes and blood-group phenotypes.

  1. The first parent supplies Iᴬ or i; the second supplies Iᴮ or i.
  2. Combine to obtain IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii, each with probability 1/4.
  3. Apply codominance of Iᴬ and Iᴮ and their dominance over i in this classroom model.

The predicted groups are AB, A, B and O, each with probability 1/4. Three allele types exist in the population, while one diploid individual has at most two at this locus.

3. Sex linkage

For a stated X-linked recessive model, cross XᴬXᵃ with XᴬY. Calculate the chance of an affected son among all offspring and among sons.

  1. List the maternal Xᴬ and Xᵃ gametes and paternal Xᴬ and Y gametes.
  2. The four equally likely outcomes are XᴬXᴬ, XᴬXᵃ, XᴬY and XᵃY in the simplified model.
  3. Count XᵃY once among all four outcomes and once among the two son outcomes.

The probability is 1/4 among all offspring and 1/2 conditional on being a son. The denominator changes with the question.

4. Many genes and environment

A fictional trait shows a broad continuous distribution rather than two sharply separated categories. What models should be considered before applying a Mendelian ratio?

  1. Check whether several loci can contribute to the trait.
  2. Consider environmental variation and measurement effects.
  3. Seek family, genotype or controlled-condition evidence that can distinguish the proposed contributions.

A polygenic and environmentally influenced model is plausible, but distribution shape alone does not prove the number of contributing genes.

5. Comparing model predictions

A heterozygote cross produces three observed phenotype categories. Compare complete dominance, incomplete dominance and codominance as possible explanations.

  1. Ask whether the heterozygote shares a homozygote's phenotype, has an intermediate phenotype or displays both defined products.
  2. Use the observed phenotype definitions to select a model.
  3. Then calculate genotype probabilities and apply that model's phenotype key.

The category count alone may suggest that simple complete dominance is inadequate, but the actual phenotype evidence distinguishes incomplete dominance from codominance.

Checkpoint

Does the same 1:2:1 ratio by itself distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance?

No. The nature of the heterozygote phenotype distinguishes the models.

Lesson 11 · Chapter 17

Pedigrees

What can family observations establish, and what must remain conditional?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Read a fictional pedigree, compare inheritance hypotheses and calculate a conditional probability with explicit limits.

Before you begin

Pedigree symbols need a legend. Phenotypes are observed; genotypes can be inferred under a model. New information changes the relevant probability sample space.

In the textbook

Chapter 17 · 612 #30–31; 614 #32; 615 Practice Problems 18–21; 617 #3–4

Open at p. 612

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

pedigree
A diagram of reported trait occurrence and relationships across generations, interpreted probabilistically and with privacy safeguards.
carrier
In simple recessive inheritance, a heterozygous individual who has one recessive allele and usually lacks the associated phenotype.
unknown genotype
An allele combination not uniquely determined by the available evidence.
probability
A numerical measure of how likely an event is under a stated model, from zero to one.

Learn · Part 1

Symbols and evidence

unknown genotype
An allele combination not uniquely determined by the available evidence.

A pedigree shows biological relationships and a scored trait across generations. Its legend defines the symbols, shading and any carrier marks. Roman numerals often label generations; numbers identify members within each generation. Lines show relationships and offspring. Read the legend first. A familiar symbol can have a specific meaning in this source that must be preserved when reasoning from it.

Affected and unaffected refer only to the trait being tracked. They do not describe a person's overall health or abilities. An unshaded symbol usually records a phenotype. It does not always show a known non-carrier genotype. If the source marks confirmed carriers, retain that distinction. Leave unknown genotypes open rather than filling every space with one certain answer.

Build the fictional pedigree from the supplied relationships before testing a genetic model. Place each person in the correct generation, join the relationships and mark only the stated traits. Add possible genotypes afterward. Show alternatives where the evidence does not settle them. This order keeps source facts separate from inference and avoids asking learners to disclose their own family histories.

Worked example

Read a fictional pedigree in which the legend defines filled symbols as a measured phenotype, a horizontal line as a reproductive partnership and a vertical line as descendants. What can be recorded before assigning genotypes?

  1. Use the legend to identify relationships and observed phenotype categories.
  2. Assign generation and individual identifiers so evidence can be cited precisely.
  3. Keep unobserved genotypes blank or conditional until an inheritance model supplies constraints.

The pedigree records relationships and phenotype observations. Genotypes are inferred under a model and should not be silently treated as directly measured.

Stop and check

Does an unfilled symbol always prove that an individual lacks a recessive allele?

Compare your thinking

No. Under a recessive model, an unfilled individual may be a heterozygous carrier. The legend and model determine the interpretation.

Advanced LearningUnknown is a meaningful category6 minutes

Unknown is a meaningful category

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced symbols and evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A blank, untested or uncertain phenotype should not be converted into unaffected merely to complete a pedigree. Add an explicit unknown symbol or note according to the legend. This preserves the difference between negative evidence and missing evidence. Model testing becomes more reliable when every constraint can be traced to an actual observation rather than a convenient assumption.

Keep unknown entries visible so every genotype constraint can be traced to an actual observation. Filling a blank as unaffected creates evidence that was never collected. A transparent pedigree separates directly recorded relationships and phenotypes from inferred allele assignments.

In the related worked example: The pedigree records relationships and phenotype observations. Genotypes are inferred under a model and should not be silently treated as directly measured. A convenient completed diagram must not convert missing information into negative evidence.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Unknown is a meaningful category — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Known unaffectedA recorded negative phenotype observation under the legend.
UnknownMissing, untested or uncertain information.

Limitation: A convenient completed diagram must not convert missing information into negative evidence.

Related worked example: Worked example: Symbols and evidence

Learn · Part 2

Autosomal hypotheses

alternative model
A different explanation that can be compared against the same observations.

Start with a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model. Fully penetrant means the genotype expected to cause the trait always shows it in this model. An affected person is aa. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, each must supply a. Both parents must therefore be Aa. Other unaffected relatives may be AA or Aa. A carrier has the recessive allele but does not show the recessive phenotype under this model.

Now test an autosomal dominant model with complete penetrance. An unaffected person is aa. An affected person may be AA or Aa. If an affected parent has an unaffected child, that parent must be able to supply a and so must be Aa. A trait in several generations may support dominance. Checking each parent–child genotype combination gives stronger evidence than relying on that pattern alone.

Keep more than one model when the pedigree cannot distinguish them. Real pedigrees may be complicated by incomplete penetrance, new mutations, few relatives or missing records. A classroom question should state when these are excluded. Write all possible genotypes instead of choosing one without evidence. Then name another observation that could test the model. A useful hypothesis explains the known relationships and predicts something you could check.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How family relationships and observed traits constrain an inheritance explanation.

Worked example

Two unaffected fictional parents have an affected child. Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model with accurate records, infer the parental and child genotypes.

  1. The affected child is aa under the stated model.
  2. Each parent must contribute a.
  3. Because both parents are unaffected in this model, each must also carry A, giving Aa × Aa.

The model supports two heterozygous parents and an aa child. It does not establish that every unaffected relative is AA or that this is the only possible real-world explanation.

Stop and check

Would the same family pattern fit a fully penetrant autosomal dominant model without new changes or record errors?

Compare your thinking

No. Under those strict assumptions, an affected child would need the relevant dominant allele from an affected parent. Relaxing assumptions can introduce other possibilities.

Advanced LearningAssumptions make exclusions conditional6 minutes

Assumptions make exclusions conditional

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced autosomal hypotheses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A pedigree can rule out a model only within the assumptions being tested. Incomplete penetrance, new mutation, uncertain parentage or inaccurate phenotype records can change the reasoning. List the classroom assumptions first so that an exclusion is precise. This does not mean every alternative is equally likely; it means that the evidence and scope of the conclusion remain visible.

State the assumptions before excluding a genotype or inheritance model. Under the classroom conditions the inference is precise, but changing penetrance or record accuracy changes the constraints. Keeping that boundary explicit is stronger than claiming that every alternative is equally likely.

In the related worked example: The model supports two heterozygous parents and an aa child. It does not establish that every unaffected relative is AA or that this is the only possible real-world explanation. A classroom exclusion is conditional on its stated model and observations.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Fully penetrant recessive modelTwo unaffected parents of an aa child are inferred Aa.

Learn · Part 3

Sex-linked hypotheses

For an X-linked recessive model, write alleles on the X chromosome explicitly. A carrier mother XᴬXᵃ and an unaffected father XᴬY can produce carrier or non-carrier daughters and affected or unaffected sons. Among sons, the affected probability is one-half. If the question also assumes equal probability of a son or daughter, the affected probability among all children is one-quarter.

An affected father's X passes to his daughters, while his Y passes to his sons in the usual XY model. A claimed direct father-to-son transfer of the same X-linked allele therefore conflicts with that transmission route. However, observing both an affected father and an affected son does not alone prove direct transfer: the son could have received an allele from his mother. Genotypes and family context are essential.

Compare X-linked, Y-linked and autosomal predictions across the whole fictional pedigree. A Y-linked model predicts transmission through the paternal Y line under its assumptions. A male-only pattern can also reflect expression differences or a small sample. State the alternative that remains possible and identify the relationship or molecular result that would distinguish it. Do not diagnose a real person's inheritance from a simplified diagram.

Worked example

A fictional pedigree shows an affected father and an affected son. Does this alone rule out an X-linked recessive explanation?

  1. In the stated X-linked model, the father supplies Y to his son rather than the father's X allele.
  2. Check whether the mother could supply the recessive X allele.
  3. Distinguish observed co-occurrence from direct father-to-son transmission of that allele.

The pair alone does not rule out X-linked recessive inheritance. An affected son could receive the allele from the mother; more family information is needed.

Stop and check

What is stronger evidence than simply noticing more affected males in a small pedigree?

Compare your thinking

Tracing which parental alleles can reach each descendant under explicit candidate models and checking the whole set of observations.

Advanced LearningSmall pedigrees can fit several models6 minutes

Small pedigrees can fit several models

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced sex-linked hypotheses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A pattern with few individuals may be compatible with both autosomal and sex-linked explanations. Preserve multiple possible genotype assignments when the observations do not distinguish them. A useful next observation targets a relationship where the models predict different possibilities. This teaches model comparison without turning a visual shortcut into an absolute rule.

Mitochondrial markers usually follow the human egg lineage and can support a different family pattern from nuclear loci. Missing relatives, uncertain parentage, new mutation and variable expression can obscure a small pedigree. Label genotype assignments as known, possible or excluded, and state what extra evidence would distinguish the remaining models.

Trace the actual allele route instead of inferring direct father-to-son X transmission from two matching phenotypes. Several inheritance models may fit a small pedigree. Choose another relative or observation where the remaining models make different predictions. A father-son phenotype pair alone does not rule out X-linked recessive inheritance.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Small pedigrees can fit several models — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Affected father and sonA relationship pattern requiring more family information.
Possible maternal contributionCan still explain the son's affected X in the stated recessive model.

Limitation: A father-son phenotype pair alone does not rule out X-linked recessive inheritance.

Learn · Part 4

Risk and information

A probability depends on the model and what is already known. In an Aa × Aa recessive cross, the carrier probability is one-half before any phenotype is given. If a child is known to be unaffected, remove aa from the possible outcomes. The carrier probability is then two-thirds. Explain the new denominator so the reader can see which question was answered.

Genetic information raises issues of privacy, consent and access. Imagine a service using anonymous examples to explain risk. A cheap automatic report could reach more people. A supported explanation might communicate uncertainty better. Accuracy is a question for evidence. The acceptable cost, access and privacy trade-offs also depend on what the people using the service value.

Compare social effects, cultural views, environmental resource use, ethical duties and economic costs. Then consider a concern about unwanted disclosure or unequal access. Revise the proposal and explain why. Keep the scientific limits in place even if the preferred option changes. A genetic probability does not decide what a person should choose or justify collecting classmates' private family information.

Worked example

An unaffected sibling of an aa child has two Aa parents under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model. Find the probability that this unaffected sibling is a carrier.

  1. Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, aA and aa with equal probability.
  2. Condition on the sibling being unaffected, removing the aa outcome.
  3. Among the three remaining equally likely outcomes, two are heterozygous.

The conditional carrier probability is 2/3. It differs from the unconditioned 1/2 probability of a heterozygote before the phenotype information is used.

Stop and check

Why is the denominator three rather than four after conditioning?

Compare your thinking

The unaffected observation excludes the aa category under the stated model. The remaining sample space contains three equally likely genotype outcomes.

Advanced LearningInformation updates the sample space6 minutes

Information updates the sample space

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced risk and information. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A probability is always tied to what is known and the model used. New phenotype or test information can remove or reweight possibilities, changing the calculation. State that information beside the answer rather than reporting a bare fraction. This classroom risk estimate applies to the fictional model and does not substitute for individualized genetic interpretation.

A genetic result can disclose information about relatives who did not choose testing. Adoption, donor conception and different cultural meanings of family make a biological pedigree only one limited representation. Use fictional cases and never collect classmates’ family health histories or DNA. Respectful interpretation keeps consent and uncertainty visible.

Evaluate the intended use of a test. Analytical validity concerns how accurately it detects the target; clinical meaning concerns its relationship to an outcome; utility concerns whether it helps a decision. A correct measurement can still be unhelpful or misunderstood. Consider uncertain findings, privacy, discrimination, access and community control of data as well as laboratory accuracy.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Information updates the sample space — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Before phenotype informationAa probability is 1/2 for Aa × Aa.
Given unaffected, full penetranceTwo Aa possibilities among three remaining equally weighted possibilities: 2/3.

Limitation: A conditional classroom risk fraction is not individualized genetic interpretation.

Lesson 12 · Chapter 17

Chromosome Mapping

How much chromosome information can recombinant offspring reveal?

Required time
120 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Classify offspring using parental phase, calculate recombination and construct a bounded three-locus map.

Before you begin

Gamete combinations can be parental or recombinant relative to a stated phase. Fractions need all relevant classes and the whole sample. Endpoint observations can miss internal events.

In the textbook

Chapter 17 · 601 #19–21

Open at p. 601

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

linked loci
Gene positions on the same chromosome; nearby positions tend to be inherited together because crossing over separates them less often.
recombinant
An offspring or gamete allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangements.
map unit
A linkage-map distance equal to a one-percent recombination frequency; also called a centimorgan.
gene order
The relative arrangement of loci along a chromosome inferred from recombination evidence or physical mapping.

test cross

First use · Core Vocabulary

linked loci

parental
Coming from a parent or original generation. In a linkage cross, parental combinations match allele arrangements present on the original parental chromosomes; distinguish that narrower use from recombinant combinations.

First use · Core Vocabulary

Learn · Part 1

Linkage and recombination

map unit
A linkage-map distance equal to a one-percent recombination frequency; also called a centimorgan.

Linked loci lie on the same chromosome. They may pass together more often than independent assortment predicts. Suppose one parental chromosome carries AB and the other carries ab. These are the parental combinations. Crossing over between the loci can make Ab and aB chromatids. These are recombinant combinations. Define the starting arrangement first. 'Parental' does not simply mean whichever trait happens to be most common.

A test cross can reveal the gametes of a heterozygous parent because the tester's contribution is known. Consider 40 AB, 40 ab, 10 Ab and 10 aB offspring. With the starting arrangement just given, AB and ab are parental; Ab and aB are recombinant. The excess of parental classes supports linkage under the model's conditions. Counts alone cannot always identify the classes without knowing the starting arrangement or having other evidence.

Linkage does not mean two alleles always stay together. Crossing over can separate them. Loci far apart on one chromosome can appear nearly independent in a two-point comparison. Other causes can also change the class counts: scoring errors, different survival rates and chance in small samples. Check these before calling every unequal ratio proof of linkage. Connect the starting chromosomes, possible gametes and observed offspring in your explanation.

Worked example

A test cross uses an AB/ab heterozygote and an ab/ab partner. Classify AB, ab, Ab and aB gamete-derived offspring types.

  1. Read AB and ab as the parental chromosome phase in the heterozygote.
  2. Identify AB and ab as parental combinations.
  3. Identify Ab and aB as recombinant combinations relative to that phase.

Parental types are AB and ab; recombinant types are Ab and aB. The same genotype letters written without phase would not supply all this information.

Stop and check

If the heterozygote instead has Ab/aB phase, do the recombinant labels stay the same?

Compare your thinking

No. The parental combinations change, so AB and ab become recombinant relative to that phase.

Advanced LearningPhase is biological information6 minutes

Phase is biological information

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced linkage and recombination. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A diploid genotype such as AaBb identifies the allele pairs but not which alleles share one homologue. Linked-locus predictions need that arrangement. Use a slash to separate homologues and keep each chromosome's allele combination together. This notation makes it clear why two individuals with the same genotype can produce different common gamete combinations when their parental phases differ.

Keep the alleles on each homologue together in the notation. AaBb alone names the two allele pairs but omits their arrangement. The omitted phase changes which gametes are common in a linked-locus model even though the unphased genotype letters look identical.

In the related worked example: Parental types are AB and ab; recombinant types are Ab and aB. The same genotype letters written without phase would not supply all this information. Linked-locus predictions need phase as well as genotype.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Phase is biological information — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
AB/ab phaseAB and ab are the parental combinations.
Ab/aB phaseAb and aB are the parental combinations.

Limitation: Linked-locus predictions need phase as well as genotype.

Related worked example: Worked example: Linkage and recombination

Learn · Part 2

Recombination frequency

recombinant count
The number of offspring classified as nonparental combinations in the stated cross.
total offspring
All offspring included in the comparison, including parental and recombinant classes.
multiple crossover
Two or more crossing-over events within the chromosome interval being studied.

Recombination frequency is the fraction of scored offspring that are recombinant in a suitable cross. First add the recombinant classes. Then divide by all offspring, including parental classes. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. In the 40, 40, 10 and 10 example, the last two classes are recombinant. Their total is 20 out of 100, so the frequency is 20%.

For short distances, 1% recombination estimates one map unit, also called one centimorgan. A 20% result therefore suggests about 20 map units under the stated model. This is a genetic distance estimate, not a count of DNA base pairs. It relies on correct class labels. The classes must also have comparable chances of surviving and being detected.

Check the denominator with a second example. There are 92 recombinants among 1,000 offspring. Divide 92 by 1,000 to get 0.092, then multiply by 100 to get 9.2%. Do not leave parental offspring out of the total. Sampling makes this an estimate. Multiple crossovers can also go undetected, making the observed recombinant fraction lower than the amount of exchange within the interval. State that limit when interpreting a map distance.

Worked example

A suitable test cross has 400 offspring: 160 AB, 160 ab, 40 Ab and 40 aB, with parental phase AB/ab. Calculate recombination frequency.

  1. Add both recombinant classes: 40 + 40 = 80.
  2. Divide by all offspring: 80/400 = 0.20.
  3. Report 20% recombination and, under the short-interval mapping approximation, about 20 map units.

The recombinant fraction is 0.20. Both reciprocal recombinant classes belong in the numerator and every scored offspring belongs in the denominator.

Stop and check

Why would 40/400 undercount recombination here?

Compare your thinking

It includes only one recombinant class. The other reciprocal recombinant class is also evidence of recombination.

Advanced LearningObserved fractions and model limits6 minutes

Observed fractions and model limits

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced recombination frequency. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Sampling can produce a recombinant fraction above 50%, especially in small samples. Report the observed value honestly rather than capping it. In the standard two-locus linkage interpretation, a value near 50% does not support a simple larger-than-50 map-distance estimate; distant linked loci and unlinked loci can look similar. More loci, larger samples or other evidence are needed to resolve the relationship.

Keep raw counts, excluded observations and denominators available beside a calculation. Describe the direction and size of any departure and compare plausible biological alternatives. A statistical difference does not by itself establish a mechanism or practical importance. Failure to detect a difference does not prove that no effect exists.

Include both reciprocal recombinant classes and preserve the denominator and exclusions. An observed fraction is a sample result, not a value to cap when it exceeds a familiar boundary. Interpretation near 50% requires care because different chromosome relationships can look alike. An observed fraction near 50% cannot distinguish distant linked from unlinked loci by itself.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Observed fractions and model limits — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Recombinant numerator40 Ab + 40 aB = 80 in the supplied example.
All scored offspring400, giving 80/400 = 0.20 or 20%.

Limitation: An observed fraction near 50% cannot distinguish distant linked from unlinked loci by itself.

Learn · Part 3

Gene order

pairwise distance
An estimated separation between two gene loci, expressed in a stated mapping unit.
gene order
The relative arrangement of loci along a chromosome inferred from recombination evidence or physical mapping.
reversed map
A map drawn in the opposite left-to-right direction while preserving the same gene order relationships and distances.

Pairwise distances can help infer the relative order of loci. Suppose the estimated distances are A–B=14, B–C=6 and A–C=20 map units. Because 14+6=20, B can lie between A and C in a simple short-distance map. Draw A–B–C with the intervals labelled. Reversing the entire drawing to C–B–A represents the same relative order.

Gene order and map orientation are different questions. Pairwise distances identify which locus is between the others in this example, but they do not establish which physical chromosome end must appear on the left of the page. Add a separate landmark if a fixed orientation is needed. Keep results from different crosses separate unless there is evidence that they describe the same loci and population.

Distances inferred from recombination are not always perfectly additive. Sampling and multiple crossovers can affect the estimates, particularly over longer intervals. More informative crosses can help identify hidden exchanges and refine order. Begin with the simplest order supported by the data, then state the limitation. A diagram should explain the calculation rather than merely presenting a memorized sequence of letters.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How recombination frequencies help infer gene order.

Worked example

Three loci have supplied short-interval distances A–B = 14, B–C = 6 and A–C = 20 map units. Construct a compatible order.

  1. Check that 14 + 6 = 20.
  2. Place B between A and C so the two shorter intervals span the longest interval.
  3. Accept the reversed orientation C—6—B—14—A as the same relative map.

A—14—B—6—C is compatible, as is its reverse. The arbitrary left-to-right direction is not a distinct biological result.

Stop and check

Would A—14—C—6—B fit the named distances?

Compare your thinking

No. It assigns the 14-unit interval to A–C even though the supplied A–C distance is 20. Labels must follow the stated pairs.

Advanced LearningAdditive maps are approximations6 minutes

Additive maps are approximations

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced gene order. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Short intervals can be combined into a useful local map, but pairwise recombinant fractions can underestimate larger distances when multiple exchanges restore parental combinations. A clean arithmetic fit does not remove that biological limit. State whether values are supplied map distances or raw recombination fractions. The distinction matters when extending a three-locus classroom map to longer chromosome regions.

A three-point test cross follows three loci in the same offspring. Under suitable survival and scoring assumptions, the largest reciprocal classes are often parental and the smallest often double crossovers. Compare allele arrangements: the locus that changes its association with the two outer markers identifies the middle gene. Count double crossovers in both adjacent intervals when estimating distances. Do not assign class roles from size alone if the assumptions fail.

Name whether the inputs are map distances or raw fractions before adding them. A tidy sum can support a local classroom order while leaving longer-interval biological limits intact. In a suitable three-point cross, double crossovers contribute to both adjacent intervals. Additive local maps are approximations, not universal conversions of raw fractions.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Additive maps are approximations — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Supplied short distances14 + 6 = 20 supports A—B—C or its reverse.
Raw pairwise recombinant fractionCan miss multiple exchanges that restore parental combinations.

Learn · Part 4

Limits of linkage estimates

fifty-percent ceiling
The maximum expected recombinant fraction between two loci under the standard mapping model; larger map distances may be obscured by multiple crossovers.

In a suitable two-locus test cross, independent assortment predicts half recombinant offspring. Loci on different chromosomes can give this pattern. Loci far apart on the same chromosome can also approach it because repeated exchanges reshuffle their combinations. A result near 50% therefore leaves two possibilities. It does not, by itself, tell you whether the loci are on the same chromosome.

Consider two markers at the ends of an interval. An even number of exchanges can restore their original combination. A two-point count may score that product as parental despite exchange inside the interval. This is why the count can underestimate longer map distances. A sample may fluctuate above 50%. Do not interpret that value as a reliable two-point distance beyond the 50% ceiling.

Before interpreting a result near the ceiling, check class labels, sample size, survival and scoring. A 49% result is close to the independent expectation, but a larger sample gives a more precise estimate than a small one. Keep three claims separate: the measured count, the map estimate under its assumptions and the physical chromosome location. A rounded percentage cannot give an exact physical position. Further evidence is needed to decide between the possible locations.

Worked example

Two loci yield about 50% recombinant offspring in a large suitable test cross. Compare two explanations.

  1. One possibility is that the loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
  2. Another is that they are far apart on the same chromosome, with multiple exchanges obscuring linkage in the two-locus result.
  3. Identify additional linked markers or other evidence that could distinguish the alternatives.

The result does not uniquely establish that the loci are on different chromosomes. About 50% is compatible with both explanations in the standard model.

Stop and check

Can a two-locus recombinant fraction reveal every crossover that occurred between those loci?

Compare your thinking

No. Multiple exchanges can restore the parental endpoint combination, so endpoint scoring can miss events within the interval.

Advanced LearningMap distance and physical distance answer different questions6 minutes

Map distance and physical distance answer different questions

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced limits of linkage estimates. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A genetic map summarizes recombination relationships, while a physical map locates DNA regions by sequence distance. Recombination rates vary across regions and biological contexts, so one map unit is not a universal fixed number of base pairs. Use the map suited to the question and avoid converting between the two with an invented constant.

Select the map that answers the question. Recombination rates vary across regions, so equal genetic intervals need not span equal sequence lengths. A near-50% result leaves more than one chromosome-location explanation possible in the standard two-locus model.

In the related worked example: The result does not uniquely establish that the loci are on different chromosomes. About 50% is compatible with both explanations in the standard model. There is no universal fixed number of base pairs per map unit.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Map distance and physical distance answer different questions — comparison

Genetic distanceSummarizes recombination relationships.
Physical distanceCounts sequence separation in base pairs.

Limitation: There is no universal fixed number of base pairs per map unit.

Illustrated walkthrough

1. Linkage and recombination

A test cross uses an AB/ab heterozygote and an ab/ab partner. Classify AB, ab, Ab and aB gamete-derived offspring types.

  1. Read AB and ab as the parental chromosome phase in the heterozygote.
  2. Identify AB and ab as parental combinations.
  3. Identify Ab and aB as recombinant combinations relative to that phase.

Parental types are AB and ab; recombinant types are Ab and aB. The same genotype letters written without phase would not supply all this information.

2. Recombination frequency

A suitable test cross has 400 offspring: 160 AB, 160 ab, 40 Ab and 40 aB, with parental phase AB/ab. Calculate recombination frequency.

  1. Add both recombinant classes: 40 + 40 = 80.
  2. Divide by all offspring: 80/400 = 0.20.
  3. Report 20% recombination and, under the short-interval mapping approximation, about 20 map units.

The recombinant fraction is 0.20. Both reciprocal recombinant classes belong in the numerator and every scored offspring belongs in the denominator.

3. Gene order

Three loci have supplied short-interval distances A–B = 14, B–C = 6 and A–C = 20 map units. Construct a compatible order.

  1. Check that 14 + 6 = 20.
  2. Place B between A and C so the two shorter intervals span the longest interval.
  3. Accept the reversed orientation C—6—B—14—A as the same relative map.

A—14—B—6—C is compatible, as is its reverse. The arbitrary left-to-right direction is not a distinct biological result.

4. Limits of linkage estimates

Two loci yield about 50% recombinant offspring in a large suitable test cross. Compare two explanations.

  1. One possibility is that the loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
  2. Another is that they are far apart on the same chromosome, with multiple exchanges obscuring linkage in the two-locus result.
  3. Identify additional linked markers or other evidence that could distinguish the alternatives.

The result does not uniquely establish that the loci are on different chromosomes. About 50% is compatible with both explanations in the standard model.

Checkpoint

Does about 50% recombination prove the loci are on different chromosomes?

Learn · Part 1

Evidence for hereditary material

transformation
Uptake and expression of external genetic material by a cell; in biotechnology it often introduces a plasmid into bacteria.
Franklin
Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray diffraction work provided important structural evidence for DNA.
Watson
James Watson, who worked with Francis Crick on a model of DNA structure informed by experimental evidence.
Crick
Francis Crick, who worked with James Watson on a model of DNA structure informed by experimental evidence.
X-ray diffraction
A method that infers molecular structure from the pattern produced when X-rays scatter through an ordered sample.
Chargaff
Erwin Chargaff, whose measurements established important base-composition relationships in DNA.
complementary
Able to match through the specified base-pairing relationships, such as A–T and G–C in DNA.

Experiments helped identify the material that carries inherited information. In Griffith's bacterial work, live non-virulent bacteria gained a heritable virulent trait when mixed with heat-killed virulent bacteria. Transformation is a change linked to uptake of external genetic material. The result showed that something from the killed cells could alter the living lineage. It did not yet identify that substance.

Avery and colleagues treated a transforming preparation in different ways. Destroying its DNA removed transforming activity in the assay. Treatments aimed at other components did not have the same effect. This supported a role for DNA. The conclusion depended on the controls and the measured change. Finding DNA in a cell alone would not have established that role.

Hershey and Chase studied viruses that infect bacteria. They used different radioactive labels linked to viral DNA and protein, then separated parts of the mixture. The DNA label was more closely linked with infected cells and the production process than most external protein. These studies together supported DNA as hereditary material in the tested systems. They did not alone reveal every feature of its structure.

Watch and make sense of it

Watch for: How an experiment distinguishes DNA from protein as hereditary material.

Worked example

Compare what bacterial transformation, selective enzyme treatment and phage labelling contributed to identifying hereditary material.

  1. Transformation showed that material from one bacterial preparation could produce a heritable change in another.
  2. Experiments that selectively disrupted candidate molecules helped test which material was needed for transformation.
  3. Phage labelling distinguished the behaviour of DNA-associated and protein-associated labels during infection.

The studies supplied different lines of evidence supporting DNA's hereditary role in the tested systems. One result should not be credited with directly proving every feature of DNA structure or every inheritance mechanism.

Stop and check

Did the original transformation observation by itself identify the double-helical structure of DNA?

Compare your thinking

No. It demonstrated a transferable heritable effect. Identifying the molecule and determining its structure required additional evidence.

Advanced LearningConverging evidence narrows alternatives6 minutes

Converging evidence narrows alternatives

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced evidence for hereditary material. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A stronger explanation can arise when different methods address different weaknesses in a hypothesis. Selective treatments test necessity in one preparation; labelled components test movement in another system. Compare the controls and limitations of each instead of treating scientific history as a list of isolated names. The conclusion gains strength from the relationship among experiments, not simply from the number of experiments cited.

Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty investigated the transforming preparation together. Their selective treatments tested its chemical identity. This question differed from the later structural question answered using base composition, diffraction and model building; credit should preserve those different contributions.

Compare each method's controls and inferential limits before combining its results. Different experiments can weaken different alternatives, making their agreement more informative than a list of names. A contribution to chemical identity should not be credited with independently establishing every structural feature. Evidence in tested systems does not prove every inheritance mechanism.

Learn · Part 2

Nucleotides and direction

phosphate
A chemical group in the nucleic-acid backbone that contributes to its negative charge and connections between sugars.
deoxyribose
The five-carbon sugar found in DNA nucleotides.
5-prime
The end/direction associated with the sugar's 5′ carbon in a nucleic-acid strand.
3-prime
The end/direction associated with the sugar's 3′ carbon; polymerases extend a strand at its available 3′ hydroxyl.
antiparallel
Describes DNA strands running in opposite 5-prime-to-3-prime directions.
hydrogen bond
A noncovalent interaction contributing to the specificity and stability of paired DNA bases.
backbone
The connected sugar-phosphate chain of a nucleic-acid strand.
5-prime to 3-prime
The direction in which a new DNA or RNA strand is extended by adding nucleotides to its 3′ end.
base pairing
Specific hydrogen-bond pairing of adenine with thymine or uracil and guanine with cytosine.
direction
The stated orientation of a process or strand; nucleic-acid answers require 5′ and 3′ labels.

A DNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine. The bases are abbreviated A, T, G and C. Nucleotides join into a strand through a sugar–phosphate backbone. Base order carries sequence information, while the backbone provides the repeated chemical structure connecting the units.

The sugar's carbon positions help define strand direction. The 5′ and 3′ labels identify different chemical ends, not left and right as permanent page positions. New DNA synthesis extends a strand at its 3′ end. A strand drawn left-to-right can therefore run either 5′→3′ or 3′→5′ depending on the labels. Always read those labels before writing a complement or predicting synthesis.

Separate sequence from orientation. For 5′-ATGC-3′, the aligned complementary strand is 3′-TACG-5′. If that complementary strand is rewritten in its own 5′→3′ direction, it becomes 5′-GCAT-3′. Complementing bases and reversing the display are different operations. A sequence without direction labels may be ambiguous for a molecular task, so state the assumption rather than silently inventing an orientation.

Worked example

A diagram shows a phosphate, deoxyribose sugar and nitrogenous base. Identify the nucleotide and explain what 5′ and 3′ labels refer to.

  1. Group the three components as one DNA nucleotide.
  2. Locate the sugar's numbered carbon positions used to name the strand ends.
  3. Use those ends to orient the sugar–phosphate backbone rather than assigning direction from the page's left edge alone.

A nucleotide contains sugar, phosphate and base. The 5′ and 3′ labels describe chemical orientation, so a sequence must carry direction labels when the diagram's orientation is ambiguous.

Stop and check

Does turning the page around change a strand's chemical 5′ and 3′ ends?

Compare your thinking

No. Page orientation changes the view, not the molecule's polarity. Keep the end labels attached to the strand.

Advanced LearningThe backbone and base order carry different information6 minutes

The backbone and base order carry different information

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced nucleotides and direction. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The repeating backbone provides a directional framework, while the sequence of bases varies along it. A diagram that shows only letters may hide the backbone, but the direction remains essential for copying and expression. Reintroduce a small sugar–phosphate key when an orientation error appears. This links the abstract sequence notation back to the chemical structure it represents.

A phosphodiester bond is the covalent linkage joining successive sugars through phosphate in the backbone. The base ratios measured by Chargaff constrain pairing in double-stranded DNA; they do not alone prove helical shape or strand orientation. Those conclusions require additional structural evidence.

Reconnect letter notation to the nucleotide structure when direction becomes unclear. Complementary bases do not remove the backbone's orientation. Composition relationships constrain pairing, but additional structural evidence is needed to infer strand arrangement and shape. Base ratios alone do not prove helicity or orientation.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 3

Structural evidence

Chargaff measured base amounts in double-stranded DNA. A was roughly equal to T, and G to C. Different organisms could have different total base compositions while keeping those paired relationships. A model had to explain both findings. Randomly pairing any base with any other would not readily explain why the same base-ratio rules kept appearing across samples.

Rosalind Franklin used X-ray diffraction to study DNA. The recorded pattern constrained its helical form and dimensions. It was evidence to interpret, not a labelled photograph of every atom. Maurice Wilkins and other researchers also supplied evidence. Name what each method showed. Giving credit to specific measurements is more accurate than treating the whole discovery as the work of one image or person.

Watson and Crick built a double-helix model using chemical and structural evidence. It had to fit the base ratios, measured width and other constraints together. The paired strands also suggested a way to copy information. That was a prediction to test with further work. Science gains strength when different methods support the same account and can expose parts that need revision.

Worked example

A double-stranded DNA sample has 30% adenine. Use the stated complementary-pairing model to infer the other base percentages and connect the result to structural evidence.

  1. Pair adenine with thymine, giving 30% thymine.
  2. Subtract 60% from the total, leaving 40% for guanine and cytosine together.
  3. Split that remainder equally: 20% each, while recognizing that composition alone does not specify the full three-dimensional structure.

T = 30%, G = 20% and C = 20% for this double-stranded sample. Base relationships constrain a model; diffraction evidence and chemical reasoning supplied additional structural constraints.

Stop and check

Would equal A and T percentages alone establish the exact base sequence?

Compare your thinking

No. Many sequences can share the same composition. Percentages describe totals, not order.

Advanced LearningCredit follows the evidence contributed6 minutes

Credit follows the evidence contributed

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced structural evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Chargaff's composition relationships, Franklin's and Wilkins's diffraction work, and Watson and Crick's model building contributed different evidence and reasoning to the DNA structure account. An accurate explanation names what each contribution constrained rather than assigning the entire result to one technique. Historical models should also be evaluated by how well they explain the evidence available and the predictions they make.

Photograph 51 was made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King’s College London in 1952. Its B-form diffraction pattern helped constrain helical structure. Wilkins showed it to Watson without Franklin’s knowledge. Explaining both the experimental contribution and how evidence was shared preserves the historical question of access and credit. It remains a diffraction pattern requiring interpretation, not a direct molecular photograph.

For the supplied double-stranded sample, 30% A requires 30% T; the remaining 40% is split equally between G and C. Explain what that calculation constrains before adding the distinct contribution of diffraction and chemical reasoning. A diffraction pattern requires interpretation and is not a direct molecular photograph.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Credit follows the evidence contributed — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Base compositionConstrains complementary-pairing proportions.
Diffraction and model buildingAdd structural constraints and a proposed arrangement.

Limitation: A diffraction pattern requires interpretation and is not a direct molecular photograph.

Learn · Part 4

The double helix

template
A strand or pattern used to specify a complementary product.
complementarity
Specific hydrogen-bond pairing of adenine with thymine or uracil and guanine with cytosine.

The DNA double helix contains two complementary, antiparallel strands. Complementary means that A pairs with T and G pairs with C in the usual DNA model. Antiparallel means that the two backbones run in opposite chemical directions. If one strand is labelled 5′→3′ across the page, its aligned partner is labelled 3′→5′.

Hydrogen bonds connect complementary bases between strands, while covalent bonds form the sugar–phosphate backbone along each strand. These are different bond relationships. Separating the strands for copying mainly disrupts the interactions between them; it does not require cutting the backbone at every nucleotide. The external backbone and internal base arrangement help explain both molecular stability and access to sequence information.

Complementarity permits a strand to act as a template for another. Knowing one oriented sequence predicts its paired sequence under the model. This is the basis for reliable copying and for reading many molecular experiments. A diagram that shows both strands running in the same direction loses an essential constraint. Label the bases, backbones and ends, then test the drawing with a short written sequence.

Worked example

Write the strand complementary to 5′-ATGC-3′ first as aligned beneath it, then separately in 5′→3′ notation.

  1. Pair A with T and G with C while keeping opposite strand directions.
  2. The aligned complement is 3′-TACG-5′.
  3. Reverse its written order to express that complementary strand from 5′ to 3′: 5′-GCAT-3′.

The aligned complement and the reverse-complement notation describe the same strand in different written directions. Both pairing and orientation must be correct.

Stop and check

Is 5′-TACG-3′ the correctly oriented aligned complement of 5′-ATGC-3′?

Compare your thinking

No. The paired complement runs antiparallel: 3′-TACG-5′. Writing it 5′→3′ requires reversing the base order.

1. Evidence for hereditary material

Compare what bacterial transformation, selective enzyme treatment and phage labelling contributed to identifying hereditary material.

  2. Experiments that selectively disrupted candidate molecules helped test which material was needed for transformation.
  3. Phage labelling distinguished the behaviour of DNA-associated and protein-associated labels during infection.

The studies supplied different lines of evidence supporting DNA's hereditary role in the tested systems. One result should not be credited with directly proving every feature of DNA structure or every inheritance mechanism.

  2. Locate the sugar's numbered carbon positions used to name the strand ends.

A nucleotide contains sugar, phosphate and base. The 5′ and 3′ labels describe chemical orientation, so a sequence must carry direction labels when the diagram's orientation is ambiguous.

T = 30%, G = 20% and C = 20% for this double-stranded sample. Base relationships constrain a model; diffraction evidence and chemical reasoning supplied additional structural constraints.

The aligned complement and the reverse-complement notation describe the same strand in different written directions. Both pairing and orientation must be correct.

DNA Replication

How can both strands be copied when their directions are opposite?

Required time
105 minutes
Advanced Learning

Learning goal

Trace semiconservative copying, enzyme roles and leading/lagging synthesis, then compare density-model predictions.

Before you begin

DNA strands are complementary and antiparallel. New strands grow from a suitable end. Strand age, chemical direction and fork movement need separate labels.

Learn · Part 1

Semiconservative replication

parental strand
An original DNA strand present before the replication event being followed.
daughter strand
A newly synthesized DNA strand produced during replication.
template strand
The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to synthesize a complementary RNA transcript.

In semiconservative replication, each new DNA double helix has one old strand and one newly made strand. The old strands separate. Each acts as a template, and new bases pair with its bases. Trace one old strand into each new molecule. This differs from a model that keeps both old strands together and makes a second molecule from two entirely new strands.

Test the models using labels. Begin with heavy-labelled DNA, then let it copy using light material. After one round, the semiconservative model predicts hybrid molecules: one heavy strand paired with one light strand. After two rounds, it predicts both hybrid and fully light molecules. The conservative model instead predicts separate heavy and light molecules after the first round. These different predictions can be compared with measured bands.

Meselson and Stahl used density labels to test replication in bacteria. Their results supported the semiconservative model. The experiment measured where labelled DNA formed bands; it did not film every base being copied. Match each band to the molecules predicted by a model. Supporting semiconservative copying does not mean copying has no errors. Nor does it show that every organism uses exactly the same helper proteins.

Worked example

Begin with one DNA duplex whose two strands are labelled old. Follow two rounds of semiconservative replication using new unlabelled nucleotides.

  1. After the first round, form two duplexes, each with one old strand and one new strand.
  2. Separate each duplex's strands for the second round and use each as a template.
  3. Count four duplexes: two retain one original old strand, while two contain only strands made after the start.

After two rounds, two of four duplexes contain an original old strand. No duplex retains both original strands paired together in this model.

Stop and check

Does semiconservative mean that each new DNA strand is half old nucleotides and half new nucleotides?

Compare your thinking

No. Each daughter duplex contains a pre-existing template strand paired with a newly synthesized strand after one round.

Advanced LearningTrack strands instead of colours alone6 minutes

Track strands instead of colours alone

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced semiconservative replication. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A colour diagram becomes confusing if “old” changes meaning between rounds. Label the original strands individually and label each later synthesis round separately. Then count which duplexes retain an original strand and which merely contain a strand from the preceding round. This makes the conservation claim precise and avoids confusing the age of a whole duplex with the age of its two strands.

Replication starts at origins and advances through forks. In addition to strand separation, proteins stabilize exposed single strands and enzymes manage twisting strain ahead of the fork. These supporting actions make templates available; the density-label experiment tests the distribution of old and new strands, not each accessory protein’s action.

After two rounds, four duplexes exist but only two contain an original strand. Label each original individually and later strands by synthesis round so the word old cannot silently change meaning. Strand conservation differs from assigning one age to an entire duplex. Density-labelling evidence does not test every accessory protein's action.

Learn · Part 2

Enzymes and direction

helicase
An enzyme that separates paired DNA strands at a replication fork.
primer
A short nucleic-acid strand providing a free 3-prime end for polymerase extension and helping define the copied region.
DNA polymerase
An enzyme that builds DNA by adding complementary nucleotides to an existing 3-prime end and often proofreads the product.
ligase
An enzyme that seals breaks in a DNA sugar-phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds.
proofreading
Detection and correction of some newly incorporated nucleotide errors during DNA replication.
initiation
The assembly and starting stage of a process, such as translation at an appropriate start site.
protein function
The biological role of a protein, depending on its structure, location, interactions and regulation.

Helicase helps unwind the DNA double helix by separating the paired strands. A primer provides an initial short nucleic-acid segment with an available 3′ end. DNA polymerase extends that end by adding complementary DNA nucleotides. The new strand grows 5′→3′ while the template is read in the opposite direction. These roles are distinct: opening the template does not itself provide the starting point needed by polymerase.

If a model shows open templates but no new DNA beginning at expected sites, missing or ineffective primers are one possible explanation. Other evidence is needed to distinguish that from a polymerase or substrate problem. Match each observation to the process directly measured. A visible replication opening is evidence of strand separation, not proof that synthesis has proceeded normally.

Describe enzyme actions precisely. Helicase does not cut the sugar–phosphate backbone into individual bases. Polymerase adds nucleotides to an existing strand end rather than constructing DNA 3′→5′. Primer removal and replacement must also be coordinated before the backbone is fully continuous. Using a source–action–product sequence makes the mechanism clearer than listing enzyme names without explaining their order and dependence.

Worked example

A template is oriented 3′→5′ along the direction a polymerase is reading. State the direction of new DNA synthesis and the role of a primer.

  1. Use complementary pairing to choose the next base.
  2. Add nucleotides to the available 3′ end of the growing new strand.
  3. Recognize that DNA polymerase extends a suitable primer rather than starting a new strand without that initial end.

The new strand grows 5′→3′ while the template is read 3′→5′. Primers provide a starting end for extension in the replication model.

Stop and check

Does a lagging-strand fragment grow 3′→5′ because it is called lagging?

Compare your thinking

No. Its new DNA also grows 5′→3′. The discontinuous arrangement resolves the opposite template orientation.

Advanced LearningRoles cooperate at a fork6 minutes

Roles cooperate at a fork

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced enzymes and direction. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Helicase-related unwinding, primer formation, polymerase extension and later joining contribute different functions. A missing role can interrupt replication even when the others are present. To diagnose a fictional model failure, identify the observed intermediate: no exposed template, no initiated fragment, incomplete extension or unjoined segments. This is more informative than attributing every replication problem to a generic “enzyme failure.”

Primase makes a short RNA primer with an available 3′ hydroxyl group, the chemical end from which DNA polymerase can extend. Complementary nucleotide selection and enzyme shape support copying accuracy. Primer production, DNA extension and later RNA replacement are separate actions. Polymerase cannot start an ordinary new DNA strand without an appropriate existing end.

Use the observed intermediate to identify the missing role in a fictional fork. Exposed template without initiated fragments suggests a different question from fragments that remain unjoined. Separating initiation, extension and joining is more informative than attributing every failure to one generic enzyme problem. A simplified fork does not represent all supporting proteins or guarantee perfect copying.
