Learn · Part 3

Leading and lagging synthesis

replication fork
The Y-shaped region where parental DNA strands separate and new DNA strands are synthesized.
leading strand
The new DNA strand synthesized continuously toward an advancing replication fork.
lagging strand
The new DNA strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments away from each advancing replication fork.
Okazaki fragment
A short DNA segment synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand and later joined by DNA ligase.

A replication fork is the region where parental strands are separating and new strands are being made. Because the templates are antiparallel but polymerase extends only 5′→3′, the two new strands follow different patterns relative to fork movement. Leading-strand synthesis can proceed continuously toward the advancing fork on its template.

Lagging-strand synthesis proceeds in short stretches called Okazaki fragments. As more template becomes available, another primer allows synthesis of another fragment, still in the 5′→3′ direction. Each fragment grows away from the current fork region. The cell coordinates removal or processing of primers, replacement with suitable DNA and joining of the remaining backbone breaks.

DNA ligase seals a backbone nick by forming the missing covalent linkage when suitable adjacent ends are available. It does not invent a missing long sequence or choose complementary bases in place of polymerase. A model showing completed fragments with unsealed junctions points to a joining problem. Label both template directions and each new fragment's direction; the lagging strand is discontinuous, not chemically synthesized backward.

Worked example

At a fork moving right, the upper template runs 3′→5′ from left to right and the lower template runs 5′→3′. Identify the continuous new-strand direction and the fragment direction.

  1. On the upper template, new DNA can grow 5′→3′ toward the moving fork.
  2. On the lower template, each new fragment still grows 5′→3′ but away from the fork over the locally exposed region.
  3. Repeated initiation allows fragments to be produced as more template is exposed.

The upper-template product is leading in this defined fork view; the lower-template product is lagging. Both products use 5′→3′ synthesis, with different arrangements relative to fork movement.

Stop and check

Can leading and lagging be assigned reliably without knowing fork direction and template polarity?

Compare your thinking

No. Their labels describe the relationship among those features. Page position alone is insufficient.

Advanced LearningTwo forks reverse the local labels6 minutes

Two forks reverse the local labels

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced leading and lagging synthesis. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Replication can proceed from an origin in two directions. A parental strand serving as a leading template at one fork can serve as a lagging template at the other. This does not change the strand's chemical polarity. Draw each fork's movement arrow separately before assigning labels. The local geometry explains the apparent reversal without inventing a polymerase that synthesizes in the opposite chemical direction.

Mark the two movement arrows before labelling leading and lagging templates. Chemical polarity remains fixed while the local fork geometry changes. Both products still grow 5′ to 3′, so the apparent reversal does not require an oppositely acting polymerase.

In the related worked example: The upper-template product is leading in this defined fork view; the lower-template product is lagging. Both products use 5′→3′ synthesis, with different arrangements relative to fork movement. Leading and lagging are local fork relationships, not permanent names for whole parental strands.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Two forks reverse the local labels — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Leading at one forkContinuous synthesis follows that fork's movement.
Lagging at the opposite forkThe same parental strand can require discontinuous synthesis there.

Limitation: Leading and lagging are local fork relationships, not permanent names for whole parental strands.

Learn · Part 4

Replication evidence

experimental prediction
A stated expected result that would follow if a proposed explanation and its assumptions were correct.

A low amount of copied DNA can have several causes. A primer may be missing, polymerase may not work or ligase may fail. Look for the stage where copying stopped. Exposed templates with no new starts suggest a different problem from many new fragments whose joins remain unsealed. Compare these patterns before choosing a cause from the total DNA amount alone.

Some polymerases can proofread: they detect and correct certain base mismatches as DNA is made. Other repair systems also help protect DNA. Together, these processes reduce errors, but they do not make copying perfect. A lasting change in genetic material is a mutation. Whether a copying error becomes a lasting change depends on repair, later copying and the cell in which it occurs.

Suppose a model without proofreading has more mismatches. You can conclude that copying was less accurate under the tested conditions. You cannot yet predict a whole-organism trait. The affected sequence, cell lineage, repair and gene expression all matter. Build the explanation in steps: name the measurement, connect it to the enzyme's job, then identify evidence that could link the DNA error to a change in function.

Watch and make sense of it

Worked example

In a simplified density-labelling experiment, DNA begins heavy and is then copied in light medium. Compare semiconservative predictions after one and two rounds.

  1. After one round, predict duplexes with one heavy original strand and one light new strand, producing an intermediate-density class.
  2. After two rounds, predict half intermediate and half light duplexes.
  3. Compare this sequence with alternative models rather than treating one intermediate result as the entire test.

The two-round pattern supports the semiconservative model under the experiment's conditions. The first round alone does not distinguish every possible alternative.

Why is the second round informative when comparing semiconservative and dispersive models?

Compare your thinking

Their predictions diverge: semiconservative replication produces separate light and intermediate duplex classes, while the simple dispersive model retains mixed material within every duplex.

Advanced LearningPredictions should precede interpretation6 minutes

Predictions should precede interpretation

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced replication evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Write each model's expected pattern before examining the result. Otherwise it is easy to modify a story after seeing the data without making a distinct testable prediction. The classic density experiment is useful because several candidate mechanisms make different patterns across rounds. A good explanation identifies the discriminating observation and the controls needed for interpreting the density classes.

A lasting change can be copied through descendants of a body cell without entering offspring. Transmission to offspring needs a route through a gamete lineage. Whether a change is harmful, neutral or useful depends on its location, expression and environment; a copying error is not automatically a disease.

Write the predicted density classes for each candidate mechanism before interpreting the observed pattern. The discriminating power comes from different predictions across rounds, not merely from fitting a story afterward. Controls must support the meaning assigned to each density class. The first round alone does not distinguish every possible alternative.

Learn · Part 1

Selecting a template

promoter
A DNA region where transcription machinery assembles to initiate transcription of a gene.
coding strand
The DNA strand whose sequence matches the RNA transcript except that DNA has thymine where RNA has uracil.
RNA polymerase
An enzyme that uses a DNA template to synthesize a complementary RNA molecule.

Transcription produces RNA using one DNA strand as a template. A promoter is a DNA region involved in positioning and regulating the transcription machinery. RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′. Which strand serves as the template depends on the gene's orientation and regulatory arrangement, rather than on a permanent label applying to an entire chromosome.

The coding strand has the same base order as the RNA for the region being transcribed, except that RNA uses U where DNA has T. The coding strand is therefore not the strand directly base-paired to the growing RNA. For coding DNA 5′-ATG GAA-3′, the aligned template is 3′-TAC CTT-5′ and the RNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′.

Gene presence and gene activity are different observations. A gene's DNA sequence can be present while little transcript is produced because initiation or regulation differs. Conversely, abundant transcript does not prove abundant functional protein. Identify what the method measures and locate it in the DNA→RNA→protein relationship. Use both strand labels and direction before writing a sequence answer.

Worked example

A gene's coding strand is 5′-ATG GAA TTT TAA-3′. Identify the aligned template and the corresponding RNA sequence in the stated orientation.

  1. Pair an antiparallel template: 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′.
  2. Read that template 3′→5′.
  3. Build RNA 5′→3′ using complementary bases, with U in place of T.

The RNA is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. It matches the coding strand's base order except for U replacing T.

Stop and check

Does coding strand mean it is the strand being read as the template for this transcript?

Compare your thinking

No. For the defined gene, the template is the complementary strand read by RNA polymerase. The coding strand corresponds to the RNA sequence.

Advanced LearningOne chromosome contains genes in both orientations6 minutes

One chromosome contains genes in both orientations

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced selecting a template. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Different genes can use different strands as templates. Calling one entire chromosome strand “the template” without naming a gene can therefore mislead. Use a local gene arrow and explicit end labels to identify the relevant transcription direction. The same double helix can support transcripts in different regions and orientations while each individual RNA is still synthesized 5′→3′.

Attach the template label to a local gene arrow rather than the entire chromosome strand. Another gene can use the opposite strand while maintaining the same chemical synthesis direction. For the supplied coding sequence, the transcript remains 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′.

In the related worked example: The RNA is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. It matches the coding strand's base order except for U replacing T. Template identity is gene-specific; a whole chromosome need not use one strand for every gene.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 2

Making RNA

uracil
The RNA base that pairs with adenine in the usual transcription model.
mRNA
An RNA molecule carrying a coding sequence from DNA transcription to a ribosome for translation.
amino acid
One of the small chemical building blocks joined into a protein chain.

RNA is a nucleic acid containing ribose sugar and the bases A, U, G and C. Uracil, abbreviated U, pairs with A in the relevant transcription relationship. RNA polymerase builds a complementary RNA strand as it follows the DNA template. The growing transcript is synthesized 5′→3′ and separates from the template as transcription progresses.

Given template DNA 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′, complementary RNA is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. Read each paired base and retain the opposite directions. If the supplied template is instead written 5′→3′, reverse the displayed order before expressing the resulting RNA in its own 5′→3′ direction. A direction label changes the task; it is not decorative punctuation.

Transcription produces an RNA molecule rather than directly assembling amino acids. Some RNAs carry a message used in translation, while others have structural or functional roles. In a sequence task, identify whether the source gives coding DNA, template DNA or RNA before applying base-pair rules. An answer that complements the coding strand and calls that product mRNA has confused the two DNA roles.

Worked example

Transcribe the template 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′ into RNA and state the base-pairing choices.

  1. Read the template in its given 3′→5′ direction.
  2. Pair T with A, A with U, C with G and G with C in RNA.
  3. Write the resulting strand 5′→3′ and retain the complete sequence.

The transcript is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. Transcription creates RNA; the amino-acid sequence is a separate later interpretation.

Stop and check

Should an RNA transcript contain thymine because the DNA template contains thymine?

Compare your thinking

No. The standard RNA alphabet uses uracil. Template T pairs with RNA A, while template A pairs with RNA U.

Advanced LearningThe chosen start and end define the transcript6 minutes

The chosen start and end define the transcript

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced making rna. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A short classroom sequence supplies a particular region to transcribe. In a cell, regulatory features help determine where transcription begins and ends. Do not assume that every displayed DNA segment is a complete gene or that every transcript begins at the first letter printed on a worksheet. Name the supplied boundary and leave unprovided upstream or downstream sequence unknown.

Transcribe only the defined template region and label the output as RNA. The first printed letter is not evidence that an entire real transcript begins there. Unknown upstream and downstream material must remain unknown rather than being added to complete a plausible-looking gene.

In the related worked example: The transcript is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. Transcription creates RNA; the amino-acid sequence is a separate later interpretation. A short supplied segment need not be a complete gene or transcript.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

The chosen start and end define the transcript — comparison

Worksheet boundaryDefines the exact segment supplied for the exercise.
Cellular transcript boundaryDepends on the gene's regulatory start and end context.

Learn · Part 3

Processing and expression

intron
A transcribed segment removed from a pre-mRNA during RNA splicing.
exon
A transcript segment retained in a mature RNA after splicing, though not every exon segment is protein-coding.
splicing
Removal of introns and joining of exons from a pre-mRNA transcript.
ribosome
An RNA-protein complex that reads mRNA codons and catalyzes polypeptide synthesis.
termination
The ending stage of a process, such as release of a polypeptide at a stop codon.
polypeptide
A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds that can fold or combine to form a functional protein.
somatic mutation
A mutation arising in a non-gamete cell lineage that can affect descendant cells but is usually not inherited by offspring.

A primary RNA transcript is the initial product made from a gene. In many eukaryotic protein-coding genes, it contains regions that will be treated differently during processing. Introns are removed from the transcript, while exons are retained and joined through splicing. An exon is a retained segment; not every nucleotide within an exon must encode an amino acid.

Processed messenger RNA, or mRNA, can carry the information used for protein synthesis. Additional processing, including end modifications, supports handling and function of many eukaryotic messages. Different splicing patterns can sometimes produce distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region. For example, two messages may share exons 1 and 3 while differing in whether exon 2 is retained.

Different tissues generally share the same inherited genome but use different genes and processing patterns. Brain and liver cells can therefore function differently without requiring entirely different inherited chromosome sets. Somatic mutations and other cell-lineage differences can qualify a claim of exact sequence identity. A comparison should distinguish DNA presence, transcript form and protein abundance, since each measurement addresses a different step in expression.

Protein abundance depends on more than mRNA abundance. Translation makes new protein, while breakdown removes protein already present. A cell can therefore contain much mRNA but little stable protein if translation is slow or breakdown is fast. Measure those processes separately to test the alternatives. A transcript measurement alone cannot show which later step limits the protein amount.

Worked example

A simplified eukaryotic precursor RNA contains exon 1, intron 1 and exon 2. Describe the processed RNA without claiming that every exon base must encode an amino acid.

  1. Identify the intron region marked for removal in the stated model.
  2. Join the retained exon regions through splicing.
  3. Keep untranslated regions and other processing features conceptually distinct from the protein-coding portion.

The processed transcript retains the joined exon sequence, while the intron is removed in this example. Exons can include untranslated regions, so exon and protein-coding sequence are not identical terms.

Stop and check

Does removal of an intron mean that the corresponding DNA region was cut out of the chromosome during ordinary RNA splicing?

Compare your thinking

No. Splicing changes the RNA transcript. The chromosome's DNA sequence remains the template source.

Advanced LearningOne gene can contribute different transcripts6 minutes

One gene can contribute different transcripts

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced processing and expression. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Alternative splicing can combine retained regions in different ways, producing distinct RNA forms from the same gene region. This extends the simple one-transcript model without changing the base-pairing rules of transcription. A diagram should show which RNA regions are retained in each form and avoid implying that every possible combination is made in every cell. Expression depends on context and regulation.

Many eukaryotic pre-mRNAs receive a modified 5′ cap and a poly-A tail, a stretch of A nucleotides added at the other end. Along with splicing, these changes affect RNA handling, stability and translation. Termination ends transcription. Removed introns are not simply useless DNA, and one gene can contribute more than one regulated transcript form.

Draw each RNA form separately and identify retained regions before interpreting translation. The base-pairing rules of transcription remain the same even when processing differs. Exon membership does not prove that every retained base encodes an amino acid. Not every possible splice combination is produced in every cell.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

SplicingJoins retained exon regions after specified introns are removed.
Alternative formsCan retain different regulated combinations from one gene.

Limitation: Not every possible splice combination is produced in every cell.

Learn · Part 4

Checking a sequence claim

RNA abundance
The amount of a specified RNA present in a sample at a stated time; it is influenced by production and breakdown.
codon
A three-nucleotide mRNA sequence that specifies an amino acid or a translation start or stop signal.
reading frame
The grouping of an RNA coding sequence into consecutive three-nucleotide codons.

A correct sequence answer must identify the molecule, strand role, direction and reading assumption. Suppose a source explicitly gives coding DNA 5′-TAC ACA TGC ATC-3′. Its corresponding RNA is 5′-UAC ACA UGC AUC-3′ for that region. Do not reinterpret the stated coding strand as a template just because its first triplet resembles a familiar classroom example.

A reading frame groups RNA bases into threes, starting at a stated base. Each group is a codon. Starting at the first base here gives UAC | ACA | UGC | AUC. Using the genetic code table, these groups specify Tyr–Thr–Cys–Ile. The next lesson teaches how to use that table. This preview assumes translation begins at the stated first base. The fragment alone does not show where a cell starts translation. A missing label needs an explicit assumption, not a guess that the source was clear.

Sequence and abundance also answer different questions. A correct RNA sequence prediction does not show how much transcript a cell produces. Low RNA abundance can reflect altered production or stability, while low protein despite abundant RNA points to later steps as possibilities. Compare the methods and intermediate evidence. A strong molecular explanation follows the specific claim through direction, pairing, expression and the limits of the observation.

Worked example

A student transcribes 3′-TAC CTT-5′ as 5′-UAC CUU-3′. Locate the error and repair the sequence.

  1. Notice that the student replaced T with U while copying the template directly.
  2. Apply complementary pairing to the template instead.
  3. Read its stated 3′→5′ direction to obtain the new RNA 5′→3′.

The correct RNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′. Direct T-to-U substitution applies to a matching coding-strand sequence, not to this template.

Stop and check

Does abundant mRNA alone prove that a large amount of active protein is present?

Compare your thinking

No. Translation, processing, degradation and other controls affect the amount and activity of the protein product.

Advanced LearningSequence correctness and expression level are separate claims6 minutes

Sequence correctness and expression level are separate claims

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced checking a sequence claim. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A correctly transcribed sequence predicts the RNA bases in the stated model. It does not by itself predict how many transcripts are produced or how long they persist. An expression study needs measurements suited to those questions. Keep sequence checking, RNA abundance and protein activity as separate evidence categories so that a strong result in one category is not used to fill an unmeasured gap in another.

RNA abundance reflects production and degradation, the mixture of cells sampled and the observation time. Record tissue, condition, timing, comparison or reference measurements and uncertainty. A change in cell composition can alter a sample’s RNA signal without the same change occurring in every individual cell.

A correct template conversion cannot establish transcript production rate or stability. Abundance also depends on degradation, timing and the cell mixture sampled. Keep these measurements separate so a strong sequence result does not supply missing evidence for expression level or protein function. Direct T-to-U replacement applies to a matching coding strand, not the supplied template.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Sequence correctness and expression level are separate claims — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Sequence checkTests the predicted order of RNA bases.
Abundance measurementTests how much RNA is present in a defined sample.

Limitation: Direct T-to-U replacement applies to a matching coding strand, not the supplied template.

Lesson 16 · Chapter 18

Translation

What does a codon table predict, and what does it leave unknown?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Translate a supplied RNA frame, explain tRNA/ribosome roles and distinguish peptide sequence from functional evidence.

Before you begin

mRNA is read in a defined 5′→3′ frame. Codons are RNA triplets. Complementary anticodons are antiparallel, and a stop signal is not an amino acid.

Learn · Part 1

Reading the genetic code

start codon
A codon, usually AUG, that establishes the translation reading frame and specifies methionine.
stop codon
An mRNA codon that recruits a release factor and ends translation rather than specifying an amino acid.
tRNA
An adaptor RNA carrying a specific amino acid and an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon.
anticodon
A three-nucleotide sequence on tRNA that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.
folding
The process by which a polypeptide adopts a three-dimensional structure influenced by sequence and conditions.
missense
A coding-sequence change that substitutes one amino acid for another in a protein.

A codon is a three-base sequence in mRNA read within a specified frame. The standard genetic code relates codons to amino acids or a termination signal. Read the mRNA 5′→3′ and divide it into triplets from the stated start. A reading frame identifies which bases belong to each triplet; shifting that grouping changes the codons even when the underlying letters are unchanged.

AUG commonly serves as the start codon and codes for methionine in the standard table used here. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. They signal termination rather than adding an amino acid called stop. Several different codons can specify the same amino acid, so some base substitutions leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged. The code table must be read using RNA bases, including U rather than T.

For mRNA 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′ in the indicated frame, translation produces Met–Glu–Phe followed by termination. Do not continue into later triplets after that stop when reading this open reading frame. A short sequence fragment without an initiation context requires a stated frame assumption. The presence of the letters AUG somewhere in a fragment does not by itself establish that a cell initiates translation there.

Worked example

Translate the supplied complete coding-region model RNA 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′ from its stated start codon.

  1. Read mRNA codons in the 5′→3′ direction using the RNA codon table.
  2. Map AUG to methionine, GAA to glutamate and UUU to phenylalanine.
  3. Treat UAA as a termination signal rather than an amino acid.

The peptide sequence is Met–Glu–Phe, followed by termination at UAA in this model.

Stop and check

Should a DNA template triplet be entered directly into an mRNA codon table?

Compare your thinking

No. First determine the correctly oriented mRNA codon. The table's input is RNA, not the DNA template or a tRNA anticodon.

Advanced LearningRedundancy is not ambiguity6 minutes

Redundancy is not ambiguity

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced reading the genetic code. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Several codons can specify the same amino acid, but a given codon has a defined interpretation within the standard code used here. That redundancy helps explain why some substitutions leave a peptide unchanged. The code table does not reveal all later processing or the final protein's function. Keep the translation result separate from those additional biological questions.

Use the specified reading frame to group the message before consulting the code. Redundancy explains how a substitution may preserve a peptide, not why a single codon could be assigned any amino acid. Later processing and activity remain separate questions.

In the related worked example: The peptide sequence is Met–Glu–Phe, followed by termination at UAA in this model. A code-table result does not establish the final protein's function.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 2

Adaptors and peptide bonds

peptide bond
The covalent bond linking amino acids in a polypeptide.
elongation
The stage in which a growing RNA or polypeptide chain is extended.
release factor
A protein that helps terminate translation at a stop codon and release the polypeptide.

Transfer RNA, or tRNA, acts as an adaptor between an mRNA codon and an amino acid. A tRNA carries an anticodon that can pair with a corresponding codon and is attached to a suitable amino acid by cellular enzymes. The mRNA supplies the codon being read; the tRNA supplies the anticodon. These names identify different molecules and should not be exchanged in a diagram.

Pairing is antiparallel. The codon 5′-GAA-3′ can align with an anticodon written 3′-CUU-5′, or equivalently 5′-UUC-3′ when written in the opposite display direction. This pairing supports delivery of glutamate in the standard code. Direction labels explain why two differently written anticodon strings can represent the same oriented sequence.

The ribosome organizes the message and tRNAs and supports peptide-bond formation. A peptide bond links amino acids into a growing polypeptide chain. Ribosomal RNA, or rRNA, has structural and catalytic roles within the ribosome. mRNA, tRNA and rRNA therefore contribute distinct functions to one process. Pairing alone does not make the whole protein; correct amino-acid loading, ribosome activity and ordered movement are also required.

Worked example

For mRNA codon 5′-GAA-3′, write an aligned anticodon and identify the role of the charged tRNA.

  1. Pair the anticodon antiparallel to the codon: 3′-CUU-5′.
  2. Recognize that a correctly charged tRNA carries the corresponding amino acid, glutamate in the standard code.
  3. Connect codon recognition with peptide-bond formation at the ribosome.

The aligned anticodon is 3′-CUU-5′, or 5′-UUC-3′ when written in its own 5′→3′ direction. The adaptor links RNA recognition with delivery of an amino acid.

Stop and check

Does the anticodon itself become part of the growing peptide?

Compare your thinking

No. The tRNA is an RNA adaptor. Its carried amino acid contributes to the peptide, while the tRNA can be reused after release and charging.

Advanced LearningCharging accuracy is another checkpoint6 minutes

Charging accuracy is another checkpoint

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced adaptors and peptide bonds. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Correct codon–anticodon pairing does not by itself demonstrate that a tRNA carries the correct amino acid. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach amino acids to suitable tRNAs, providing another important specificity step. A simplified model can separate charging from codon recognition to show why both matter. The mRNA sequence supplies instructions, but the cellular machinery must implement them accurately.

The ribosome’s A site accepts an incoming charged tRNA during elongation. The P site holds the tRNA bearing the chain before transfer, and the E site is an exit position. Movement shifts these relationships as the message advances one codon. These site names describe molecular positions; recognition and catalysis do not require conscious choices by the ribosome.

Consider charging and pairing as distinct specificity steps. Correct base recognition alone cannot show what amino acid is attached to the adaptor. Keeping both visible explains why a correct message still depends on cellular machinery to implement it accurately. Codon–anticodon pairing alone does not verify the attached amino acid.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Charging accuracy is another checkpoint — comparison

Limitation: Codon–anticodon pairing alone does not verify the attached amino acid.

Learn · Part 3

Initiation to termination

Initiation establishes the translation machinery at a suitable start region and fixes the reading frame. The mRNA, ribosomal subunits and an initiating tRNA assemble in a coordinated way. Once the start frame is established, the ribosome progresses through successive codons. The same message can be used repeatedly, allowing more than one polypeptide molecule to be produced from its information.

During elongation, a suitable charged tRNA enters, its anticodon pairs with the next codon and the growing chain is transferred through peptide-bond formation. The ribosome moves along the mRNA so that the next codon can be read. The sequence of codons therefore helps determine the order of amino acids rather than merely the overall number of each amino-acid type.

When a stop codon enters the decoding region, a release factor supports termination and release of the chain. There is no ordinary amino-acid-carrying tRNA that adds a stop amino acid at that point. The completed chain can then fold and undergo further processing. Sequence prediction describes the immediate chain under the stated code and frame; it does not by itself prove that a mature functional protein accumulates in a cell.

Worked example

Sequence initiation, elongation and termination for a model transcript with an AUG start and a later UGA in the same reading frame.

  1. Establish the translation machinery and reading frame at the supplied start region.
  2. Add amino acids as successive codons are read during elongation.
  3. Use the in-frame stop codon to recruit termination machinery and release the peptide.

Translation proceeds through a defined frame until a stop signal is reached. UGA does not require a normal tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid.”

Stop and check

Would a UGA sequence outside the current reading frame necessarily terminate this translation?

Compare your thinking

No. The codons actually read are defined by the established frame. The same letters grouped differently form different codons.

Advanced LearningFinding AUG is not the entire initiation mechanism6 minutes

Finding AUG is not the entire initiation mechanism

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced initiation to termination. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A short teaching sequence often marks its start codon explicitly. Real initiation also depends on surrounding signals and cellular machinery, so scanning any arbitrary DNA or RNA fragment for its first AUG is not a complete prediction. In an exercise, state whether the sequence is a full coding region or a fragment with a specified frame. That boundary prevents invented start sites and overconfident peptide predictions.

A premature stop can shorten the predicted chain, but RNA surveillance may instead reduce the abundance of that message. Test whether a transcript and product actually accumulate before inferring a particular cellular result from the shortened sequence prediction.

Do not declare the first AUG in an arbitrary fragment to be a complete initiation prediction. A marked frame supports a bounded peptide interpretation; an unprovided start context remains uncertain. A premature stop may also alter message abundance rather than simply yield a stable short product. A stop codon is a termination signal, not a codon for a normal stop amino acid.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Finding AUG is not the entire initiation mechanism — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Specified classroom startDefines the frame of the supplied coding-region model.
Real initiationAlso requires surrounding signals and appropriate machinery.

Models and Data Lab: Compare coding changes and peptide predictions

Learn · Part 4

From sequence to function

deletion
Loss of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.
sequence comparison
An analysis of appropriately aligned nucleotide sequences to identify similarities and differences.

A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Its sequence influences how it folds and interacts with other molecules. Amino acids differ in properties such as charge, size and interactions with water. A change at one position can therefore have a different effect from the same type of change at another position, depending on the protein's structure and role.

Folding produces a three-dimensional arrangement that helps determine function. Some proteins also require processing, partner molecules or assembly with other chains. A correct coding sequence is one part of the pathway. Transcription, RNA handling, translation, folding and stability all influence how much functional product is available. Low protein abundance does not uniquely establish a DNA deletion or a transcription defect.

A missense change replaces one encoded amino acid with another. Its effect may be small, substantial or undetected under the conditions measured. Compare sequence evidence with protein amount, activity and cellular response before inferring a phenotype. The most useful explanation identifies the immediate predicted change and the next experiment needed to test its consequence, rather than treating any amino-acid difference as automatically harmful.

Worked example

Translate 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′, then evaluate the claim that the sequence alone proves a functional enzyme.

  1. Use the standard code to obtain Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop.
  2. Distinguish this short classroom peptide model from a complete functional protein.
  3. Identify additional evidence about folding, processing, localization and activity that would address function.

The sequence supports the stated translation result. It does not establish enzyme activity or the complete behaviour of a protein in a cell.

Stop and check

Would two identical short peptide segments prove that the full proteins are identical?

Compare your thinking

No. Unprovided regions and processing may differ. A short match establishes only the compared segment.

Advanced LearningFunction requires an appropriate assay6 minutes

Function requires an appropriate assay

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced from sequence to function. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A sequence comparison can suggest a hypothesis about function, but an activity claim requires evidence suited to the proposed function. A binding measurement, localization image or catalytic assay answers a different question from base sequencing. Combining these approaches can strengthen an explanation. The claim should remain tied to what each method actually measured rather than treating the central-dogma sequence as a guarantee of every later outcome.

A chain may be cleaved, chemically modified, combined with other subunits or moved to a particular cell compartment. Chaperone proteins help other proteins fold under suitable conditions. Amount, location, timing and interactions all matter to function. Compare a sequence prediction with measurements that test the proposed later step.

Select the assay that corresponds to the claimed function. Folding, modification, localization and interactions can intervene after translation. Combining a sequence with an appropriate activity measurement strengthens the explanation while keeping the contribution of each method explicit. The predicted Met–Glu–Phe sequence does not prove enzyme activity.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Function requires an appropriate assay — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Sequence predictionIdentifies the peptide in the stated translation model.
Functional assayTests binding, catalysis, location or another proposed activity.

Limitation: The predicted Met–Glu–Phe sequence does not prove enzyme activity.

Illustrated walkthrough

1. Reading the genetic code

Translate the supplied complete coding-region model RNA 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′ from its stated start codon.

  1. Read mRNA codons in the 5′→3′ direction using the RNA codon table.
  2. Map AUG to methionine, GAA to glutamate and UUU to phenylalanine.
  3. Treat UAA as a termination signal rather than an amino acid.

The peptide sequence is Met–Glu–Phe, followed by termination at UAA in this model.

2. Adaptors and peptide bonds

For mRNA codon 5′-GAA-3′, write an aligned anticodon and identify the role of the charged tRNA.

  1. Pair the anticodon antiparallel to the codon: 3′-CUU-5′.
  2. Recognize that a correctly charged tRNA carries the corresponding amino acid, glutamate in the standard code.
  3. Connect codon recognition with peptide-bond formation at the ribosome.

The aligned anticodon is 3′-CUU-5′, or 5′-UUC-3′ when written in its own 5′→3′ direction. The adaptor links RNA recognition with delivery of an amino acid.

3. Initiation to termination

Sequence initiation, elongation and termination for a model transcript with an AUG start and a later UGA in the same reading frame.

  1. Establish the translation machinery and reading frame at the supplied start region.
  2. Add amino acids as successive codons are read during elongation.
  3. Use the in-frame stop codon to recruit termination machinery and release the peptide.

Translation proceeds through a defined frame until a stop signal is reached. UGA does not require a normal tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid.”

4. From sequence to function

Translate 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′, then evaluate the claim that the sequence alone proves a functional enzyme.

  1. Use the standard code to obtain Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop.
  2. Distinguish this short classroom peptide model from a complete functional protein.
  3. Identify additional evidence about folding, processing, localization and activity that would address function.

The sequence supports the stated translation result. It does not establish enzyme activity or the complete behaviour of a protein in a cell.

Lesson 17 · Chapter 18

Mutations

Why can different sequence changes have very different consequences?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Trace substitution and insertion examples through expression while separating origin, transmission and selection.

Before you begin

DNA sequence, RNA sequence and peptide sequence are linked but distinct. Coding context and frame determine triplet interpretation. Somatic and germline lineages have different inheritance routes.

In the textbook

Chapter 18 · 644 #18–19; 651 #1,2,6

Open at p. 644

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

substitution
Replacement of one nucleotide or chromosome segment with another.
insertion
Addition of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.
frameshift
A reading-frame change caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in a multiple of three within a coding region.
germ-line mutation
A mutation in a gamete-producing lineage that can be transmitted to offspring.

Learn · Part 1

Types of sequence change

insertion
Addition of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.
frameshift
A reading-frame change caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in a multiple of three within a coding region.
nonsense
A coding-sequence change that converts an amino-acid codon into a stop codon.

A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. An insertion adds nucleotide sequence, while a deletion removes sequence. The effect depends on where the change occurs and which biological process uses that region. A change within a protein-coding region must be interpreted relative to a stated reading frame. Changes in regulatory or RNA-processing regions require a different kind of prediction.

An insertion or deletion whose length is not a multiple of three can shift the downstream reading frame within a coding region. This frameshift changes how later bases are grouped into codons and may alter later amino acids or stop placement. A three-base insertion preserves the downstream frame, although it can add amino-acid information and affect a codon at the insertion boundary.

Write the original and changed sequence with aligned positions before translating. For coding DNA ATGGAATTTTAA, a single added A after ATG gives ATGAGAATTTTAA. In the first-base frame, the later triplets differ from the reference. This prediction assumes the segment lies in a translated region with the stated frame. A one-base change outside that region is not automatically a protein frameshift.

Worked example

Compare coding DNA reference ATGGAATTTTAA with substitution ATGGAGTTTTAA and insertion ATGAGAATTTTAA in the stated frame beginning at the first base.

  1. The substitution changes one base without changing the total length.
  2. The insertion adds one base after ATG, changing later triplet grouping.
  3. Separate the type of sequence change from its effect on the translated product.

The substitution preserves the reading frame; the one-base insertion shifts downstream grouping in this coding-region model. Neither label alone determines every functional effect.

Stop and check

Does every insertion shift the downstream reading frame?

Compare your thinking

No. An insertion of a multiple of three bases within a coding region preserves downstream grouping, though it can still change the peptide and function.

Advanced LearningLocation changes the prediction6 minutes

Location changes the prediction

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced types of sequence change. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The same number of altered bases can have different consequences in a coding region, a splice-related region or a regulatory region. A classroom frameshift claim therefore needs a defined coding frame and position. Do not apply it automatically to every DNA insertion. Identify the affected sequence context first, then trace the mechanism supported by that context.

Changes also occur at larger scales. Duplication repeats a region; inversion reverses a segment; translocation moves material between chromosome locations. Copy-number changes alter how many copies of a region are present, while chromosome-number changes affect whole chromosomes. Copying, damage, repair or movement of mobile DNA elements can produce changes. Naming their scale does not establish their effect.

Locate the alteration before assigning its consequence. A one-base insertion in a supplied coding frame supports a frameshift prediction, but the same label cannot be applied to every DNA insertion. Scale and position identify the question; they do not settle every functional effect. An alteration's name or size alone does not determine its biological outcome.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Location changes the prediction — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
One-base coding insertionShifts downstream grouping in a defined reading frame.
Regulatory or splice-context changeRequires a mechanism appropriate to that location.

Limitation: An alteration's name or size alone does not determine its biological outcome.

Models and Data Lab: Compare coding changes and peptide predictions

Learn · Part 2

Effects on gene products

silent
A coding substitution that leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the specified frame; other effects are still possible.
regulatory mutation
A DNA change that affects when, where or how much a gene is expressed.
mutagen
An agent that can increase the chance of changes to genetic material.
dose
The amount of an agent delivered or received, with its units and exposure conditions stated.

A synonymous, or silent, substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the stated frame. For example, RNA GAA and GAG both specify glutamate in the standard code. A missense substitution changes the amino acid, while a nonsense substitution creates a premature stop codon. These terms describe immediate coding consequences; they do not independently establish an organism's full phenotype.

A regulatory mutation can change when, where or how strongly a gene is expressed without changing its encoded amino-acid sequence. A change at a splice boundary can alter the mature transcript. Even a synonymous substitution may have RNA-related effects in some contexts. Therefore, no amino-acid change means no change to that predicted sequence, rather than proof of no possible biological effect anywhere.

Effects can be harmful, neutral or beneficial under specific conditions. Compare the changed sequence with RNA, protein and functional evidence. If the measurements show no difference under tested conditions, report no detected effect in that assay. If a shortened product is predicted, test whether it is produced and functional. The strength of the conclusion depends on the level of evidence, not simply on the mutation category.

Worked example

Compare translation of the reference coding DNA ATGGAATTTTAA and the substitution ATGGAGTTTTAA in the supplied standard-code model.

  1. Convert coding DNA to matching RNA with T replaced by U.
  2. Read reference AUG GAA UUU UAA and variant AUG GAG UUU UAA in the same frame.
  3. Use the code table to note that GAA and GAG both specify glutamate.

Both produce Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop in this model. The substitution is synonymous for this peptide sequence, which does not prove that every possible regulatory or expression effect is absent.

Does synonymous mean that the DNA sequence did not change?

Compare your thinking

No. The DNA changed, but the codon substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged under the stated code and frame.

Advanced LearningAn unchanged peptide narrows one claim6 minutes

An unchanged peptide narrows one claim

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced effects on gene products. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

If translation is unchanged, a claim that this substitution changes the amino acid at that position is unsupported. Other possible effects require different evidence and should not be invented simply to make the variant seem harmful. Distinguish an established peptide result from hypotheses about RNA processing, stability or expression. A precise explanation can say what stayed the same while leaving untested effects unknown.

Use the unchanged peptide to reject the specific claim that this substitution changes that amino acid. Do not invent an unmeasured harmful effect to replace the rejected claim. Processing or abundance effects can remain testable possibilities without being reported as established facts.

In the related worked example: Both produce Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop in this model. The substitution is synonymous for this peptide sequence, which does not prove that every possible regulatory or expression effect is absent. Synonymous for this peptide does not prove every possible expression effect is absent.

Learn · Part 3

Inheritance and variation

germ-line mutation
A mutation in a gamete-producing lineage that can be transmitted to offspring.
random origin
The idea that a mutation does not arise because the organism anticipates a useful outcome.
selection
Change in representation associated with differences in survival or reproductive success under stated conditions.

A somatic mutation occurs in a body-cell lineage. As that cell divides, daughter cells may receive the change. A mutation confined to body tissue usually does not pass to offspring through gametes. A germ-line mutation occurs in cells that contribute to gametes, so it may pass to offspring. Before predicting inheritance, identify the cell lineage where the change occurred.

Mutation can create a new allele sequence. Recombination usually puts existing sequence variants into new combinations during meiosis. Errors in chromosome processes can also create changes, but rearranging existing alleles is not the same as making a new allele at every locus. Compare the sequence itself with the combination inherited from the parents. They describe different sources of variation.

Mutations do not arise because an organism knows it will need a trait. Their origin is not directed toward a future benefit. Later, selection can change how common an inherited variant becomes. This can happen when the variant affects reproductive success in that environment. Separate the two questions: how did a variant arise, and why did its frequency change? Unit D uses counts, inheritance and environmental evidence to study the second question.

Worked example

A fictional sequence change occurs in one skin-cell lineage, while a separate change occurs in a cell lineage contributing to gametes. Compare their potential inheritance.

  1. Track the skin-cell change through its descendant somatic cells.
  2. Track the gamete-lineage change into possible reproductive cells.
  3. Distinguish the origin of a variant from later selection on carriers and from whether a particular gamete participates in fertilization.

A somatic change is generally confined to that lineage and is not normally inherited through gametes. A germline change can be transmitted if it enters a gamete that contributes to offspring.

Stop and check

Do organisms create a specific helpful mutation because their environment requires it?

Compare your thinking

No. Mutation supplies variants without anticipating need. Selection can later change their representation through differences in survival and reproduction.

Advanced LearningTransmission is a chain of events6 minutes

Transmission is a chain of events

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced inheritance and variation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Calling a change germline identifies a route by which inheritance is possible, not a guarantee that every offspring receives it. The changed lineage must contribute to a gamete, that gamete must participate in fertilization, and subsequent development must proceed. Trace these steps when comparing possible and observed inheritance. This keeps origin, transmission and later population change as distinct questions.

Mosaicism means different cell populations within an organism have different genetic material. Developmental timing, sampled tissue and the fraction of cells carrying a variant help test its lineage. A blood sample may not represent every tissue. Distinguish a new change, its spread through cell descendants and its possible transmission through gametes.

Follow the change through lineage, gamete contribution and fertilization rather than equating germline with guaranteed transmission. Sampling one tissue addresses that lineage, not every cell in the organism. Origin, within-body spread and inherited population change are distinct events. Potential inheritance is not proof that every offspring receives the change.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Transmission is a chain of events — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Somatic lineage changeCan spread through descendants of that body-cell lineage.
Gamete-lineage changeHas a possible route into offspring if a contributing gamete carries it.

Limitation: Potential inheritance is not proof that every offspring receives the change.

Related worked example: Worked example: Inheritance and variation

Learn · Part 4

Evaluating mutation evidence

A mutagen is an agent that can increase the frequency of genetic changes under specified conditions. Dose, exposure route, duration, biological system and the measured endpoint all affect explanation. A controlled comparison should include a reference condition and use the same detection method. An association between exposure and a change does not by itself identify the exact molecular mechanism.

Consider a variant found repeatedly in tumour samples. Recurrence alone can suggest a research question, but functional evidence strengthens a proposed role. If the variant changes a growth pathway in cells and reducing that activity changes growth in matched models, the observations converge on a possible mechanism. The result still has a scope: tumour context, other variants and model limitations matter.

Communicate evidence in layers: sequence change, RNA or protein effect, cell behaviour and broader outcome. Name uncertainty at each transition. A mutation presentation should include sources and types, specific sequence examples, effects, inheritance routes and a misconception correction. Use fictional sequences and supplied data for the classroom task. Neither an exposure model nor a tumour example provides a diagnosis or treatment decision for an individual.

Worked example

Translate the insertion sequence's coding-region excerpt ATGAGAATTTTAA in the stated frame and compare it with the reference ATGGAATTTTAA.

  1. The insertion RNA is AUGAGAAUUUUAA.
  2. Group complete codons from the first base: AUG AGA AUU UUA, with one trailing A.
  3. Translate Met–Arg–Ile–Leu and report that no stop codon is supplied in this short shifted frame.

The insertion changes the peptide segment and leaves an incomplete trailing codon. Do not invent a downstream stop or claim this excerpt defines the full variant protein.

Stop and check

Can the short DNA excerpt's 12 or 13 bases be treated as the entire 1000- or 1001-base fragment in the separate gel model?

Compare your thinking

No. The excerpt and the larger fragment model operate at different scales. Their relationship must be stated without equating their lengths.

Advanced LearningEvidence at two scales6 minutes

Evidence at two scales

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced evaluating mutation evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A sequence excerpt makes the coding consequence readable, while a larger-fragment model illustrates cutting or separation. Keeping both scales explicit avoids a false numerical contradiction. A one-base length difference may also be unresolved in a particular gel method, so the displayed fragment diagram must state its idealized resolution. Use sequence evidence for the base change and a suitable assay for any claimed size distinction.

Cancer-related changes can affect growth, repair, cell death, genome stability, immune interactions, resource use and invasion. Inherited susceptibility and acquired changes have different routes. Compare a tumour variant with matched tissue and functional evidence before assigning a driver role. Its sequence alone is not a complete cause or prognosis. Plan sampling, repeat measurements, classification and recording rules before examining results. Positive controls test detection of a known result; negative controls reveal background; randomized order or masked scoring can reduce some biases. Use supplied observations and safe fictional models, not personal biological material.

A report should connect question, method, evidence, reasoning, safety and conclusion. Identify analyses planned beforehand and questions explored after seeing results. State what would strengthen, weaken or change the explanation. Peer feedback should improve traceability. Permission to share a method is not permission to share identifiable genetic information.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Evidence at two scales — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Coding excerptSupports base grouping and a bounded peptide-segment prediction.
Larger fragment assayTests size at the method's actual resolution.

Limitation: Do not invent a downstream stop or a resolvable gel difference from an incomplete excerpt.

30 optional minutes

Learning goal

Explain cutting, joining, transformation, PCR and separation with controls, then evaluate bounded relatedness and application claims.

Before you begin

Methods measure particular features at particular resolutions. Compatible sequence ends, sample identity and assay function are separate conditions. A match or missing signal needs context.

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

restriction enzyme
An enzyme that recognizes a particular DNA sequence and cuts the phosphodiester backbone at or near that site.
plasmid
A usually circular DNA molecule that replicates separately from a cell's main chromosome and can serve as a biotechnology vector.
PCR
Polymerase chain reaction; a laboratory method that uses primers and repeated temperature cycles to amplify a selected DNA region.
gel electrophoresis
A method that separates charged molecules through a gel, commonly resolving DNA fragments mainly by length.

Learn · Part 1

Cutting and joining DNA

restriction enzyme
An enzyme that recognizes a particular DNA sequence and cuts the phosphodiester backbone at or near that site.
recognition site
A specific DNA sequence bound and cut by a particular restriction endonuclease.
sticky end
A single-stranded DNA overhang produced by staggered cutting and capable of complementary base pairing.
insert
The DNA segment placed into a vector or other specified DNA construct.

Restriction enzymes recognize specific DNA sequences and cut the backbone at characteristic positions. A recognition site is the sequence pattern associated with an enzyme's action. Some cuts produce short single-stranded overhangs, called sticky ends, while others produce blunt ends. The resulting fragments depend on where the recognition sites occur in the original DNA, so the source sequence constrains the products.

Compatible sticky ends can pair through complementary bases, bringing fragments into an arrangement suitable for joining. DNA ligase then seals suitable breaks in the sugar–phosphate backbone. Pairing and joining are different steps: base interactions align the ends, while ligase forms a covalent connection. Ligase does not invent the required base sequence or make every unrelated end immediately compatible.

For a recombinant-DNA plan, specify the DNA source, recognition sites, intended insert and receiving molecule. Predict the fragments before describing a successful construct. Cutting with a familiar enzyme name is not proof that the intended gene was isolated. A later sequence or fragment check is needed to confirm the product. The most useful diagram shows the original, the cut ends and the verified joined arrangement.

Worked example

A fictional linear 1000-base DNA fragment has one defined cut producing 400- and 600-base products. Predict the count and total length, then contrast a one-cut circular molecule.

  1. For the linear molecule, one internal cut creates two pieces.
  2. Check conservation: 400 + 600 = 1000 bases.
  3. For a circular molecule, one cut opens the circle into one linear piece rather than creating two separate pieces.

The linear case gives two fragments totalling 1000 bases. The one-cut circular case gives one linear molecule of the original total length.

Stop and check

Does using the same sticky-ended cut guarantee that any two fragments will join in the desired orientation and produce a working gene?

Compare your thinking

No. Compatible ends permit joining, but orientation, sequence context and later expression still require checks.

Advanced LearningCounting sites needs molecular shape6 minutes

Counting sites needs molecular shape

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced cutting and joining dna. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

The relation between cut sites and fragment number differs for linear and circular DNA. A diagram should show the molecule's shape before a learner counts products. Multiple molecules, repeated sites and incomplete cutting add further possibilities. Begin with the stated idealized complete-cut model, then label any extension that relaxes those assumptions so unexpected bands are not assigned a single cause prematurely.

Draw the molecule's shape before counting products, then check conservation of total length. The same number of cut sites has different consequences when a molecule starts with free ends or forms a circle. Incomplete cutting and mixed molecules would require an expanded model.

In the related worked example: The linear case gives two fragments totalling 1000 bases. The one-cut circular case gives one linear molecule of the original total length. The count assumes one molecule and the specified complete cuts.

Learn · Part 2

Transforming cells

vector
A DNA molecule used to carry and replicate or express inserted genetic material in a host cell.
plasmid
A usually circular DNA molecule that replicates separately from a cell's main chromosome and can serve as a biotechnology vector.
PCR
Polymerase chain reaction; a laboratory method that uses primers and repeated temperature cycles to amplify a selected DNA region.

A vector is a DNA vehicle used to carry selected genetic material into a cell or maintain it there. A plasmid is a DNA molecule that can replicate separately from the main chromosome in a suitable host. A recombinant plasmid may contain an insert, a selectable feature and sequences needed for its intended expression. Each element serves a different purpose in the experimental design.

Transformation is uptake of external genetic material by a cell in the context used here. Uptake does not guarantee that every cell receives the intended construct or expresses the inserted gene. Selection identifies cells with a feature linked to survival or detection under specified conditions. A surviving colony can contain a vector without the desired insert, so selection must be followed by suitable verification.

Check insert presence, orientation, sequence and expression separately. A failed insert-specific PCR result is consistent with an absent insert but can also reflect a failed assay; controls are needed. A plasmid's presence does not mean it necessarily integrated into the host chromosome. Some constructs remain separate, while stable integration requires its own mechanism and evidence. Trace each claim from uptake through persistence and expression before concluding that a cell's function changed as intended.

Worked example

A fictional recombinant-DNA workflow joins an insert to a vector, introduces the material into cells and selects surviving colonies. Does survival alone prove the intended insert is correct and expressed?

  1. Separate joining, cellular uptake and selection as different steps.
  2. Identify exactly what the selection marker tests in the supplied model.
  3. Use additional checks for insert presence, orientation, sequence and expression as needed for the claim.

Selection can identify cells with a relevant marker, but it does not by itself prove a correct functional insert. Appropriate positive, negative and identity checks remain necessary.

Stop and check

Why include a vector-only comparison when assessing a claimed insert-dependent result?

Compare your thinking

It helps distinguish effects associated with the vector or selection procedure from effects requiring the insert.

Advanced LearningControls test competing explanations6 minutes

Controls test competing explanations

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced transforming cells. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A positive control shows that a procedure can produce the expected signal under known conditions. A negative control helps reveal contamination or background. A vector-only control addresses another specific alternative. These controls are not interchangeable decorations. Match each one to a possible explanation for the observed result and state which uncertainty remains after it is considered.

An expression vector can include an origin that permits replication, a marker for selection, a cloning site and regulatory sequences around an insert. Insert orientation and reading frame matter to expression. A reporter produces a detectable signal; a selectable marker permits detection or survival under a condition. Neither proves that the full insert sequence and product are correct.

Match each control to the alternative it can address. Surviving colonies can support a marker claim while leaving insert identity, orientation and expression unresolved. A correct-looking signal therefore needs the appropriate identity and functional checks rather than decorative control labels. Selection alone does not prove that the intended insert is correct and expressed.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Controls test competing explanations — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation

Negative or vector-only controlTests a particular background or alternative explanation.

Limitation: Selection alone does not prove that the intended insert is correct and expressed.

Learn · Part 3

Amplifying and separating

gel electrophoresis
A method that separates charged molecules through a gel, commonly resolving DNA fragments mainly by length.
fragment size
The length of a DNA fragment, commonly measured in base pairs.
ladder
A set of DNA fragments of known sizes used as a gel reference.

PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction. It makes many copies of a selected DNA region. Follow one temperature cycle: the strands separate, primers bind to matching sites, and a heat-tolerant polymerase extends them. Repeat the cycle to make more copies. The primer positions help define the target region. Detecting a signal depends both on that target being present and on the method working under the chosen conditions.

Gel electrophoresis uses an electric field to separate DNA or RNA fragments. In the standard DNA comparison here, smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel. A ladder of known fragment sizes helps estimate the sample's sizes. A band contains many molecules that moved about the same distance. It gives size evidence, but it does not reveal every base in those molecules.

Compare the controls before interpreting a sample. A negative control checks for contamination or copying where none is expected. A known positive control checks that the method can produce the expected signal. A band in the negative control makes sample bands harder to trust. Also check the gel's resolution. An ordinary gel may not clearly separate fragments just one base apart. Report what the bands show before claiming a sequence change or identity.

Worked example

A fictional PCR lane shows no target band. Compare “the target is absent” with “the assay failed,” then identify needed controls.

  1. Recognize that no visible band can result from either missing target or failure of amplification/detection.
  2. Check a positive control for assay function and a negative control for contamination.
  3. Consider sample-specific quality or an appropriate internal control before concluding absence.

The negative lane is consistent with absence or assay failure until controls narrow the alternatives. In a gel, interpret migration against the stated size standard and method resolution.

Stop and check

Does a smaller DNA fragment normally travel less far than a larger one in the standard classroom gel model?

Compare your thinking

No. Smaller fragments generally travel farther through the gel under the stated conditions. Direction and ladder labels must be shown.

Advanced LearningResolution limits a size claim6 minutes

Resolution limits a size claim

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced amplifying and separating. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Two fragments close in length may be indistinguishable in one separation method. A schematic drawing with visibly separate 1000- and 1001-base bands can therefore overstate the assay's resolution unless explicitly presented as an idealized model. Report what the method can resolve and choose another measurement if the question requires a finer distinction. A clear picture is not itself evidence that the laboratory method could make that separation.

Sequencing identifies nucleotide order rather than only fragment size. Short tandem repeats, or STRs, are repeated DNA patterns used at selected markers. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs, are single-position variants. Mitochondrial and Y-chromosome markers track particular inheritance routes. Sample quality, target choice, reference data and method error limit every comparison.

Ask whether the method could resolve the difference before interpreting a schematic gap between bands. A positive detection control helps test failure as an alternative to absence, while sequencing answers a finer base-order question. The most visually clear diagram is not automatically the strongest measurement. A drawing of separate 1000- and 1001-base bands is not evidence of real assay resolution.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Case or measureBiological interpretation

Size comparisonDepends on a standard and the separation method's resolution.

Limitation: A drawing of separate 1000- and 1001-base bands is not evidence of real assay resolution.

Learn · Part 4

Genetic evidence and relatedness

chloroplast DNA
DNA contained in chloroplasts, useful alongside other sequences when comparing related organisms.

DNA can help test relatedness when matching regions are compared. Alignment places corresponding positions together. Greater similarity may support a closer relationship under the chosen model. The result also depends on the region, its rate of change and the sample. A short sequence match is not proof that two whole genomes are identical or that only one relationship is possible.

Nuclear DNA usually includes contributions from both parents in a sexual cross. Human mitochondrial DNA is passed mainly through the maternal line. Chloroplast DNA comes from a plant organelle; its inheritance varies by species and is often from one parent. These sources can record different histories. State which was sampled instead of treating all DNA as one interchangeable measure.

The supplied investigation gives both a short coding segment and separate measurements of larger fragments. Reference and substitution models have lengths 400+600 bases; the insertion model has 401+600. An ordinary gel may not resolve that one-base change. Use oriented sequences to identify the precise change. Do not derive the full fragment lengths from the short excerpt or treat a size match as complete sequence identity.

For a source comparison, matching one DNA marker can leave many possible sources. Comparing additional informative, independent markers can improve discrimination. Check the method with suitable controls and consider related samples that may share alleles. More markers do not turn one band into a whole-genome match; the strength of the inference depends on the combined evidence and its quality.

Worked example

Three fictional sequences of the same region differ from a reference at one, three and six aligned positions. What relationship claim can this comparison support?

  1. Confirm that the same homologous region and alignment are being compared.
  2. Count differences using one stated rule and equal sequence coverage.
  3. Treat fewer differences as evidence of closer similarity for this region, while retaining sampling and evolutionary-model limits.

The one-difference sequence is most similar to the reference in the compared region. This alone does not establish a complete family relationship or the history of the whole genome.

Stop and check

Do mitochondrial or chloroplast sequences represent every independently inherited nuclear region?

Compare your thinking

No. Organelle inheritance can follow different patterns and represents particular lineages. Broader relationship claims need appropriately sampled evidence.

Advanced LearningA gene history can differ from a whole-organism history6 minutes

A gene history can differ from a whole-organism history

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced genetic evidence and relatedness. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A short region supplies one historical signal. Different inheritance paths, sampling and evolutionary processes can make that signal incomplete for a broader relationship question. Compare several suitable regions and explain the model used to interpret differences. This does not make sequence comparison uninformative; it prevents one convenient marker from being treated as the entire ancestry record.

For identity or relationship questions, compare the evidence under explicitly different source hypotheses and a suitable reference population. Close relatives, identical twins, mixtures, mutation and incomplete measurements can change the comparison. A profile match is not automatically a unique identity or a whole-genome match. An ancestry estimate depends on reference samples and does not establish culture, nation or personal identity.

Keep the aligned region and reference population visible in the conclusion. Different markers can track different inheritance routes, and close relatives or mixtures can change interpretation. A match or short similarity ranking is informative without becoming a unique whole-genome history. Sequence similarity does not establish guilt, culture, nation or personal identity.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

A gene history can differ from a whole-organism history — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
One compared regionSupports a local sequence-similarity statement.
Whole ancestry or identity claimRequires broader evidence, suitable hypotheses and reference data.

Limitation: Sequence similarity does not establish guilt, culture, nation or personal identity.
